parts.answer: Result: after an eight-week mindfulness programme, brain scans showed increased grey matter in areas such as the hippocampus, which is linked to learning and memory. Caution: the study used an eight-week course, not a single ten-minute exercise, so it cannot show that a short exercise has the same effect.
parts.working: 1 mark: result described (grey-matter change after an 8-week course); 1 mark: brain area named and linked to learning or memory; 1 mark: caution based on the length of the course or the difference in intervention; 1 mark: developed link to the university's claim.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hospital in Quetta plans to move its nurses to night shifts only, to cover staff shortages. Explain two ways that research into sleep stages (for example Dement and Kleitman) could help the hospital plan the rota fairly and safely.
parts.answer: Any two developed points, e.g.: sleep research shows that sleep occurs in cycles that include REM sleep, so disrupted daytime sleep may reduce the quality of rest; nurses on night shifts may need protected rest periods and time to recover before driving home; staff should not be scheduled for long unbroken night runs without breaks; the hospital could check that workers are getting enough sleep, as REM sleep is needed for memory and emotional processing.
parts.working: 2 marks per developed point: 1 mark for the sleep-research idea, 1 mark for applying it to the rota. Accept any well-explained link.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest one way a kindergarten in Islamabad could use the study by Bandura et al. to encourage kind behaviour among its children.
parts.answer: Teachers and older children can model kind behaviour (sharing, helping) in front of the children, and praise or reward children who copy it, so that the imitation is reinforced.
parts.working: 1 mark: modelling kind behaviour by adults or older children (observational learning); 1 mark: praise or reward for imitation (vicarious or direct reinforcement).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one limitation of applying Milgram's findings directly to workplaces in Karachi.
parts.answer: Milgram's study was carried out in one laboratory setting in the USA in the early 1960s with adult men; workplaces today have different rules, cultures and forms of authority, and the findings may not transfer to women or to other settings, so applying them directly may be misleading.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying a limitation (sample, era, culture or setting); 1 mark for explaining why it matters for workplaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one everyday setting, other than a laboratory, in which people might obey an authority figure, as shown in Milgram's study. Explain your choice.
parts.answer: For example a hospital, a school, a police station or a government office. The authority figure has legitimate power, so people follow instructions without questioning them.
parts.working: 1 mark for a relevant setting; 1 mark for explaining it with reference to legitimacy or authority.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one way in which the Bobo doll used by Bandura et al. (aggression) helped the researchers to follow the ethical guideline of protection from harm.
parts.answer: The doll could be hit and knocked over without any person being physically hurt, so the researchers could observe aggressive behaviour while protecting the children and adults from physical harm. A real person as the target would have risked injury, which the guideline of protection from harm forbids.
parts.working: 1 mark: the doll cannot be physically hurt; 1 mark: aggressive behaviour could still be observed and measured; 1 mark: a real person would have been harmed, which breaks protection from harm. Max 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the ethical guideline of 'debriefing'.
parts.answer: After a study, participants are told the true aims of the research, given the chance to ask questions, and any harmful effects of participating are addressed.
parts.working: 1 mark: told the aims or what the study was about; 1 mark: chance to ask questions or support is given after participating.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether the deception used in Milgram's study was justified. Use the study to support your answer.
parts.answer: Justification: the findings showed how far ordinary people will follow an authority figure, which is valuable for understanding real-world harm; deception was needed because telling participants the true aim would have changed their behaviour. Against: participants were misled and many showed severe distress, and the risk of lasting harm was not fully removed by debriefing, so the cost to participants may outweigh the benefit.
parts.working: Level-based: 5-6 marks for a balanced, justified judgement that weighs the value of the findings against the harm to participants, using details of the study; 3-4 marks for one developed point; 1-2 marks for a basic statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the field study by Piliavin et al. (subway Samaritans) did not meet the ethical guideline of informed consent.
parts.answer: The passengers did not know they were taking part in a study, so they could not agree to it beforehand. Once the 'victim' had collapsed they could not refuse to be involved or withdraw without leaving the situation, so they were not able to give informed consent.
parts.working: 1 mark: passengers did not know they were in a study; 1 mark: they could not give consent in advance; 1 mark: they could not refuse or withdraw once the 'victim' collapsed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways researchers can reduce the ethical problems caused by using deception in a study of helping behaviour.
parts.answer: Any two of: use a pilot study to check the level of distress; keep the deception to the minimum needed; give a full debriefing and explain why deception was used; let participants withdraw their data after debriefing; have the study approved by an ethics committee and weigh costs and benefits first.
parts.working: 2 marks for each way: 1 mark to name the strategy, 1 mark to explain how it reduces the ethical problem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the ethical guidelines of informed consent and protection from harm can conflict in a study of obedience like Milgram's.
parts.answer: Full informed consent would tell participants the real aim, which would change the behaviour being studied and make the findings invalid; so researchers must withhold information. But withholding information means participants cannot judge the risk, so they may suffer more harm, which conflicts with protection from harm.
parts.working: 2 marks for explaining the conflict from the consent side (full disclosure would alter the behaviour); 2 marks for the harm side (withholding information makes harm more likely and participants cannot judge the risk).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ethical issues raised by the study by Dement and Kleitman (sleep and dreams).
parts.answer: Any two of: participants were woken repeatedly during sleep, which disrupts sleep and may cause distress; participants must give informed consent to be woken, including knowing the procedure; sleep deprivation or disturbance may affect their health; the right to withdraw must be respected if they wanted to stop during the night.
parts.working: 1 mark per issue correctly identified, linked to a named guideline (protection from harm, informed consent or right to withdraw).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that the right to withdraw is harder to apply in a field study like Piliavin et al.'s than in a laboratory study like Milgram's.
parts.answer: Supports the view: in the field, passengers were never told they were in a study and could not be asked to withdraw; the researchers could not stop the situation once it began; in Milgram's lab the participants could leave at any time, so the right to withdraw was explicitly given. Challenges the view: in a lab study, the right to withdraw may still be hard to use because participants may feel pressured by the experimenter's authority; field studies can still allow withdrawal in a limited way (e.g. the data are not used), so the difficulty is not total.
parts.working: Level-based: 5-6 marks for a balanced evaluation with at least one developed point on each side, using the two studies; 3-4 marks for one developed side; 1-2 marks for a basic statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bus company in Rawalpindi wants passengers to stop ignoring a passenger who has collapsed. Using the study by Piliavin et al., explain two factors that might make bystanders on the bus more likely to help, and one reason why the company's plan might still fail.
parts.answer: Any two factors, e.g.: a victim who appears genuinely ill is more likely to be helped than one who seems drunk, so a clear, visible need increases helping; helping is more likely when the cost to the bystander is low, such as a simple action like calling for the driver (Piliavin's cost-reward idea). Reason the plan may fail: many passengers may assume someone else will act (diffusion of responsibility), or may fear helping a victim who seems drunk, so the company's message may not change behaviour.
parts.working: 2 marks for each factor (1 to name it, 1 to link it to Piliavin's findings or the cost-reward idea); 1 mark for a reason the plan might fail, linked to bystander behaviour (diffusion of responsibility, or fear about helping a victim who seems drunk). Max 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why the study by Hassett et al. (monkey toy preferences) would need approval from an animal ethics committee before it could begin.
parts.answer: The study uses living monkeys, so an ethics committee must weigh the costs to the animals (for example confinement or stress during testing) against the benefit of understanding toy preferences, and check the housing, procedures and welfare before approval.
parts.working: 1 mark: the study involves living animals whose welfare must be protected; 1 mark: the committee weighs costs to the animals against the expected benefits; 1 mark: the committee checks housing, procedures or the 3Rs before approval.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an individual explanation of behaviour, and give one example from psychology.
parts.answer: An individual explanation says that behaviour is caused by factors within the person, such as personality, genes or brain structure. Example: explaining aggression by a person's personality, or by a genetic factor.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition (causes within the person, e.g. traits, biology); 1 mark: a valid example from a study or theory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the study by Bandura et al. (aggression) supports a situational explanation of behaviour.
parts.answer: The children's aggression depended on what they saw in the situation: children who watched an adult model act aggressively, in the same room, copied it, while children who did not see the model were less aggressive. The behaviour was caused by the environment the children were in rather than by a fixed trait.
parts.working: 1 mark: the aggression varied with the situation (presence of a model); 1 mark: comparison of the groups; 1 mark: conclusion that the environment, not a fixed trait, produced the behaviour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Piliavin et al. found that bystanders were more likely to help a victim who appeared ill than one who appeared drunk. Explain whether this finding supports an individual or a situational explanation of helping.
parts.answer: A situational explanation: the same bystanders responded differently depending on the cue presented by the victim, so the situation (how the victim looked) changed the helping, rather than a fixed trait in the bystanders. Some individual explanation remains possible, as not everyone helped, but the difference between victim conditions points to situational causes.
parts.working: 1 mark: the finding involved only the victim's appearance changing (situational cue); 1 mark: the same people responded differently; 1 mark: an acknowledgement that individuals still varied; 1 mark: conclusion (situational explanation is better supported).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Findings about REM sleep and dream reports, such as those of Dement and Kleitman, are often used to support an individual, biological explanation of dreaming. Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: Support: dreaming occurs in an internal physiological state (REM sleep) that is recorded in every person, so the explanation sits within the person's brain. Limitation: the environment still affects dreams (e.g. noise or a worry can enter dreams), and dream content depends on experience, so a purely biological explanation is incomplete; the interactionist view of both internal and external factors is more balanced.
parts.working: Level-based: 5-6 marks for a balanced, developed evaluation with support and a limitation linked to the study; 3-4 marks for one developed point; 1-2 marks for a basic statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one individual factor that may affect whether a bystander helps someone in an emergency.
parts.answer: Any one of: personality (for example empathy or altruism), mood, previous experience of helping, or gender.
parts.working: 1 mark for a named individual factor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why an individual factor may be less important than the situation in helping.
parts.answer: Two people in the same situation may respond very differently, but a situation such as a visibly ill victim often produces helping regardless of who the bystander is.
parts.working: 1 mark: states that situational cues (e.g. how the victim looks, or the number of bystanders) can change behaviour across many different people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the interactionist view approaches the debate between individual and situational explanations.
parts.answer: The interactionist view says behaviour results from the interaction between the person and the situation. A person's traits (for example, assertiveness) influence how they respond to a situation, and the situation changes how their traits show up.
parts.working: 1 mark: behaviour caused by both person and situation; 1 mark: example of a trait interacting with the situation; 1 mark: the point that the two cannot easily be separated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the individual versus situational debate, using the studies by Milgram (obedience) and Piliavin et al. (subway Samaritans).
parts.answer: Situational: obedience changed with the proximity of the learner, the location and the authority of the experimenter; helping changed with the victim's apparent condition and the number of bystanders, so both studies show situational factors shape behaviour. Individual: some participants refused to obey and some bystanders helped while others did not, suggesting individual differences such as personality or values; neither study measured personality directly, so individual causes are hard to test. Discussion: both studies show that the situation is powerful, but the individual variation shows the person also matters; the interactionist view is a better fit to both.
parts.working: Level-based: 7-8 marks for a balanced discussion using both studies, with situational and individual points each developed, and a conclusion; 4-6 marks for one side developed well with some balance; 1-3 marks for description only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two situational factors that Milgram varied in his obedience studies.
parts.answer: Any two of: proximity of the learner (how close the teacher was to the learner); location (the prestigious Yale setting compared with a run-down office in Bridgeport); the presence or absence of the experimenter in the room.
parts.working: 1 mark per factor correctly named with a detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it is difficult for researchers to separate individual and situational explanations of behaviour.
parts.answer: Behaviour usually results from both the person and the situation, and the two interact, so changing one variable alters the other; for example, a shy person may respond differently to a crowd than a confident one. Researchers cannot easily hold the situation constant while varying only the person.
parts.working: 1 mark: behaviour is caused by both person and situation; 1 mark: they interact so that effects cannot be separated; 1 mark: example or explanation of why controlled comparison is hard.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A head teacher in Multan argues that bullying among pupils is caused by 'bad character' (an individual explanation). Using one study from the learning or social approach, evaluate this view.
parts.answer: Against the view: Bandura's study showed that children copied aggression after watching an adult model, so the situation (what they observed) can produce bullying-like behaviour in children with ordinary personalities. For the view: not all children who saw aggression copied it, which suggests individual differences matter. Balanced conclusion: a person's character and the situation both matter, so the teacher should consider the school environment as well as individual pupils.
parts.working: Level-based: 5-6 marks for a developed, balanced evaluation that uses a named study and considers both sides; 3-4 marks for one developed side; 1-2 marks for a basic statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a researcher could test whether personality or the situation is the main cause of aggressive behaviour in a group of pupils in Peshawar.
parts.answer: The researcher could measure personality (e.g. with a questionnaire) and observe the same pupils in different situations (e.g. a classroom with a rule against fighting, and a playground with no supervision); if aggression varies much more between situations than between personalities, the situation is the main cause. Alternatively, the researcher could run an experiment that changes the situation while keeping participants the same.
parts.working: 1 mark: a measure of personality (e.g. questionnaire); 1 mark: observation in different situations; 1 mark: comparison of variation between persons and between situations; 1 mark: a conclusion or experimental design that controls the other factor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one limitation of explaining aggression only by a person's personality.
parts.answer: Personality explanations ignore the situation, so they cannot explain why the same person behaves differently in different settings; they also do not explain why whole groups of people act aggressively when the situation changes.
parts.working: 1 mark: states the limitation (ignores situations, or cannot explain variation across settings); 1 mark: explains why it matters with a link to evidence (e.g. Bandura's children copied aggression).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by ecological validity.
parts.answer: Ecological validity is the extent to which the findings of a study can be applied to real-life settings and everyday behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark: relates to real-life or everyday settings; 1 mark: relates to applicability of findings beyond the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A psychologist measures the reaction times of 30 drivers in Lahore using a computer test in a laboratory. Explain one reason why the findings may have low ecological validity.
parts.answer: The computer task does not involve real traffic, hazards or the pressure of driving, so the reaction times may be different from those on the road; participants also know they are being tested, which may change their speed or care.
parts.working: 2 marks: a reason why the lab task is unlike real driving (no real hazards, no traffic); 1 mark: effect on behaviour (reaction times would differ); 1 mark: demand characteristics or awareness of being tested.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two observers watch the same child in a nursery and count the number of aggressive acts. Their counts are 14 and 11. Explain what this shows about inter-observer reliability, and suggest one way to improve it.
parts.answer: The counts differ, so inter-observer reliability is low: the observers did not record the behaviour in the same way. Improve it by training the observers with clear behavioural categories (e.g. what counts as a hit) and practice sessions, then checking agreement before the main study.
parts.working: 1 mark: low inter-observer reliability identified; 1 mark: reason (different interpretation of the behaviour); 1 mark: suitable improvement (training with clear operational definitions, pilot or practice).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why a study with low population validity could mislead a government planning a health campaign in Pakistan.
parts.answer: The findings may come from a narrow group, such as urban university students, who differ from rural families or older adults; a campaign designed on those findings may then fail to reach or suit the people it is meant for.
parts.working: 1 mark: the sample is not representative of the wider population (low population validity); 1 mark: a campaign based on these findings may not work for the people it targets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher tests the same 20 participants on a memory task today and again two weeks later, to check test–retest reliability. Explain how the researcher would use the results to decide the reliability of the test, and give one reason why the scores might differ between the two tests even if the test is reliable.
parts.answer: Reliability is shown if the two sets of scores are strongly correlated (similar rankings for the same participants at both times). Scores may differ because participants' memories, mood or learning between sessions change, or practice effects occur, not because the test is unreliable.
parts.working: 1 mark: correlate the two sets of scores (strong positive correlation = reliable); 1 mark: a reliable test should show consistent rankings; 1 mark: a reason for difference (practice effects, changed mood or learning, time passing); 1 mark: explanation that such difference does not automatically mean unreliability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by demand characteristics, and explain one way they can reduce the validity of a study.
parts.answer: Demand characteristics are cues in a study that tell participants what the researcher expects, so they change their behaviour to fit (e.g. being helpful or hiding their true views).
parts.working: 1 mark: definition (cues that reveal the expected result); 1 mark: participants change behaviour to fit; 1 mark: the findings then measure the participants' reaction to the study rather than the variable being studied (low validity).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a survey of 250 people in Lahore, 180 said they would take part in future research. Calculate this as a percentage, to the nearest whole number. Explain why this result alone cannot be generalised to all Pakistanis.
parts.answer: 180 ÷ 250 × 100 = 72%. The sample came from one city, so it may not represent people in rural areas, other provinces, other age groups or people with different education levels, so the result cannot be generalised to all Pakistanis.
parts.working: 1 mark: 72% calculated correctly; 1 mark: sample limited to one city (or one type of person); 1 mark: effect on generalisation (not representative); 1 mark: a relevant example of a group not included.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one way a researcher could improve the internal validity of a laboratory experiment on memory.
parts.answer: Any one of: standardise the instructions and procedure for every participant; use a control group; control extraneous variables such as noise or time of day; use random allocation to conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark for a named improvement; 1 mark for how it removes or controls an extraneous variable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how using only students from one university limits the generalisability of findings about exam stress. Give one way to improve generalisability.
parts.answer: Students from one university are a narrow group in terms of age, education and background, so stress levels and coping may differ from those of school pupils, workers or students at other universities; the findings can therefore be applied only to similar people.
parts.working: 2 marks: explanation of the limit (narrow sample in age/background/education, so not representative); 2 marks for an improvement (e.g. a random sample from several universities and schools, or stratified sampling).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the claim that a study with high reliability must also have high validity.
parts.answer: Reliability means consistency, and validity means measuring what is intended, so a study can be reliable but not valid. Example: a scale that always shows the same wrong weight is reliable but not valid. Reliability is necessary for validity (a measure that gives random results cannot be valid), but it does not guarantee validity. Therefore the claim is not correct.
parts.working: Level-based: 5-6 marks for a clear, balanced judgement that defines both terms, gives an example of reliable but invalid measure, and explains that reliability is necessary but not sufficient; 3-4 marks for one developed point; 1-2 marks for a basic definition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the difference between temporal validity and population validity.
parts.answer: Temporal validity: whether findings still apply at a different time, because social behaviour changes over time. Population validity: whether findings apply to a different group of people from the sample.
parts.working: 1 mark for temporal validity (time/era); 1 mark for population validity (other groups of people).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a field study such as Piliavin et al.'s subway study may have higher ecological validity but lower reliability than a laboratory study.
parts.answer: Higher ecological validity: the behaviour happens in a real setting, with real people who did not know they were being studied. Lower reliability: because the setting cannot be controlled, the situation (number of passengers, the victim, the time of day) cannot be repeated exactly, so the study is harder to replicate.
parts.working: 2 marks: ecological validity explained (natural setting, participants unaware); 2 marks: reliability explained (uncontrolled variables, difficult to replicate exactly).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why children may be unable to give fully informed consent.
parts.answer: Any two of: children may not understand the purpose or risks of the study; they may feel pressured by adults to take part; they may not understand that they can withdraw at any time.
parts.working: 1 mark per reason, from the three listed or a similar one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one reason why parental consent is needed before a child takes part in a study.
parts.answer: Children are not legally or developmentally able to give full consent for themselves, so a parent or guardian gives consent on the child's behalf.
parts.working: 1 mark: children cannot give full legal/informed consent; 1 mark: a parent or guardian acts for the child.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A psychologist in Hyderabad wants to observe 8-year-old children in a school playground and count cooperative behaviour between them. Explain one ethical issue with this study and one way to address it.
parts.answer: Issue: the children are being observed without knowing it, so they cannot give informed consent. Way to address it: obtain consent from the school and parents and tell the children about the observation in age-appropriate language; allow children who do not wish to take part to be excluded from the count; or use a public-observation approach with the school's approval and no identifying data.
parts.working: 2 marks for the issue (identified and explained with reference to consent or privacy); 2 marks for a suitable way to address it (named and explained).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways that a study using children to investigate aggression, such as the Bobo doll study by Bandura et al., could be made more ethical.
parts.answer: Any two developed ways, e.g.: use a more gentle model of aggression that is less likely to cause distress; check that children are comfortable before and after the procedure; obtain consent from parents and assent from the children; allow children to stop at any time; provide a full debriefing with a calm activity after the study; limit the number of trials or the amount of exposure to aggression.
parts.working: 3 marks per way: 1 mark to name it, 1 mark to describe how it is done, 1 mark to explain how it protects the child. Level-based: 5-6 marks where two ways are fully developed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why an adult model's aggressive behaviour could place children at greater risk of harm than it would place adults.
parts.answer: Children are less able to understand that the aggression is pretend and may be more frightened or more likely to imitate it, so the risk of distress or of learning harmful behaviour is greater.
parts.working: 1 mark: children may not understand that the behaviour is pretend; 1 mark: children are more easily frightened or influenced; 1 mark: this increases the risk of distress or of learned harm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the term 'assent' when children take part in research.
parts.answer: Assent is a child's own agreement to take part, given with an understanding suited to the child's age, in addition to the parent's consent.
parts.working: 1 mark: child's own agreement; 1 mark: understanding suited to age, in addition to parental consent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school study in Multan uses 46 pupils aged 8 to 10. 19 of the pupils are girls. Calculate the percentage of girls. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for dividing 19 by 46; 1 mark for multiplying by 100; 1 mark for 41.3% (1 d.p.).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some psychologists argue that findings from research with children cannot be generalised to adults, so child research has little value. Discuss this view, using at least one study with children (for example Bandura et al.).
parts.answer: Against the view: many psychological processes such as imitation and observational learning develop early and continue in adults, so findings from children can show basic principles that apply later; studying children can reveal how behaviour develops. For the view: children's cognitive and emotional development differs from adults', so results may not transfer; the Bandura sample was small and from one nursery school, which further limits generalisation. Balanced conclusion: child research can be valuable for developmental questions but results should be checked with adult samples before being applied to adults.
parts.working: Level-based: 7-8 marks for a balanced discussion, using a named study, with both sides developed and a reasoned conclusion; 4-6 marks for one side well developed; 1-3 marks for description only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the right to withdraw may be difficult for a child to use in a school study.
parts.answer: Children may not know they have the right to leave, and may feel they must follow a teacher or parent who is present; they may also be unable to judge the consequences of stopping, so they may stay in the study even if they are unhappy.
parts.working: 1 mark: child may not know the right exists; 1 mark: pressure from adults or the school setting; 1 mark: child cannot judge consequences or feels obliged to continue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one methodological reason why researchers study young children rather than adults when investigating early language development.
parts.answer: Young children are at the stage where language is developing, so studying them shows how language is acquired; adults already have full language, so their results would not reveal how it develops. Researchers can compare children at different ages to see the sequence of development.
parts.working: 2 marks: reason based on developmental stage (adults have already acquired language); 2 marks: explanation of what the child study shows (sequence, change with age, or development over time).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways in which a researcher could check that a child understands what taking part in a study involves, before the study starts.
parts.answer: Any two of: ask the child to explain the study in their own words; use simple, child-friendly language or pictures to describe the tasks; ask a few short questions to check understanding; invite questions and repeat the explanation before starting.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid check, e.g. child explains the study back, child-friendly explanation or pictures, short comprehension questions, invitation to ask questions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a psychologist in Karachi tests 8-year-old pupils on a memory task during lesson time. The head teacher agrees to the study, but the parents are not asked. Explain one ethical problem with this procedure.
parts.answer: Parents have not given consent, and the children cannot give fully informed consent alone. The school's agreement may not represent the children's own interests, and the study takes time away from lessons without parental knowledge.
parts.working: 1 mark: parents (who are legally responsible) were not asked for consent; 1 mark: the head teacher cannot replace the children's or parents' informed consent, or the study disrupts school time without parents knowing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the researcher could address this problem.
parts.answer: Ask each child's parents or guardians for written consent before the study, explain the task in simple language to the parents and the child, and let the child stop at any time.
parts.working: 1 mark for a sensible step (asking parents for written consent); 1 mark for a supporting detail (explaining the study in child-friendly language, or giving the child a right to withdraw).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why researchers may choose to use children as participants when studying the effects of violent media on aggression.
parts.answer: Children are still forming their behaviour, so the effect of media on learning aggression can be studied in the developing stage; findings may show how aggression is acquired early in life, which adults who already have set habits would not show.
parts.working: 1 mark: children are at a developmental stage where behaviour is still being learned; 1 mark: studies of children show how aggression is acquired; 1 mark: adults already have established behaviour, so effects are harder to observe.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate one ethical issue of using children in this type of study.
parts.answer: Children may be exposed to distressing or harmful content, and they cannot fully understand the risks, so protection from harm is harder to guarantee. Even a short exposure could make a child more anxious afterwards, so a careful debrief is essential.
parts.working: 1 mark: names an issue (harm or distress from violent content); 1 mark: explains why children are more vulnerable (cannot fully judge risk); 1 mark: evaluates, e.g. debriefing and parental consent may reduce but not remove the risk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the "nature" side of the nature versus nurture debate.
parts.answer: Nature is the view that behaviour is largely inherited or biologically determined, through genes and the physical structure of the brain.
parts.working: 1 mark: inherited or genetic influence; 1 mark: biological or innate determinism (not learned from experience). Accept the equivalent for nurture: behaviour learned from the environment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one biological factor and one environmental factor that can influence human behaviour.
parts.answer: Biological: genes (or hormones or brain structure). Environmental: upbringing, family or school (or peers, culture).
parts.working: 1 mark for a biological factor; 1 mark for an environmental factor. Accept any sensible example of each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one way in which the study by Bandura et al. (aggression) supports the nurture side of the debate.
parts.answer: Children who watched an adult model act aggressively towards a Bobo doll copied the aggressive behaviour, including actions they had not seen before. This suggests aggression is learned through observation rather than being innate.
parts.working: 1 mark: children imitated the adult model's aggression; 1 mark: imitation included novel behaviour, so it was not just a pre-existing response; 1 mark: conclusion that aggression was learned from the environment (social learning).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a heritability estimate of 0.5 for a trait.
parts.answer: About half of the differences between people in that trait, within the studied population, are due to genetic differences; the other half is due to environmental differences.
parts.working: 1 mark: genetic differences account for about half of the variation; 1 mark: the remaining variation is due to environmental influences. Do not accept "half of a person's trait is inherited".

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: 50 adopted children in Lahore are compared with their biological parents and their adoptive parents on a measure of reading ability. Explain how this design helps separate the influence of nature from nurture.
parts.answer: Children share genes with their biological parents but not their adoptive parents, while they share the home environment with the adoptive parents. If the children's scores are more like the biological parents, nature is more influential; if more like the adoptive parents, nurture is more influential.
parts.working: 1 mark: biological parents share genes with the children; 1 mark: adoptive parents share the home environment; 1 mark: comparison of similarity with each group; 1 mark: conclusion about which influence is stronger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one ethical or practical limitation of this design.
parts.answer: Adoption agencies may not give access to records, or the adoptive home may differ from the biological family in ways other than the environment; families may also be hard to recruit.
parts.working: 1 mark for any sensible limitation, e.g. difficulty recruiting families, adoption placements are not random, or an ethical issue of contacting families about their adoption history.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the interactionist approach can be seen as a compromise between the nature and nurture positions.
parts.answer: Interactionism accepts that genes influence behaviour (nature) and that experience shapes how those genetic tendencies develop (nurture). It does not treat either as the only cause, so it accepts both kinds of influence working together.
parts.working: 1 mark: accepts biological influence; 1 mark: accepts environmental influence; 1 mark: says the two work together or interact, neither acting alone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one limitation of using the study by Dement and Kleitman (sleep and dreams) as evidence for the nature side of the nature versus nurture debate.
parts.answer: The study mainly links REM sleep to dream reports; it does not show that the content of dreams is fixed by biology, because dream content is also shaped by a person's experiences, so the evidence supports only part of the nature view.
parts.working: 1 mark: REM sleep is linked to dream reports, but this does not show what the dreams contain; 1 mark: dream content is shaped by experience (nurture); 1 mark: conclusion that the study supports nature only partly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it is difficult to separate nature and nurture when studying language development in children.
parts.answer: Children inherit the biological capacity to learn language, but they only learn a particular language through the speech they hear. Parents also pass on their genes and provide the environment, so the two influences are correlated and hard to separate.
parts.working: 1 mark: language needs both an inherited capacity and exposure to speech; 1 mark: genes and environment are correlated (parents provide both); 1 mark: experiments that separate them would be unethical in humans.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher in Peshawar measures the reading time at home and the language score of 200 children at age 6. She finds a positive correlation. Explain why this correlation cannot show whether nature or nurture caused the difference in language scores.
parts.answer: A correlation shows only an association. Children with more reading time may have parents with stronger verbal ability, who also passed on genes that affect language. So the correlation may reflect shared genes as well as the home environment.
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation shows association, not cause; 1 mark: a third factor (parents' genes or ability) may explain both; 1 mark: the design does not separate genetic from environmental influence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans) found changes in brain structure after an eight-week mindfulness course. Explain how this study can be used as evidence for the nurture side of the debate, and identify one limitation of the study.
parts.answer: Brain structure changed after experience (mindfulness training), so the brain is shaped by practice, which supports nurture. A limitation is that the sample was small, so the results may not generalise and some of the change could be due to chance or to individual differences.
parts.working: 1 mark: brain changed after training (experience shaped structure); 1 mark: link to nurture or plasticity; 1 mark: limitation identified (small sample); 1 mark: limitation explained (results may not generalise or may reflect chance).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a researcher might argue that the change could also reflect nature.
parts.answer: People who are naturally more able to focus or regulate attention may be more likely to take up and stick with mindfulness, so some of the difference may reflect inherited traits rather than the training alone.
parts.working: 1 mark: individual differences in genetic traits may make some people more likely to benefit; 1 mark: this suggests the training effect and the trait interact.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the interactionist view of behaviour, using one named study to support your answer.
parts.answer: Interactionism says behaviour results from the combination of inherited tendencies and environmental experiences, which cannot be separated. A named study can illustrate this, for example the Bandura et al. (aggression) study: children may have different tendencies to be aggressive (nature), but whether they show aggression depends on the model they observe and the situation (nurture), so both interact. Evaluation: the approach accepts complexity, but it is harder to test and to predict individual behaviour than either pure nature or pure nurture view.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks. AO1: definition of interactionism (up to 2 marks). AO1: relevant named study described accurately (up to 2 marks). AO2/AO3: explains how the study shows both influences interact, or evaluates the view (up to 2 marks). Credit reasonable alternative studies that are correctly described.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two students argue. Student A says: "Behaviour is entirely learned." Student B says: "Behaviour is entirely innate." Evaluate both claims, using evidence from one study.
parts.answer: Both claims are too extreme. Evidence from a study such as Bandura et al. supports learning through observation, but it does not show that every behaviour is learned, since children may have biological tendencies that affect how they respond to a model. Evidence from biological studies such as Dement and Kleitman shows innate processes, but experience also affects behaviour. The best conclusion is that both nature and nurture contribute.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks. 1 mark each for: a reasoned rejection of the "entirely" claim; use of an accurately described named study; a point supporting the learned claim; a point supporting the innate claim; a justified overall conclusion (interactionist or balanced).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher in Hyderabad compares the personality scores of 60 pairs of identical twins raised together with 60 pairs of non-identical twins raised together. Identical twins share almost all their genes, non-identical twins share about half. Explain how a greater similarity in identical twins would support the nature side of the debate, and state one limitation of this design.
parts.answer: If identical twins are more similar on personality than non-identical twins, the extra shared genes suggest a genetic influence (nature). A limitation is that identical twins may also be treated more alike by parents and others, so the shared environment may explain some of the similarity rather than genes alone.
parts.working: 1 mark: identical twins share more genes, so greater similarity suggests genetic influence; 1 mark: comparison with non-identical twins is the key control; 1 mark: limitation that identical twins experience more similar environments; 1 mark: clear conclusion about nature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by "competence" as an ethical consideration when recruiting participants.
parts.answer: Competence means that participants must be able to understand the information given and make a decision about taking part, so researchers must consider whether they are able to give informed consent (for example, because of age, illness or language).
parts.working: 1 mark: participants must be able to understand the study and the information given; 1 mark: the ability to decide freely or give consent (e.g. considering age, illness or language).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why a researcher should tell participants that they may refuse to answer any particular question.
parts.answer: It protects their right to withdraw or not disclose personal information, so that they do not feel forced to share sensitive details; it also helps ensure the consent given is voluntary and informed.
parts.working: 1 mark for each: protects voluntary participation or freedom to refuse; protects privacy or prevents discomfort with sensitive questions. Accept reasonable equivalents.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a school counsellor in Lahore wants to record how 40 students interact in the school canteen. The students are not told they are being observed. Explain how this breaches the ethical guideline of informed consent.
parts.answer: Students have not been told they are being observed, so they cannot decide whether to take part, and they cannot give informed consent.
parts.working: 1 mark: students are not told about the study; 1 mark: so they cannot give informed consent or withdraw.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the counsellor could follow the ethical guidelines while still studying natural interaction.
parts.answer: Tell the school and students that the study will observe general behaviour in the canteen, obtain consent from students and parents, and use a debrief afterwards, with the option to remove their data.
parts.working: 1 mark for a suitable step (e.g. obtain consent from students and parents, or a general explanation of the study). 1 mark for a justification, e.g. the debriefing and the right to withdraw still allow ethical study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: an online questionnaire about sleep is completed by 500 adults in Karachi. The researcher stores each respondent's IP address with their answers. Explain one ethical issue with storing IP addresses and suggest how the researcher can address it.
parts.answer: An IP address can identify an individual, so storing it means that participants could be identified, which breaches confidentiality. The researcher should not collect IP addresses or should remove them as soon as possible, and store the data securely with anonymous codes.
parts.working: 1 mark: IP addresses can identify people, so confidentiality is at risk; 1 mark: suggestion to avoid collecting or delete them; 1 mark: secure anonymous coding or storage of responses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A university department offers students extra course credit to take part in a study on memory. Explain why offering a very large reward could be unethical.
parts.answer: A very large reward could pressure students into taking part even if they do not want to, so their consent is not truly voluntary. Students who need the credit most may feel unable to refuse, which breaches the guideline on voluntary participation.
parts.working: 1 mark: undue pressure or inducement; 1 mark: consent is not voluntary; 1 mark: students in need feel unable to refuse or withdraw.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher exposes students in Islamabad to a short task designed to create mild anxiety (a timed mental arithmetic test with a loud noise), in order to measure heart rate. The study may tell us how anxiety affects heart rate, a finding useful for stress management. Evaluate whether the study is ethical, using a cost-benefit analysis.
parts.answer: Benefits: the findings may help people understand and manage stress; the task is short and standard. Costs: students may feel distress and some may be more anxious than expected; the heart rate measurement carries little physical risk for healthy people. The study can be justified only if the distress is short-lived, participants can stop at any time, and a careful debrief is given. If the risk of lasting harm is low and the benefit is clear, the study is more likely to be ethical, but the researcher must monitor participants throughout.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying benefits; up to 2 for identifying costs or risks; up to 2 for a justified judgement with the cost-benefit balance, including safeguards such as the right to withdraw, debriefing or monitoring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the ethical guideline of debriefing should be used in a study that involved deception, and explain why a debrief may not fully restore a participant's trust in the researcher.
parts.answer: Debriefing should explain the true purpose of the study and why deception was needed, let participants ask questions, and offer the option to withdraw their data. However, participants may still feel foolish or upset, and the researcher may be seen as untrustworthy even after the debrief, so trust may not be fully restored.
parts.working: 1 mark: explains the true purpose and why deception was used; 1 mark: gives participants the chance to ask questions or withdraw data; 1 mark: explains that participants may still feel embarrassed or distrustful; 1 mark: the effect on trust is hard to undo.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by "replacement" in the 3Rs of animal research.
parts.answer: Replacement means using non-animal methods, such as cell cultures, computer models or human volunteers, instead of animals wherever possible.
parts.working: 1 mark: uses alternatives to animals; 1 mark: examples of alternatives (cell culture, computer simulation, or human studies where ethical).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the three Rs of animal research.
parts.answer: Replacement, reduction and refinement.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of the three correctly named.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by "reduction" in the 3Rs, and give one example of how it can be achieved.
parts.answer: Reduction means using the smallest number of animals needed to obtain valid results, for example by using a power calculation to decide the sample size, or by sharing data between studies.
parts.working: 1 mark: the minimum number of animals needed for valid results; 1 mark: example (power analysis, sharing data, or improved design so fewer animals are needed).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why researchers may justify using animals in psychological research.
parts.answer: Animals can be studied in ways that would be unethical with humans, for example to study brain damage or early development; animals may have biological systems similar enough to humans to give useful findings.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid reason (ethically impossible in humans; similar biology; control over environment and genetics). Do not accept "animals are cheaper".

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by "animal welfare" in research.
parts.answer: Animal welfare is the physical and psychological well-being of the animal, including keeping it free from pain, distress and unnecessary suffering while it is in the study.
parts.working: 1 mark: physical well-being (health, pain, housing); 1 mark: psychological well-being (freedom from distress or fear).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one way in which animal research differs from human research in relation to informed consent.
parts.answer: Animals cannot give informed consent, so researchers must rely on ethical approval and welfare judgements made by committees on the animals' behalf.
parts.working: 1 mark: animals cannot give informed consent; 1 mark: researchers rely on ethics committees or welfare standards instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways in which animal research may benefit humans.
parts.answer: It may lead to treatments for mental health conditions such as anxiety or depression, and it may improve understanding of how the brain controls memory and learning.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid benefit: development of treatments; understanding of brain or genetic processes; improved understanding of learning or development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher at a university in Lahore uses 60 rats, split into 3 groups of 20, to test whether a new drug improves maze learning. Explain how the researcher could apply "reduction" and "refinement" in this study.
parts.answer: Reduction: a power calculation or a within-subjects design could allow fewer rats per group while still giving valid results. Refinement: the rats could be housed in enriched cages, handled gently, and given the maze test in a way that causes the least stress and no lasting harm.
parts.working: 1 mark: suggests a way to reduce numbers (power analysis or within-subjects design); 1 mark: explains why this keeps results valid; 1 mark: refinement to housing or handling; 1 mark: refinement to reduce stress or pain in the task.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher plans to remove part of the hippocampus from rats to study memory. Explain why this procedure must be justified using a cost-benefit analysis.
parts.answer: The procedure causes harm and distress to the rats, so the expected scientific benefit must outweigh the costs to the animals. The researcher must show that the knowledge gained cannot be obtained another way and that the number of animals is kept to a minimum.
parts.working: 1 mark: procedure causes harm to the animal (cost); 1 mark: the benefit must outweigh the harm; 1 mark: justification that no alternative would give the same knowledge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one way the researcher could refine this procedure to reduce harm.
parts.answer: Use anaesthetic and pain relief during and after surgery, and monitor the animals daily for signs of distress or infection, ending the study early at humane endpoints.
parts.working: 1 mark: anaesthesia or pain relief; 1 mark: monitoring with humane endpoints or post-operative care.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher uses cultured rat neurons in a laboratory dish, rather than live rats, to test one part of a memory theory. Name which of the 3Rs this illustrates, and explain why.
parts.answer: Replacement: the study uses cell cultures instead of whole living animals for one part of the research.
parts.working: 1 mark: replacement; 1 mark: uses a non-animal (cell culture) method instead of live animals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why researchers should use the minimum number of animals needed in a study.
parts.answer: Fewer animals means less overall suffering, which is an ethical duty; using more animals than needed wastes resources and may not give more reliable results; it also makes a study easier to justify to ethics committees.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid reason, up to 2: less suffering or harm to animals; ethical obligation; avoids wasting resources or unnecessary procedures; easier to justify to an ethics committee. Do not accept reasons that ignore the animals' welfare.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: monkeys in a primate centre in Sindh are used to test whether a new treatment reduces fear responses. Describe two welfare factors the researcher should monitor throughout the study.
parts.answer: Physical health: weight, appetite, signs of injury or illness, and behaviour such as self-harm. Psychological well-being: signs of extreme fear or distress such as repeated pacing, withdrawal or abnormal behaviour, and whether the animals are able to behave naturally in their enclosure.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two factors and 1 mark for each of two specific signs. Accept any valid welfare indicator. Maximum 4 marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a cost-benefit analysis for an animal study, and give one example of a cost and one of a benefit.
parts.answer: A cost-benefit analysis weighs the harm done to the animals against the expected scientific or human benefit. Cost example: pain or distress from a procedure. Benefit example: a better understanding of an anxiety disorder that could help people.
parts.working: 1 mark: weighs harm to the animals against benefits; 1 mark: cost example; 1 mark: benefit example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a laboratory in Peshawar reduces its rat colony from 80 animals to 56 animals after redesigning its experiment. Calculate the percentage reduction in the number of animals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A research team plans four groups of animals. Each group must have at least 12 animals completing the study. The team expects 25% of the animals to be lost during the study in each group. Calculate the total number of animals that must start the study.
parts.answer: 64 animals (16 per group).
parts.working: 1 mark for 12 ÷ 0.75 = 16 animals per group (or 12 ÷ (1 − 0.25)); 1 mark for 16 × 4 = 64; 1 mark for the correct total with the unit (animals) stated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways in which the living conditions of laboratory animals can be refined to improve their welfare.
parts.answer: Provide enrichment such as toys, tunnels or nesting material; allow social housing with compatible animals; keep a regular light–dark cycle.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid refinement, e.g. environmental enrichment, social housing, appropriate lighting, handling by trained staff.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the number of animals used should be kept to a minimum even if more animals would give more reliable results.
parts.answer: Each animal used is a cost to its welfare, and an ethical guideline requires researchers to avoid unnecessary harm; a larger sample is only justified if the extra benefit is worth the additional cost to animals, so the researcher must balance reliability with welfare.
parts.working: 1 mark: animal welfare or harm is a cost; 1 mark: ethical principle to avoid unnecessary use; 1 mark: balance or justification of reliability against harm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how two of the 3Rs can conflict with each other in an animal study.
parts.answer: Replacement with cell cultures or computer models may reduce animal use but may not give a whole-organism response, so the researcher may still need live animals to observe behaviour; reducing the number of animals may mean fewer groups or less data, which can be a problem if refining the procedure requires more time or more monitoring.
parts.working: 1 mark: names two Rs; 1 mark: explains a conflict between them (e.g. replacement cannot give whole-organism behaviour so animals are still needed); 1 mark: a second example of a conflict (e.g. reduction limiting data needed for careful refinement); 1 mark: a reasoned outcome.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of animals in psychological research, with reference to the benefits to humans and the costs to animals.
parts.answer: Benefits: animal studies can give knowledge about brain function, learning and development that could help treatments, and they allow experimental control that is not possible with humans. Costs: animals may suffer pain or distress, and they cannot consent; results may not generalise to humans because of differences in biology and behaviour. A balanced view is that animal research can be justified where benefits are substantial, there is no alternative, and the 3Rs are followed.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks. Up to 2 marks for benefits; up to 2 for costs or limitations (including generalisation); up to 2 for a justified evaluation, e.g. the 3Rs and cost-benefit analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two researchers disagree about a planned study. Researcher A says the study is justified because the benefits to people with phobias outweigh the costs to the animals. Researcher B says the costs are too high because animals cannot consent. Evaluate both views.
parts.answer: Researcher A is right that the benefits can be large, but benefits must be judged against costs to animals, and cannot simply outweigh them without limits. Researcher B is right that animals cannot consent, but the absence of consent does not mean research is always wrong; it means the costs must be minimised and justified. A reasonable judgement depends on whether the benefit is significant, whether alternatives exist and whether the 3Rs are applied.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks. 1 mark each for: a reasoned point supporting Researcher A; a reasoned point supporting Researcher B; reference to cost-benefit analysis or the 3Rs; evaluation of whether alternatives exist; a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a primate researcher wants to use an electric shock on monkeys to study learned fear. Describe two ethical concerns with this procedure and one way the researcher could refine it.
parts.answer: Concerns: the shock causes pain and distress, which the monkeys cannot consent to; the fear may last after the study, causing long-term harm. Refinement: use the lowest intensity that gives a valid response, or use a non-aversive alternative, with pain relief and close monitoring.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two concerns (pain or distress; cannot consent; lasting harm); 1 mark for a refinement with a reason (lower intensity, non-aversive alternative, monitoring).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher reports that a new compound reduces anxiety in mice. Explain why the researcher should not treat this finding alone as sufficient justification for using animals in all future anxiety research.
parts.answer: The finding may not generalise to humans because of biological differences; there may be an alternative method (such as a computer model or a human study) that gives the same knowledge; each further study adds costs to animals, so the benefit of repeating it must be re-justified.
parts.working: 1 mark: animal results may not generalise to humans; 1 mark: alternatives (replacement) may be available; 1 mark: each new study must be justified by cost-benefit analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of ethics committees in animal research, and describe how they judge whether a study should be approved.
parts.answer: Ethics committees review proposals before research starts, checking the scientific justification and the number of animals, and deciding whether the costs to animals are justified by the expected benefits and whether the 3Rs have been applied. They can refuse approval or set conditions, and monitor the study while it runs.
parts.working: 1 mark: reviews the proposal before research begins; 1 mark: checks justification and numbers; 1 mark: judges cost-benefit and the 3Rs; 1 mark: can set conditions, refuse approval or monitor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what is meant by "ergonomics" in the design of work.
parts.answer: Ergonomics is the study of how work tasks and equipment can be designed to fit the physical and mental abilities of workers, reducing strain and error.
parts.working: 1 mark: fitting the work and equipment to people; 1 mark: aim of reducing strain, fatigue or error.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by the "Hawthorne effect".
parts.answer: The Hawthorne effect is the tendency for people to change their behaviour because they know they are being observed or studied, rather than because of the variable being tested.
parts.working: 1 mark: change in behaviour caused by being observed or studied; 1 mark: the change is not caused by the independent variable itself.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the job demand–control model of work stress (Karasek) predicts stress in workers.
parts.answer: The model predicts that stress is highest when job demands are high and the worker has little control over how the work is done (high strain). Stress is lower when demands are high but control is also high (an active job), or when demands are low.
parts.working: 1 mark: high demands; 1 mark: low control produces high strain; 1 mark: high demands combined with high control, or low demands, reduces strain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why workers on a night shift may make more errors than workers on a day shift.
parts.answer: Night workers are working against their circadian rhythm, when body temperature and alertness are naturally lower, so they are more tired. Daytime sleep is often shorter and of lower quality, which increases fatigue and reduces attention.
parts.working: 1 mark: circadian rhythm or body clock works against the night shift; 1 mark: fatigue and reduced alertness; 1 mark: disrupted or shorter daytime sleep increases errors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what psychologists have found about the effect of high temperatures on work performance.
parts.answer: Performance on simple tasks may be maintained up to a point, but as temperatures rise, performance on complex tasks, concentration and decision-making tends to fall; in very high heat, errors and accidents increase.
parts.working: 1 mark: performance falls on complex tasks or concentration; 1 mark: effect is not linear, with a point beyond which performance worsens; 1 mark: errors or accidents increase in extreme heat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a textile factory in Faisalabad had 24 accidents among 600 workers in one year. Calculate the accident rate per 100 workers.
parts.answer: 4 accidents per 100 workers.
parts.working: 1 mark for 24 ÷ 600 × 100 = 4; 1 mark for the answer with the unit (per 100 workers).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the usefulness of research into accident proneness as an explanation for workplace accidents, including a discussion of individual and situational explanations.
parts.answer: Accident proneness suggests that some people have personal traits that make them more likely to have accidents, which is useful for selecting workers. However, it is an individual explanation and does not consider the situation: accidents are often caused by equipment design, workload or shift patterns. Accident proneness is also hard to measure reliably, since accidents have many causes. A balanced view is that both individual and situational factors matter, and a systems approach that improves the work environment may be more effective than screening workers.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks. Up to 2 marks for describing accident proneness; up to 2 for evaluating it as an individual explanation, noting the situational alternative; up to 2 for a justified conclusion, e.g. interactionist or systems view.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the difference between job satisfaction and job involvement.
parts.answer: Job satisfaction is how positively a person feels about their job or its aspects; job involvement is how central work is to a person's identity and how much they are absorbed in it.
parts.working: 1 mark: satisfaction is an emotional evaluation of the job; 1 mark: involvement is the importance of work to self-identity or absorption.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a "Likert-type scale" in a job satisfaction questionnaire.
parts.answer: A rating scale with a set of ordered response options (for example, from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree") that respondents choose between to show how much they agree with a statement.
parts.working: 1 mark: ordered set of response options; 1 mark: respondents rate how much they agree or disagree with each statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two reasons why responses to a job satisfaction questionnaire may be affected by social desirability bias.
parts.answer: Employees may not want to criticise their employer if they think answers are seen by managers, or may give answers they think are expected; they may fear losing their job or reputation.
parts.working: 1 mark for each: fear of being identified or of consequences; wish to give a socially acceptable or expected answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nadia is a nurse in a hospital in Karachi. She reports low satisfaction with her pay but high satisfaction with her colleagues and the work itself. Explain how a facet approach to job satisfaction helps to describe this pattern.
parts.answer: The facet approach measures satisfaction with separate aspects of the job, so Nadia can be dissatisfied with pay but satisfied with other facets. A single overall score would hide these differences, which may suggest where changes are needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: facets are measured separately; 1 mark: Nadia can be satisfied on some facets and not others; 1 mark: an overall score would hide this, so the facet approach is more useful for identifying what to change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a high level of job satisfaction does not always lead to high job performance.
parts.answer: Performance depends on other factors, such as ability, skills, the tools available and the rewards linked to effort. A satisfied worker may still perform poorly if the job does not require much effort, and performance may lead to satisfaction rather than the reverse.
parts.working: 1 mark: performance depends on ability, skills or resources as well as satisfaction; 1 mark: the relationship can run in either direction; 1 mark: the link between satisfaction and performance is weak or moderated by other factors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the link that psychologists have found between job satisfaction and labour turnover (staff leaving an organisation).
parts.answer: Lower job satisfaction is associated with higher intention to leave and with actual turnover. Satisfied employees are more likely to stay, although other factors such as pay offers or alternative jobs also influence leaving.
parts.working: 1 mark: low satisfaction is linked to higher turnover or intention to leave; 1 mark: satisfaction is one of several factors; 1 mark: the relationship is correlational / not the only cause.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: five employees in a call centre in Lahore rate their satisfaction on a scale from 1 (very dissatisfied) to 5 (very satisfied). Their scores are 4, 2, 5, 3 and 4. Calculate the mean satisfaction score.
parts.working: 1 mark for (4 + 2 + 5 + 3 + 4) ÷ 5 = 18 ÷ 5 = 3.6; 1 mark for the answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of self-report questionnaires to measure job satisfaction, with reference to the usefulness of research in this area.
parts.answer: Strengths: questionnaires are quick and cheap, can be used with large samples, and allow comparisons across organisations; standardised scales such as the JDI have been tested for reliability. Weaknesses: responses may reflect mood on the day or social desirability; people may not be honest about dissatisfaction; a single score may not capture satisfaction across all facets. The findings are useful for organisations that want to identify problems, but they are a snapshot and should be combined with other measures such as turnover or observation.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks. Up to 2 marks for strengths; up to 2 for weaknesses (e.g. social desirability, mood, reliability of self-report); up to 2 for a justified evaluation of usefulness, e.g. combined with other evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a psychologist wants to compare job satisfaction between staff in two factories in Sialkot, one with a new shift system and one with the old system. Describe one suitable research design for the study and justify your choice.
parts.answer: A quasi-experimental or natural experiment design would compare the two factories with and without the new system. Measure satisfaction before and after the change in both factories. This controls for some of the factors that might affect satisfaction, although the groups are not randomly assigned.
parts.working: 1 mark: names a suitable design (natural experiment, quasi-experiment, or independent measures with pre/post test); 1 mark: description of the procedure; 1 mark: justification of the design (no random allocation possible); 1 mark: a limitation or control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two needs described in McClelland's theory of motivation.
parts.answer: Need for achievement; need for affiliation (also accepted: need for power).
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two needs: achievement, affiliation, power.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by "equity" in Adams' equity theory.
parts.answer: Equity is the perception that the ratio of a worker's outcomes (such as pay) to inputs (such as effort) is fair compared with the ratio for others.
parts.working: 1 mark: ratio of outcomes to inputs; 1 mark: comparison with others (perceived fairness).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the "expectancy" component of Vroom's expectancy (VIE) theory.
parts.answer: Expectancy is the worker's belief that increased effort will lead to a successful performance (effort → performance).
parts.working: 1 mark: belief about effort leading to performance; 1 mark: a probability or subjective estimate between 0 and 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Umar works in a warehouse in Multan. He notices that a colleague who works more slowly earns the same wage as he does. Explain how equity theory predicts Umar may respond.
parts.answer: Umar sees his outcome-to-input ratio as less fair than his colleague's, because he puts in more effort for the same pay. Equity theory predicts he may feel under-rewarded and may reduce his effort, ask for a pay rise, or move to another job to restore fairness.
parts.working: 1 mark: perceives inequity (same outcome for less input or greater input for same outcome); 1 mark: feeling of under-reward or distress; 1 mark: prediction of a behavioural response (reduce effort, seek change, or leave).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a piece-rate pay system relates to extrinsic motivation, and identify one possible drawback of the system.
parts.answer: Piece-rate pay gives workers money for each unit produced, so their motivation comes from the external reward rather than the task itself. A possible drawback is that workers may focus on quantity rather than quality, or the intrinsic enjoyment of the work may be reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark: pay depends on output so it is an extrinsic reward; 1 mark: a drawback, e.g. quality is ignored or intrinsic motivation falls; 1 mark: a second drawback, e.g. competition or stress.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by job enrichment as an approach to motivating workers.
parts.answer: Job enrichment gives workers more responsibility, variety, autonomy and control over their work, for example by letting them plan their own tasks or check their own quality. It aims to increase intrinsic motivation by making the work more meaningful.
parts.working: 1 mark: more responsibility, autonomy or decision-making; 1 mark: greater variety or task significance; 1 mark: aims to increase intrinsic motivation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a garment factory manager in Gujranwala wants to use positive reinforcement to reduce late arrivals. Describe how he could apply positive reinforcement and name one schedule of reinforcement he could use.
parts.answer: He could reward punctual arrival, for example with a small bonus or a visible reward after each week without lateness. A fixed-interval or variable-ratio schedule could be used; a variable schedule may be more resistant to extinction. The reward should follow the desired behaviour immediately to be effective.
parts.working: 1 mark: reward follows punctual arrival (positive reinforcement); 1 mark: example of reward; 1 mark: names a schedule (fixed ratio, fixed interval, variable ratio or variable interval); 1 mark: explains timing or why it works.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In Vroom's expectancy (VIE) theory, motivational force = expectancy × instrumentality × valence. A sales worker in Peshawar has two options. Option A: expectancy 0.6, instrumentality 0.7, valence 0.9. Option B: expectancy 0.8, instrumentality 0.4, valence 0.9. Calculate the motivational force of each option and state which option has the higher force.
parts.answer: Option A: 0.6 × 0.7 × 0.9 = 0.378; Option B: 0.8 × 0.4 × 0.9 = 0.288. Option A has the higher motivational force (0.378 against 0.288); the values have no units.
parts.working: 1 mark for 0.6 × 0.7 × 0.9 = 0.378; 1 mark for 0.8 × 0.4 × 0.9 = 0.288; 1 mark for stating that Option A is higher, with no units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate process theories of motivation to work (such as equity theory and expectancy theory), including a discussion of the usefulness of research in this area.
parts.answer: Equity theory explains why workers react to unfair pay, and this has been supported in many workplace studies, so it is useful for managers. However, it is hard to measure how people perceive fairness and the theory does not explain why some people put up with inequity. Expectancy theory explains how choices depend on beliefs and values, and it is useful for setting rewards, but its variables are difficult to measure and the estimates are subjective. Both are cognitive, which gives strengths in explaining decisions, but they have less to say about the influence of needs. Overall, the theories are useful but limited.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks. Up to 2 marks for describing equity or expectancy theory; up to 2 for strengths (usefulness for management, research support); up to 2 for weaknesses and a justified conclusion (measurement difficulty, subjective estimates, limited scope).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the "democratic" leadership style in Lewin, Lippitt and White's study.
