parts.answer: Democratic leaders involve group members in decisions, encouraging discussion and allowing them to share in planning the work.
parts.working: 1 mark: group members take part in decisions; 1 mark: encourages discussion or shared planning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two components of transformational leadership.
parts.answer: Idealised influence (acting as a role model); inspirational motivation; intellectual stimulation; individualised consideration.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two components named correctly (accept any of the four).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the difference between transactional and transformational leadership.
parts.answer: Transactional leadership relies on exchanges, such as rewards for meeting targets and punishment for failure; transformational leadership inspires followers to go beyond their own interests by developing their ideas and commitment.
parts.working: 1 mark: transactional = exchange of rewards and punishment; 1 mark: transformational = inspiration, development and commitment beyond expectations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tariq is a site manager for a construction firm in Karachi. He pays bonuses to crews who meet weekly targets and warns those who fall behind. Identify the leadership style he is using and explain one reason for your answer.
parts.answer: Transactional leadership, because he uses an exchange of rewards for meeting targets and warnings or sanctions for failing to meet them.
parts.working: 1 mark: transactional leadership; 1 mark: rewards linked to targets (contingent reward); 1 mark: warnings for failure (management by exception).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by "leader–member exchange" (LMX) theory.
parts.answer: LMX theory proposes that leaders develop different working relationships with each follower. Some members form high-quality relationships with more trust and responsibility, while others have only the standard, formal exchange; these differences influence performance and satisfaction.
parts.working: 1 mark: leaders form different relationships with different followers; 1 mark: high-quality relationships involve trust and extra responsibility; 1 mark: differences affect performance or satisfaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why trait theories of leadership were criticised.
parts.answer: Trait theories assume that good leaders have fixed personal characteristics, but many people with those traits are not effective leaders, and the theory ignores the situation and the followers. Traits such as intelligence show only weak links to leadership effectiveness.
parts.working: 1 mark: a reason (leaders with the traits are not always effective; the theory ignores situations); 1 mark: a supporting point (e.g. traits show weak correlation with leadership outcomes); 1 mark: explanation of why this weakens the theory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: the head teacher of a girls' school in Quetta wants to lead her staff in a transformational way. Describe two behaviours she could use.
parts.answer: She could act as a role model by showing commitment to the school's goals; she could communicate an inspiring vision for improving student results; she could encourage staff to try new teaching ideas (intellectual stimulation); and she could give each teacher individual support and feedback.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two behaviours and 1 mark for each linked component of transformational leadership (idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualised consideration). Maximum 4 marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher in Karachi gives a questionnaire to bank staff to find out whether they see their branch manager as a transformational leader. Identify two sources of bias the researcher should consider, and suggest how each could be reduced.
parts.answer: Social desirability: employees may rate their supervisor more favourably if they fear consequences; reduce by guaranteeing anonymity. Acquiescence: employees may agree with statements automatically; reduce by using reverse-scored items and a balanced range of questions. Halo effect: a generally positive view may colour specific ratings; reduce by asking about each behaviour separately.
parts.working: 1 mark for each source (social desirability, acquiescence, halo effect, demand characteristics); 1 mark for each suitable way to reduce it (anonymity, reverse-scored items, separate items, pilot test).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate transactional and transformational leadership, with reference to research evidence and cultural factors.
parts.answer: Transformational leadership is linked in many studies to higher follower satisfaction and performance, which supports its usefulness. However, the evidence is largely correlational and often based on self-report, so causation is unclear. Cultural factors matter: in cultures with high power distance, followers may expect leaders to direct them, so a transactional approach may be more acceptable; in other cultures, a more participative style may work better. Transactional leadership is easier to measure and can be effective for routine tasks, but it may not encourage creativity or commitment. A balanced view is that the effectiveness of each style depends on the context.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks. Up to 2 marks for research evidence for transformational leadership and its limits (correlational, self-report); up to 2 for a discussion of cultural factors; up to 2 for a justified conclusion, e.g. both styles, context-dependent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two of the nine team roles described by Belbin.
parts.answer: Any two of: plant, resource investigator, coordinator, shaper, monitor evaluator, teamworker, implementer, completer finisher, specialist.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correctly named team role.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two conditions under which social loafing is more likely to occur in a work group.
parts.answer: When group members are not individually identifiable; when the group is large; when individual contributions are not evaluated; when the task seems unimportant or unlikely to be missed.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid condition, e.g. large group size, individual effort not identifiable, no individual evaluation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by "groupthink".
parts.answer: Groupthink is a pattern of thinking in highly cohesive groups where the desire for agreement overrides realistic evaluation of alternatives, so poor decisions are made.
parts.working: 1 mark: desire for agreement or cohesion overrides critical thinking; 1 mark: leads to poor or unrealistic decisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two symptoms of groupthink that Janis identified.
parts.answer: Illusion of invulnerability (the group believes it cannot fail); self-censorship (members hold back doubts); pressure on dissenters (members who disagree are persuaded or excluded); illusion of unanimity (silence is taken as agreement).
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two symptoms correctly described (up to 2), and 1 mark for accurate detail. Any two of the four named symptoms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how group cohesion can both help and harm the decisions a group makes.
parts.answer: Cohesion helps because members trust each other, communicate well and are motivated to complete tasks. However, high cohesion can cause groupthink, in which members avoid disagreement and fail to consider alternative options.
parts.working: 1 mark: cohesion improves communication, trust or motivation; 1 mark: high cohesion may suppress disagreement; 1 mark: link to poor decisions (groupthink).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a textile company in Faisalabad has a six-person design team in which one member, Ayesha, consistently organises the team, sets agendas and keeps the group focused on deadlines. Explain which Belbin team role Ayesha is likely to be playing and why this role is useful.
parts.answer: Coordinator. The coordinator clarifies goals, sets agendas and delegates tasks, which helps the team stay focused and work together effectively.
parts.working: 1 mark: coordinator; 1 mark: organises the team and clarifies goals; 1 mark: helps the team to stay focused and work effectively.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what psychologists mean by "avoiding" as a conflict-handling style, and give one situation in which it may be appropriate.
parts.answer: Avoiding means ignoring or withdrawing from the disagreement, so the conflict is neither confronted nor resolved. It may be appropriate when the issue is trivial, when emotions are high and a delay would help, or when someone else can handle the problem better.
parts.working: 1 mark: avoiding involves ignoring, postponing or withdrawing from the conflict; 1 mark: example of an appropriate situation (trivial issue, cooling-off period, better-placed person); 1 mark: an explanation of why it helps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a student group in Lahore is asked to clap and shout as loudly as possible, alone and in a group of six. Each student's average output is 12 units when alone and 7.5 units in the group. Calculate the percentage drop in individual output.
parts.working: 1 mark for (12 − 7.5) ÷ 12 × 100 = 37.5; 1 mark for the answer with the % sign.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a six-person volunteer team at a charity in Quetta is working on a flood-relief project, and some members are doing much less than others. Suggest two steps the team leader could take to reduce social loafing.
parts.answer: Make each member's contribution identifiable, for example by assigning named tasks with individual deadlines; set a clear group goal with individual responsibilities; give feedback to individuals on their contribution; keep the group small or split it into smaller sub-teams.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two suitable steps (identifiable contributions, individual tasks, feedback, clear goals, smaller sub-teams); 1 mark for a suitable explanation of each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the research into groupthink, including a discussion of the usefulness of research in this area.
parts.answer: Janis's account is based on detailed case studies of political and military decisions, such as the Bay of Pigs invasion, which gave rich insight into how decisions are made. However, the case studies are retrospective, so the evidence relies on documents and memories and may be biased. There is little experimental control, so it is difficult to show that cohesion causes poor decisions rather than being correlated with them. The model has been useful to organisations, since it suggests safeguards such as encouraging dissent and appointing a devil's advocate, but its real-world usefulness depends on how it is applied.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks. Up to 2 marks for describing Janis's research (case studies, examples); up to 2 for evaluation (retrospective data, lack of experimental control, bias, correlation); up to 2 for a justified conclusion about usefulness, e.g. practical safeguards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a software team in Karachi has been working on a new app for three months. Members have begun arguing openly about who should lead the project and how the work should be divided. Using Tuckman's model, identify the stage the team has reached and explain how the team manager should respond.
parts.answer: The team has reached the storming stage, when conflict and competition for roles emerge. The manager should encourage open discussion of the roles and goals, set clear rules for decision-making, and help the team agree on responsibilities so that it can move on to the norming stage.
parts.working: 1 mark: storming stage; 1 mark: conflict over roles or goals is typical of this stage; 1 mark: manager encourages open discussion or clarifies roles; 1 mark: aims to move the team forward to norming and performing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two physiological measures that Dement and Kleitman recorded during participants' sleep.
parts.answer: EEG (brain-wave activity) and eye movements (EOG).
parts.working: 1 mark each: EEG / electroencephalogram (brain waves); eye movement recording (EOG). Accept 'electrical activity of the brain' for EEG.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the researchers woke participants during both REM and non-REM sleep.
parts.answer: So that dream reports from REM sleep could be compared with reports from non-REM sleep, to test whether dreaming is linked to REM.
parts.working: 1 mark for a comparison of dream reports from REM and NREM awakenings; 1 mark for linking the comparison to testing whether REM sleep is associated with dreaming.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical replication (these figures are invented for practice, not from the original study) woke participants 40 times from REM sleep and 40 times from non-REM sleep. Dream reports followed 33 REM awakenings and 4 non-REM awakenings. Calculate the percentage of REM awakenings that produced a dream report.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of non-REM awakenings that produced a dream report.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one conclusion the researcher could draw from these results.
parts.answer: Dream reports were much more likely after REM awakenings than after non-REM awakenings, so dreaming appears to be linked to REM sleep.
parts.working: 1 mark for a conclusion that compares the two conditions and links dreaming to REM sleep.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A friend claims that people only dream while their brain is inactive and that dreams have no link to the body's sleep cycle. Explain one reason, based on the study, why this claim is not supported.
parts.answer: Dream reports were linked to REM periods, which occur in a regular cycle during the night, so dreaming is connected to a physiological sleep stage.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reference to REM periods occurring in a cycle during sleep; 1 mark for explaining that dreaming was linked to this physiological stage, so it is not independent of the body's sleep cycle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the researchers used EEG recordings as well as eye-movement recordings to identify REM sleep.
parts.answer: EEG shows the pattern of brain-wave activity that characterises each sleep stage, while eye movements show the rapid eye movements typical of REM; using both gives a more reliable identification of the stage.
parts.working: 1 mark for each: EEG identifies the brain-wave pattern of the sleep stage; eye movements identify REM. Accept that combining the two increases reliability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After waking, participants estimated how long they had been dreaming. Explain one reason why the researchers compared these estimates with the length of the REM period before waking.
parts.answer: To test whether the estimated dream length was related to the actual length of the REM period, i.e. whether dream time matches real time.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying the comparison (estimate against actual REM length); 1 mark for explaining what it tests (whether dream duration corresponds to the length of REM sleep).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one limitation of conducting sleep research in a laboratory, as in Dement and Kleitman's study.
parts.answer: Participants wired to electrodes in an unfamiliar room may not sleep as they normally would, so the findings may have low ecological validity.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying the limitation (artificial setting or electrodes disturb sleep); 1 mark for explaining its effect (sleep not typical of home sleep; low ecological validity).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Six REM periods (in minutes) from a hypothetical sleep study were: 12, 18, 15, 22, 9, 14. Calculate the mean length of these REM periods.
parts.answer: 15 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the median length of these REM periods.
parts.answer: 14.5 minutes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of physiological measures in Dement and Kleitman's study of sleep and dreams. Refer to the reliability and objectivity of the EEG and eye-movement recordings, and discuss whether the measures show that REM sleep causes dreaming.
parts.answer: Strengths: EEG and eye-movement recordings are objective and recorded in the same way for each participant, so they are less affected by bias than self-report; sleep stage can be checked against both brain-wave and eye-movement patterns, which improves the reliability of stage identification. Weaknesses: the link between REM periods and dream reports is correlational, so it cannot show that REM causes dreaming; the content of dreams still depends on participants' memory, which the physiological records cannot check; and wires and the laboratory may disturb sleep, so the recordings may not be typical of normal sleep. Conclude with a justified judgement of how far the physiological evidence supports a link between REM sleep and dreaming.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): clear evaluation of the objectivity and reliability of the measures and of the causal limit, with at least two strengths and two weaknesses developed and a supported conclusion. Level 2 (5–8): some evaluation, with one area developed or both areas covered briefly. Level 1 (1–4): description of the study or of EEG with little evaluation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Dement and Kleitman's findings support the view that dreaming has a biological basis.
parts.answer: REM sleep is a physiological state with a characteristic brain-wave and eye-movement pattern; dream reports were far more frequent when participants were woken from REM than from non-REM sleep; so dreaming is linked to a measurable brain state that occurs in cycles during sleep, which supports a biological explanation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: REM is a physiological state identified by EEG and eye movements; dream reports were more frequent after REM awakenings; REM occurs in a regular cycle; this links dreaming to brain activity, supporting a biological basis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concludes: 'Dement and Kleitman showed that rapid eye movements cause dreams.' Explain why the study does not justify this conclusion.
parts.answer: The study found an association between REM sleep (which includes rapid eye movements) and dream reports. Eye movements and dreaming both occur during REM, so they are correlated, not shown to cause each other. A third factor, the brain state of REM, may explain both.
parts.working: 1 mark for stating that the study shows an association (correlation), not causation; 1 mark for noting that both occur in REM sleep so a third factor could explain both; 1 mark for a clear statement that causation has not been demonstrated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one way a researcher could test whether a participant's dream report is accurate, and suggest one problem with this method.
parts.answer: The researcher could ask the participant to describe the dream in detail after a short delay, or compare the report with a second report of the same dream given at a different time, or use a consistency check (such as later questions about the dream's details). Problem: the dream cannot be observed directly, so there is no objective check; the participant's memory may be altered by the questioning itself.
parts.working: 1 mark for a suitable method (repeat or consistency check of the report); 1 mark for explaining how it tests accuracy; 1 mark for a problem stated; 1 mark for explaining why the problem limits accuracy (dreams cannot be verified objectively; memory can be distorted).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the researchers measured toy preference by observing what the monkeys did, rather than by asking the monkeys which toy they preferred.
parts.answer: Monkeys cannot say which toy they like, so preference must be inferred from behaviour. Observing and recording how much time each monkey spends with each toy gives an objective, measurable indicator of preference.
parts.working: 1 mark: monkeys cannot self-report, so behaviour is the only available measure. 1 mark: observation gives an objective, quantifiable measure (for example, time spent with each toy).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two types of toy that the monkeys could choose between in the study.
parts.answer: A wheeled toy (for example a toy car) and a plush toy (a soft toy).
parts.working: 1 mark for each: wheeled toy; plush (soft) toy. Accept 'a toy vehicle' for wheeled toy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A replication wants to be sure that the observers recording each monkey's toy use do not bias their results. Suggest one way to achieve this.
parts.answer: The observers could be kept unaware of each monkey's sex (or of the hypothesis), so that their expectations cannot influence what they record; a second observer could also check the recordings.
parts.working: 1 mark for a suitable method (observers unaware of sex/hypothesis, or blind observation); 1 mark for explaining how this reduces bias. Accept inter-observer reliability checks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how the biological approach would explain a sex difference in toy preferences found in monkeys.
parts.answer: Hormones such as testosterone, especially during early development, could influence brain development and so make some toys more attractive to one sex than the other.
parts.working: 1 mark for a biological mechanism (hormones, e.g. prenatal androgens or testosterone); 1 mark for explaining how this affects brain development and preference.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a finding of sex differences in toy preferences in monkeys could contribute to the nature versus nurture debate.
parts.answer: Because the differences appear in monkeys, which were not raised in a human gender-role environment, they suggest some influence of biology (nature) rather than only learned gender roles (nurture).
parts.working: 1 mark for stating the finding is found in a non-human species with no human gender socialisation; 1 mark for explaining this points towards biological (nature) influences.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical replication (invented figures), juvenile males spent 62 of 90 observed minutes with the wheeled toy, and juvenile females spent 28 of 90 observed minutes with it. Calculate the percentage of observed time that males spent with the wheeled toy, to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of observed time that females spent with the wheeled toy, to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the two percentages, in percentage points.
parts.answer: 37.8 percentage points
parts.working: 68.9 − 31.1 = 37.8 percentage points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one ethical consideration that researchers must address when using rhesus monkeys in a study of this kind.
parts.answer: Animal welfare: the researchers must minimise any distress and harm, justify the use of animals, and return the monkeys safely to their group. Accept the 3Rs (replacement, reduction, refinement).
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying a consideration (welfare, minimising distress, justification, 3Rs); 1 mark for explaining how it is addressed in practice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of observation to record toy preferences in Hassett et al.'s study. Refer to the validity and reliability of the observations, and discuss whether the findings can be generalised to human children.
parts.answer: Strengths: observation records what the monkeys actually do, which gives an objective, direct measure of behaviour; inter-observer checks can improve reliability; observing animals in a social setting can add to ecological validity. Weaknesses: observers' expectations may bias what is recorded unless they are unaware of each monkey's sex; the toys offered were limited, so a recorded preference may reflect what was available; and the animals are not a representative sample of all monkeys. Generalisation: monkeys differ from human children in biology and upbringing (language, culture, gender norms), so the findings apply only with caution. Conclude with a justified judgement of how far the observations support the view that toy preferences have a biological basis.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): balanced evaluation of observation (validity and reliability) with at least two developed strengths and weaknesses, and a reasoned discussion of generalisation to children, with a supported conclusion. Level 2 (5–8): some evaluation, with one area developed. Level 1 (1–4): mainly description of the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the findings of a study on rhesus monkeys may not generalise to human children.
parts.answer: Monkeys and humans differ biologically, so hormonal and brain development may differ. Human children also grow up with language, culture and a wider range of toys and gender stereotypes, which can shape preferences in ways not present in monkeys.
parts.working: 1 mark for a biological difference between species; 1 mark for a difference in environment or upbringing (culture, language, gender norms); 1 mark for explaining why this limits generalisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a study of sex differences must compare males and females of the same age, and explain one problem that would arise if the male and female groups differed in age.
parts.answer: A sex difference can only be attributed to sex if the groups are otherwise similar. If the males and females differed in age, age could cause the difference in toy use, because play and social behaviour change as monkeys grow. Age would then be a confounding variable, so the comparison would not show a true sex difference.
parts.working: 1 mark: a sex difference can only be concluded if other variables (such as age) are kept equal. 1 mark: age would be a confounding variable. 1 mark: age changes play or social behaviour, so it could produce the observed difference. 1 mark: the comparison would not then reflect sex alone.

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the brain-scanning technique used in Hölzel et al.'s study and state what it measures.
parts.answer: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which measures brain structure, for example the volume or density of grey matter.
parts.working: 1 mark for MRI; 1 mark for stating that it measures brain structure (grey matter volume or density).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the study included a control group that did not take part in the mindfulness programme.
parts.answer: The control group allowed the researchers to compare changes in the experimental group with changes in people who had not done the programme, so that changes caused by time, practice effects or repeated scanning could be ruled out.
parts.working: 1 mark for comparison of the two groups; 1 mark for explaining that it controls for other causes of change (time, repeated scanning, expectations).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two extraneous variables that the researchers would need to control when scanning participants before and after the programme.
parts.answer: For example: time of day of the scan, the scanner settings, how the head is positioned in the scanner, the participant's caffeine intake, or their stress level before the scan.
parts.working: 1 mark for each suitable extraneous variable (any two of: time of day; scanner settings; head position; caffeine or food intake; stress or fatigue).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical example (figures invented for practice), a participant's hippocampal grey matter volume rose from 4.10 cm³ before the programme to 4.25 cm³ after it. Calculate the percentage increase, to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: Increase = 4.25 − 4.10 = 0.15 cm³. Percentage increase = 0.15 ÷ 4.10 × 100 = 3.7%. 1 mark for the method (increase ÷ original × 100), 1 mark for the answer.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the researchers needed a brain scan taken before the mindfulness programme began, as well as one taken after it.
parts.answer: A before-programme scan gives each participant a baseline, so any change in grey matter can be measured as a difference from their own starting point. Without a baseline, a single after-programme scan could not show whether the brain had changed.
parts.working: 1 mark: the baseline provides a starting point for comparison. 1 mark: change can only be shown as a difference from that starting point (a single scan cannot show change).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher finds that participants with higher mindfulness scores also have more grey matter in the hippocampus. Explain why this correlation alone would not show that the mindfulness programme caused the brain changes.
parts.answer: A correlation shows an association but not direction or cause: people with more grey matter might have become more mindful, or a third variable (such as personality or prior brain structure) might explain both. Without an experimental design comparing pre- and post-programme scans with a control group, causation cannot be shown.
parts.working: 1 mark for stating that correlation shows association, not causation; 1 mark for a third-variable or reverse-causation explanation; 1 mark for noting that the experimental design (before and after, with control group) is needed to show cause.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Hölzel et al.'s study of mindfulness and brain scans. Discuss whether the findings can be generalised to people with long-term stress or to people who already have a long meditation practice.
parts.answer: Points to include: the sample had no prior meditation experience, so the findings may not apply to experienced meditators; the sample may not be representative of people with long-term stress; the programme was short (eight weeks) and the long-term effects are unknown; strengths include the controlled design with a control group and objective MRI measures; weaknesses include small samples, the possibility that expectations affected self-report, and that structural change does not automatically mean a change in behaviour. Conclude with a justified view on generalisability.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): clear evaluation of generalisability to both groups, using strengths and weaknesses of the design, with a supported conclusion. Level 2 (5–8): some evaluation of generalisability with limited development. Level 1 (1–4): description of the study only.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the findings of Hölzel et al. support the biological approach's assumption that changes in behaviour and mental processes are linked to changes in the brain's structure.
parts.answer: Participants' practice of mindfulness was linked to changes in grey matter in the hippocampus and other regions, so an experience (psychological training) was associated with a structural brain change. This supports the idea that mental processes are linked to brain structure. However, the change was correlational with the programme and the direction of cause cannot be fully confirmed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: a psychological practice was linked to brain structure change; grey matter change in named regions (e.g. hippocampus); evidence the brain is affected by experience; the change is a physiological basis for mental processes; a limitation about causation or direction.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Look at this question: "Do you usually sleep for at least seven hours a night? Yes / No". Identify whether it is an open or a closed question, and explain one advantage of using this type of question.
parts.answer: Closed question: it offers a fixed choice (yes or no). Advantage: quick to answer and easy to analyse (for example, count the "yes" answers), so the data are quantitative.
parts.working: 1 mark: closed. 2 marks: one advantage developed (quick to complete, easy to code and compare, reduces variation in how answers are written).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the term social desirability bias as it applies to self-reports.
parts.answer: The tendency for participants to answer in a way that makes them look good or fits what they think is socially acceptable, rather than giving their true answer.
parts.working: 2 marks: participants answer to look good / in a socially acceptable way, not truthfully. 1 mark for a vague idea without the link to the answer given.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Outline one way a researcher could reduce social desirability bias in a questionnaire.
parts.answer: Guarantee anonymity or confidentiality so that participants feel less pressure to look good. Other valid options: neutral wording, asking about "most people" rather than the participant, or indirect questions.
parts.working: 2 marks: one method clearly outlined with the reason it reduces bias. Accept any sensible method.

stem: A researcher in Lahore asks 8 students to rate how much they agree with the statement "I exercise regularly" on a five-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). The scores are: 4, 5, 3, 4, 2, 5, 4, 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean score. Show your working.
parts.working: 1 mark for the total of 30. 1 mark for 30 ÷ 8 = 3.75.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the data from a five-point Likert scale are usually treated as ordinal rather than interval data.
parts.answer: The scale puts responses in order (strongly disagree to strongly agree), but the distance between points, for example between "agree" and "strongly agree", may not be equal for every respondent, so only the order is secure.
parts.working: 1 mark: ordinal means ranked or ordered. 1 mark: the gaps between points may not be equal. 1 mark: linked to the Likert scale in this study.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the mean may give a misleading picture of these students' exercise habits.
parts.answer: The sample is small (only 8 students), so the mean may not represent students in general. Also, the mean hides the spread of answers, which runs from 2 to 5.
parts.working: 2 marks: any one valid reason linked to the data, such as the small sample, or that the average hides the range of scores. "The mean is wrong" alone earns no marks.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher gives a happiness questionnaire (scores out of 30) to six adults in Karachi, then gives the same questionnaire again two weeks later. Time 1 scores: 22, 30, 18, 25, 27, 15. Time 2 scores: 24, 29, 20, 26, 25, 17. The pairs are (Time 1, Time 2): (22,24), (30,29), (18,20), (25,26), (27,25), (15,17).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by test-retest reliability.
parts.answer: The consistency of a measure over time: the same people complete the same test on two occasions, and their scores should be similar.
parts.working: 2 marks: consistency over time; same participants and same test on two occasions with similar scores. 1 mark for "it gives the same result".

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) for these scores, using the formula for Pearson's r. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Method: find the means (Time 1 = 22.83, Time 2 = 23.5), then sum of products of deviations divided by the square root of the product of the sums of squared deviations. 1 mark for correct method; 1 mark for correct sums; 1 mark for r = 0.97 (accept ±0.01).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why a high test-retest correlation does not, on its own, show that the questionnaire is valid.
parts.answer: A questionnaire can be consistent (reliable) and still measure the wrong thing, for example social desirability or a general mood rather than happiness. Reliability does not prove validity.
parts.working: 2 marks: reliable does not mean valid, with an explanation (for example, a consistent measure of the wrong construct).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between a structured interview and an unstructured interview.
parts.answer: Structured: the interviewer asks a fixed set of pre-set questions in the same order, and answers are often closed, which makes them easy to compare. Unstructured: the interview is flexible, follow-up questions are asked depending on the conversation, and answers are open, giving richer detail.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each type: structured = fixed questions, same order, quantitative or comparable; unstructured = flexible, follow-up questions, open-ended, rich qualitative data. Accept any clear contrast.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way that interviewer bias could affect the responses in a structured interview.
parts.answer: The interviewer's tone, facial expression or slight changes in wording may encourage some answers over others, so the responses reflect the interviewer as well as the participant, reducing validity.
parts.working: 2 marks: a specific interviewer behaviour (tone, expression, rewording) shapes participants' answers; linked to lower validity or accuracy.

stem: A questionnaire on sleep asks: "How satisfied are you with your sleep?" Participants circle one number: 1 = very dissatisfied, 2 = dissatisfied, 3 = neutral, 4 = satisfied, 5 = very satisfied.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of scale used in this question.
parts.answer: A rating scale (a numerical scale with five points), which is a closed-question format.
parts.working: 1 mark: rating (Likert-style) scale; accept "closed question with a numbered scale".

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a researcher might include a neutral midpoint (3) on this five-point scale.
parts.answer: A neutral midpoint lets participants who are undecided give a true answer, rather than being forced to choose a side, which could distort the data.
parts.working: 2 marks: a neutral option lets undecided participants answer honestly; avoids forced choice distorting results.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Outline one limitation of this type of scale.
parts.answer: The distance between points may not be equal for every respondent, and some people cluster answers near the middle or avoid the extremes (response style bias).
parts.working: 2 marks: one limitation (unequal intervals, response style bias such as central tendency or extreme responding) outlined.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term "case study" as used in psychological research.
parts.answer: An in-depth investigation of one individual, a small group or an event, using one or more methods to collect detailed data, often over time.
parts.working: 2 marks: in-depth/detailed study of one individual, group or event. 1 mark for "studying one person" with no detail on depth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one strength of using a case study to research a rare condition.
parts.answer: It gives rich, detailed data about a condition that few people have, which could not be studied in a large sample.
parts.working: 2 marks: a strength (rich detail or rare cases) with a brief explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one ethical issue that a researcher must consider when writing up a case study of a patient with brain damage.
parts.answer: Privacy and confidentiality: the patient's identity must be protected, for example by changing name and details. Informed consent must come from the patient or, if they lack capacity, from a legal representative acting in the patient's best interests.
parts.working: 2 marks: one ethical issue outlined (confidentiality, consent, risk of psychological harm, the right to withdraw). Accept any one with an explanation.

stem: Psychologists are writing a case study of Ayesha, a 17-year-old from Multan with a rare memory condition. They collect data from interviews with Ayesha and her parents, a memory test completed at two time points, and a diary kept by Ayesha.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one type of data collected in this case study.
parts.answer: Qualitative data from the interviews or the diary, or quantitative data from the memory test scores.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one valid type: interview (qualitative), diary (qualitative), memory test score (quantitative).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the researcher could improve the reliability of the case study's findings.
parts.answer: Use multiple sources of data (triangulation) and check that they agree. Or use the same standard memory test at both time points, under the same conditions.
parts.working: 2 marks: one valid suggestion with a reason, for example triangulation, a standardised test, or an independent researcher checking the coding.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one limitation of drawing general conclusions about human memory from a case study of one person.
parts.answer: Each person's brain and life experiences differ, so one person may not be typical of all people. The findings may be unique to this individual and their circumstances (low generalisability), so a general conclusion about humans could be wrong.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 for a named limitation (generalisability); 1 for explaining individual differences; 1 for linking to memory research; 1 for developing the point with an example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two methods a researcher could use to collect data in a case study of a person who has lost the use of a limb after an accident.
parts.answer: For example: a structured interview or questionnaire about daily activities (self-report); observation of the person completing everyday tasks; a psychometric test of mood or memory; a diary kept by the participant; brain imaging to see the extent of damage.
parts.working: 2 marks for each described method: 1 for naming it, 1 for how it is used in this case. Accept any two valid methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why data from a retrospective case study may be less accurate than data collected at the time of events.
parts.answer: Memories are reconstructed over time, so details can be forgotten or distorted. The person may also present events in a favourable light (social desirability), so the account can be biased.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for the memory point (forgetting, reconstruction, distortion). Up to 2 marks for the bias point (self-presentation, social desirability). Each point must be developed.

stem: A longitudinal case study follows a child, Hamza, who was raised with very limited language exposure. He is assessed at regular intervals from age 4 to age 12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength of using a longitudinal case study that follows Hamza from age 4 to age 12, rather than a single assessment.
parts.answer: The researcher can track how language develops over time, so changes can be seen. Repeated data can show whether early limited exposure has a lasting effect, which a single snapshot would miss.
parts.working: 4 marks: strength identified (1); explained (1); linked to Hamza's development and change over time (1); developed with a clear point about what a single assessment would miss (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one ethical issue specific to following a child's development over eight years.
parts.answer: The child cannot give fully informed consent, so parents or guardians must consent, and the child's privacy must be protected over the long term.
parts.working: 2 marks: one issue with an explanation (consent by guardians, long-term confidentiality, risk of later identification, or the right to withdraw).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a researcher could use a case study to investigate the effects of a rare brain injury on language. Include how the patient would be chosen and what data would be collected, and explain how the analysis would be checked for reliability.
parts.answer: Select one patient with a documented injury, obtain consent and assess their suitability. Collect baseline data (medical history, brain scan) and repeated data over time using standardised language tests, interviews, recorded speech and observation. Analyse qualitative and quantitative data, and use triangulation and a second coder to check reliability. Apply ethical safeguards such as anonymity and the right to withdraw.
parts.working: Up to 10 marks: 4 for patient selection and procedure; 3 for relevant data collection (named tools, timing); 2 for analysis and reliability; 1 for ethics. Credit any sound design.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate one strength and one weakness of your approach.
parts.answer: Strength: detailed, rich data about a rare injury that could not be obtained from a large sample. Weakness: findings cannot be generalised to other patients, and retrospective information about language before the injury may be inaccurate.
parts.working: 4 marks: one strength (2 marks, developed) and one weakness (2 marks, developed and linked to the scenario).

stem: A teacher writes a case study of Sana, a 10-year-old with dyslexia, using her school reports and the teacher's own observations of her reading in class.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one reason why the teacher's case study may be biased.
parts.answer: The teacher knows Sana and may have expectations about her progress, so observations and interpretation may be influenced (observer or researcher bias).
parts.working: 2 marks: one reason linked to the scenario (teacher expectations, reliance on school reports written by the same teacher).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to make the case study more objective.
parts.answer: Use an independent observer, or compare the teacher's notes with a standardised reading assessment.
parts.working: 2 marks: one suggestion with a reason (independent researcher, standardised test, inter-rater check).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why a researcher who is also the participant's physiotherapist may have a conflict of interest when writing up a case study of Ibrahim, a former athlete who has had a stroke.
parts.answer: The physiotherapist may want the case study to show that the treatment works, so may interpret results favourably. A personal relationship with Ibrahim may also influence what is recorded and what is left out.
parts.working: 4 marks: 1 for naming the conflict of interest; 2 for explaining how it could bias the data or interpretation, linked to the scenario; 1 for the effect on validity or objectivity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how this bias could be reduced.
parts.answer: A researcher who is not involved in Ibrahim's treatment could collect or analyse the data, or a second researcher could check the write-up.
parts.working: 2 marks: one valid suggestion with a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define covert observation.
parts.answer: The participants do not know that they are being observed, or that the observer is recording their behaviour.
parts.working: 2 marks: participants unaware / observation is hidden. 1 mark for "secret" without linking it to participants' knowledge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one ethical issue with covert observation.
parts.answer: Participants cannot give informed consent and cannot withdraw, so their privacy is invaded.
parts.working: 2 marks: one issue (consent, privacy, right to withdraw, deception) outlined with a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define time sampling.
parts.answer: Recording behaviour at fixed intervals of time (for example every 30 seconds), noting which behaviours occur in each interval.
parts.working: 2 marks: fixed intervals of time; behaviours recorded in each interval. 1 mark for "recording at set times" only.

stem: A researcher records children's play in a school playground by watching from a classroom window, without the children knowing they are being observed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify whether this is a naturalistic or a controlled observation, and whether the observer is a participant or a non-participant.
parts.answer: Naturalistic observation (in a natural setting, with no manipulation of conditions); non-participant observation (the researcher does not join in the play).
parts.working: 1 mark: naturalistic. 1 mark: non-participant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one disadvantage of the observer's position in this study.
parts.answer: The observer is far from the children, so may miss what they say or may misinterpret their behaviour without knowing the context.
parts.working: 2 marks: one valid disadvantage with an outline (cannot hear speech, misreads intent, too far away to see detail).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two observers independently recorded whether aggression occurred in each of 20 ten-second intervals in a playground. They agreed on 17 of the 20 intervals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage agreement (inter-observer reliability). Show your working.
parts.working: 1 mark for 17 ÷ 20 (or 17/20). 1 mark for 85%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why inter-observer reliability is important in an observational study.
parts.answer: It shows that different observers record the same behaviour in the same way, so the data are objective and not the result of one observer's bias. This makes the findings more trustworthy.
parts.working: 2 marks: consistency between observers, with a link to objectivity or reduced observer bias.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Operationalise "aggressive behaviour" for a time-sampled observation of children. Give two behavioural categories that are observable, specific and do not overlap.
parts.answer: For example: "Hits another child with a hand or an object." and "Pushes another child so that they move or fall." Each category describes an action that could be seen and recorded, and the two do not overlap.
parts.working: 2 marks for two categories (1 each). 1 mark for each being observable/specific, and 1 mark for the categories not overlapping. Maximum 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength of participant observation compared with non-participant observation.
parts.answer: The observer shares the group's experience, which can give an insider view of what behaviour means to the group, improving validity.
parts.working: 2 marks: strength with a clear explanation (insider understanding, richer data, better validity).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of participant observation.
parts.answer: The observer may lose objectivity, becoming too involved with the group, or may change the group's behaviour by taking part. It is also harder to record data while taking part.
parts.working: 2 marks: one weakness with an explanation (loss of objectivity, observer effect, difficulty recording).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how observer bias could affect the findings of a study on children's sharing behaviour.
parts.answer: If the observer expects boys to share less than girls, they may record more "not sharing" for boys, or interpret an ambiguous act as not sharing. The results would then reflect the observer's expectations rather than what the children actually did, reducing validity.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: definition of observer bias (1); how expectations shape recording or interpretation (1); example linked to sharing (1); effect on validity (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a researcher could carry out a naturalistic observation of children's cooperation in a primary school classroom in Lahore. Include the sampling method, the behavioural categories, how reliability would be checked and one ethical safeguard.
parts.answer: Choose a sampling method (for example time sampling every 30 seconds, using a fixed sample of children observed in turn). Define cooperation as observable behaviours (for example taking turns, helping, sharing materials), each with a clear example and non-overlapping. Two trained observers code the same lessons, and inter-observer reliability is calculated as percentage agreement. Ethics: obtain consent from the school, parents and teacher, anonymise the children, and remove any identifiable recordings.
parts.working: Up to 10 marks: 4 for a suitable sampling method and procedure; 3 for operationalised categories; 2 for reliability (inter-observer agreement); 1 for an ethical safeguard in context.

stem: A researcher observes one child for 10 minutes using time sampling with 30-second intervals. "Sharing toys" is recorded in 6 of the 20 intervals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of intervals in which sharing was recorded.
parts.working: 1 mark for 6 out of 20 intervals. 1 mark for 30%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of time sampling in this study.
parts.answer: Advantage: the observer records every interval in the same way, so the data are systematic and easy to quantify, and no interval is skipped. Disadvantage: a brief act of sharing that happens between two intervals is missed, and the record depends on the observer keeping accurate time.
parts.working: 2 marks for the advantage (systematic, quantifiable, equal coverage). 2 marks for the disadvantage (short behaviours missed between intervals, timing errors).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A supermarket researcher covertly watches shoppers and records items placed in trolleys to study impulse buying.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether covert observation of shoppers is ethically acceptable. Refer to two ethical guidelines in your answer.
parts.answer: Against: shoppers do not give informed consent, have no right to withdraw, and are deceived about being observed, which invades privacy. For: shopping takes place in a public place where people have limited expectations of privacy, and if no identifiable data are recorded and no harm results, the invasion is small; but without debriefing the shoppers cannot be told about the study afterwards.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: a named guideline with explanation (informed consent or deception, 2 marks); a second guideline (privacy, right to withdraw, debrief, harm, 2 marks); a balanced judgement based on public setting or anonymity (2 marks).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one alternative method that would avoid covert observation.
parts.answer: Use an overt observation with the shoppers' consent, or ask shoppers to complete a survey about their impulse purchases.
parts.working: 2 marks: one valid method with a brief justification.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether you would expect a positive, negative or zero correlation for each of these pairs of variables: (i) hours of revision and exam score; (ii) hours of television watched and the price of rice in a city; (iii) time spent exercising and resting heart rate.
parts.answer: (i) positive; (ii) zero; (iii) negative.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept reasoned answers that are consistent with the expected direction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term "correlation coefficient".
parts.answer: A number between −1 and +1 that shows the strength and direction of the relationship between two co-variables.
parts.working: 2 marks: a number that gives strength and direction of the relationship. 1 mark for "a measure of relationship" only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the range of values a correlation coefficient can take.
parts.answer: −1 to +1 (inclusive).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a correlation cannot establish that one variable causes the other.
parts.answer: A correlation only shows that two variables are related. Neither variable is manipulated, so the direction of cause cannot be determined, and a third variable may be causing both.
parts.working: 2 marks: no manipulation / direction of cause unknown; third variable could explain the link. Accept either with explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define "third variable" and give an example from a study of exam stress.
parts.answer: A variable that is not measured in the study but influences both of the measured co-variables. For example, a student's general motivation could affect both how many hours they revise and how well they perform in the exam.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition (not measured, affects both co-variables). 1 mark: explained link to both variables. 1 mark: valid example in an exam-stress context.

stem: A psychologist asks 7 students how many hours a week they spent on social media (X) and records their scores on a wellbeing scale out of 100 (Y). The pairs (hours, score) are: (4, 78), (10, 60), (6, 70), (12, 52), (8, 66), (2, 88), (15, 58).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rank the scores for each variable (rank 1 = lowest). Calculate Spearman's rho, showing the differences in ranks (d), d² and the sum of d². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: ranks correct for both variables. 1 mark: d and d² correct. 1 mark: Σd² = 110. 1 mark: rho = 1 − (6 × 110) ÷ (7 × 48) = -0.96 (accept ±0.01).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a conclusion about the relationship, using the value of rho. Refer to correlation rather than cause.
parts.answer: There is a strong negative correlation: students who spend more hours on social media tend to have lower wellbeing scores. This does not show that social media use causes lower wellbeing.
parts.working: 1 mark: direction and strength of the relationship (strong negative, matching the value of rho). 1 mark: a correlation does not show cause.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Spearman's rho is used rather than Pearson's r when the data are ranks or ordinal.
parts.answer: Pearson's r assumes interval or ratio data with a linear relationship. Spearman's rho works on ranks and does not assume equal intervals between values.
parts.working: 2 marks: Pearson's needs interval/ratio data; Spearman's uses ranks and suits ordinal data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis for a study of hours of social media use and wellbeing.
parts.answer: There is no relationship between hours of social media use and wellbeing scores.
parts.working: 2 marks: "no relationship" with both variables named. 1 mark if "no difference" is written (wrong for a correlation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write one directional (one-tailed) hypothesis and one non-directional (two-tailed) hypothesis for a study of phone use before bed and sleep quality in teenagers in Karachi.
parts.answer: Directional: Teenagers who use their phone in bed for more than one hour before sleep will report poorer sleep quality. Non-directional: There is a relationship between phone use in bed and sleep quality.
parts.working: 2 marks: directional hypothesis with direction and both variables operationalised. 2 marks: non-directional hypothesis stating a relationship without a direction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A scattergram of 30 participants shows points closely clustered around a line sloping downward from left to right. Describe the correlation shown.
parts.answer: A strong negative correlation: as one variable increases, the other decreases consistently.
parts.working: 1 mark: negative. 1 mark: strong (points closely clustered around the line).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the researcher should check the scattergram for outliers before reporting the correlation.
parts.answer: An outlier is an extreme pair of scores that lies far from the rest. It can pull the line of best fit and change the value of r, so the researcher should check whether an outlier is an error or a genuine score, and report how it was treated.
parts.working: 2 marks: outlier defined as an extreme score; it can distort r (strength or direction), so it should be checked or reported before the result is interpreted.

stem: A researcher records weekly practice hours (X) and reaction time in milliseconds (Y) for 8 students. The pairs (practice hours, reaction time) are: (2, 410), (5, 380), (1, 450), (8, 330), (4, 395), (7, 355), (3, 420), (6, 362).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rho for these 8 pairs. Show your working for the sum of d². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for correct ranks; 1 mark for d and d²; 1 mark for Σd² = 166; 1 mark for rho = -0.98 (accept ±0.01).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Interpret the value of rho. Comment on the size of the sample (n = 8) when deciding how much confidence to place in the result.
parts.answer: The value shows a strong negative correlation: more practice hours go with shorter reaction times. With only 8 pairs, one or two unusual scores could change rho substantially, so the result is uncertain and should be tested with a larger sample.
parts.working: 1 mark: strong negative relationship (direction and strength). 1 mark: correlational, not causal. 1 mark: small sample means results are unstable or may not generalise.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A study of 200 teenagers in Lahore found a correlation of +0.62 between daily screen time and anxiety scores. Explain two reasons why this correlation does not show that screen time causes anxiety.
parts.answer: A third variable, such as lack of physical activity or family pressure, could cause both more screen time and more anxiety. Reverse causation is also possible: anxious teenagers may use screens more to cope with their feelings.
parts.working: 2 marks per reason: naming the reason (third variable, reverse causation, or sample/measurement issue) and explaining how it accounts for the correlation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how an experiment could test whether screen time causes anxiety.
parts.answer: Randomly allocate participants to a limited screen-time condition or a normal screen-time condition. Measure anxiety before and after, and control extraneous variables such as sleep and exercise.
parts.working: 1 mark: screen time is manipulated as the IV. 1 mark: random allocation and control of extraneous variables. 1 mark: anxiety measured as the DV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a coefficient of +0.85 and a coefficient of −0.85 in terms of direction and strength.
parts.answer: Both show equally strong relationships (the size of the number, 0.85, is the same, so the strength is equal). The sign shows direction: +0.85 is a strong positive relationship, where the variables rise together, and −0.85 is a strong negative relationship, where one rises as the other falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: strength is the same (value sizes equal). 1 mark: positive means both rise together. 1 mark: negative means one rises as the other falls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A researcher reports rho = 0.20 for 500 participants and describes the relationship as "strong". Evaluate this claim in two or three sentences.
parts.answer: The claim is not justified. A coefficient of 0.20 is a weak relationship, even though the sample is large. Large samples can make small correlations statistically significant, but significance does not make the relationship strong.
parts.working: 1 mark: 0.20 is weak. 1 mark: a large sample does not change the strength of the correlation. 1 mark: significance and strength are different things.

stem: In a hypothetical study, 40 students are divided into three groups. Each group memorises a list of 20 words, then recalls as many as possible. The groups had been awake for 0, 1 or 5 hours before the task. The number of words recalled is counted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this study.
parts.answer: IV: hours of sleep deprivation (0, 1 or 5 hours). DV: the number of words recalled.
parts.working: 1 mark for the IV (the variable the researcher changes). 1 mark for the DV (the variable measured).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define an extraneous variable and give one example from this study.
parts.answer: A variable other than the IV that could affect the DV if it is not controlled, for example the time of day the students were tested, or how easy the words were to remember.
parts.working: 1 mark: a variable (not the IV) that could affect the DV. 1 mark: a valid example from this study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a confounding variable.
parts.answer: A variable that changes systematically with the IV, so that its effect on the DV cannot be separated from the effect of the IV.
parts.working: 2 marks: changes systematically with the IV and makes the effect of the IV impossible to separate. 1 mark for "an extra variable" alone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by random allocation and why it is used.
parts.answer: Each participant has an equal chance of being placed in any condition, for example by using a random number generator or drawing names from a hat. This spreads individual differences, such as intelligence or memory skill, evenly across the groups, so they are less likely to act as confounding variables.
parts.working: 2 marks for what random allocation is (equal chance of each condition). 2 marks for why it is used (spreads individual differences, reduces confounding).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of a repeated measures design compared with an independent groups design.
parts.answer: Advantage: each participant acts as their own control, so individual differences are removed and fewer participants are needed. Disadvantage: order effects, such as practice or fatigue, may affect the second performance, although counterbalancing can reduce this.
parts.working: 2 marks for the advantage (controls individual differences, fewer participants) with explanation. 2 marks for the disadvantage (order effects) with explanation.

stem: Four participants each complete two conditions in a repeated measures design: condition A (a quiet room) and condition B (a noisy room), both with the same reading test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how counterbalancing would be used for these four participants, and why it is used.
parts.answer: Two participants (for example 1 and 2) complete condition A (quiet room) and then condition B (noisy room). The other two (3 and 4) complete B and then A. Each condition is done first equally often, so any practice or fatigue effect is spread evenly across both conditions and cannot be the sole cause of the difference.
parts.working: 1 mark: participants split into two orders. 1 mark: example for four participants. 2 marks: explains that order effects are balanced across conditions so they do not bias the comparison.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a hypothetical study, participants memorised a list of 20 words. Group A (imagery instructions) recalled a mean of 12.5 words. Group B (repetition instructions) recalled a mean of 9.0 words.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the two means. Then calculate the percentage by which Group A's mean is higher than Group B's mean. Give the percentage to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Difference = 3.5 words; 3.5 ÷ 9.0 × 100 = 38.9% higher
parts.working: 1 mark: difference = 3.5 words. 1 mark: divide by Group B's mean (the baseline), not Group A's. 1 mark: 38.9%.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a study on the effect of noise on concentration, participants knew they were in the "noisy" group and were told that the researcher expected them to perform worse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how demand characteristics could affect the results in this study.
parts.answer: The participants may work out the hypothesis (that noise affects performance) and try to please the researcher, or deliberately perform worse, so the results reflect their guesses rather than the effect of noise.
parts.working: 2 marks: participants become aware of the hypothesis; their behaviour changes to fit or please. 1 mark for a vague mention of "participants guessing".

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to reduce demand characteristics in this study.
parts.answer: Use a single-blind design, so participants do not know which condition they are in, or give a cover story about the purpose of the study.
parts.working: 2 marks: one valid method with a reason (single-blind, cover story, more natural task).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A field experiment tests whether a "Please don't litter" sign reduces litter in a park in Karachi. The sign is present in one park and absent in another park of similar size.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength of this field experiment compared with a laboratory experiment.
parts.answer: It has high ecological validity: the littering happens in a natural setting and the visitors do not know they are in a study, so their behaviour is less affected by demand characteristics.
parts.working: 4 marks: strength named (1); explained (1); linked to the park setting and the sign (1); developed with the effect on the results (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of this field experiment.
parts.answer: Many extraneous variables cannot be controlled, such as the weather, the number of visitors, or differences between the parks, so it is hard to be sure that the sign caused any difference. Visitors also cannot give informed consent.
parts.working: 4 marks: weakness named (1); explained (1); linked to the scenario (1); developed (1). Accept lack of control or ethical issues.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a matched pairs design could be used to test whether caffeine improves reaction time in adults. Explain how the participants would be matched.
parts.answer: Pair participants on a relevant variable, such as baseline reaction time measured in a first session or age. Within each pair, randomly allocate one participant to the caffeine drink and the other to a placebo drink. Measure reaction time under standard conditions. Because each pair starts with similar baseline reactions, individual differences are controlled, and the difference between pair members can be attributed to caffeine.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: a relevant matching variable chosen and justified (2); random allocation within pairs with a placebo control (2); measurement and control of the procedure (2).

stem: A researcher tests reading speed (words per minute) in three conditions: no music, classical music and rap music, with 12 participants in each condition. The mean reading speeds are: no music 210, classical 198, rap 183.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in reading speed from the "no music" condition to the "rap music" condition. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark: difference of 27 words per minute. 1 mark: 12.9% (divide by the no-music mean).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an independent groups design may be used here, and identify one extraneous variable that should be controlled.
parts.answer: An independent groups design means each condition uses different participants, so participants do not read the same passage three times and practice effects are avoided. Individual differences, such as reading ability, must then be spread evenly by random allocation. One extraneous variable is the difficulty of the passage, which should be kept the same across conditions.
parts.working: 2 marks: independent groups design justified (no repeated reading, no order effects). 2 marks: an extraneous variable identified and a control explained (for example standardised passage, same room, random allocation of reading ability).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher predicts that background music reduces reading comprehension. Participants read a passage and then answer questions on it; the score is the DV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a directional hypothesis and a null hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: Directional: Participants who read with background music will score lower on a comprehension test than participants who read in silence. Null: There is no difference in comprehension test scores between participants who read with background music and those who read in silence.
parts.working: 1 mark: directional hypothesis with IV and DV named. 1 mark: null hypothesis. 1 mark: comprehension test named as the measure (operationalised DV).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one extraneous variable and explain how standardising the procedure controls it.
parts.answer: Prior reading ability differs between people. Using the same text, the same time limit, the same instructions and the same room for everyone makes sure that only the presence of music varies between conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: a named extraneous variable (for example prior reading ability). 2 marks: standardisation explained as keeping everything else the same, so only the music differs.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two physiological measures used in psychological research.
parts.answer: For example: heart rate, skin conductance (galvanic skin response), cortisol levels in saliva, EEG, or fMRI.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid measure named (any two of the above or similar).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define objectivity in the context of physiological measures.
parts.answer: Physiological measures are recorded by equipment, so the data do not depend on the researcher's interpretation or the participant's own report of how they feel.
parts.working: 2 marks: recorded by machines or without judgement; not dependent on subjective reports or the researcher's interpretation. 1 mark for "not biased" alone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one ethical issue when using a physiological measure such as blood sampling.
parts.answer: The procedure is invasive, so it may cause discomfort, pain or anxiety, and the participant must give informed consent and be free to withdraw.
parts.working: 2 marks: one ethical issue (invasive, discomfort, consent, right to withdraw, data protection) with a link to blood sampling.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what skin conductance (galvanic skin response) measures, and why a change in it could indicate arousal.
parts.answer: It measures the electrical conductance of the skin, which increases when sweat glands become more active. Sweat gland activity increases under sympathetic nervous system arousal, so higher conductance indicates higher arousal.
parts.working: 2 marks: measures skin conductance (sweat gland activity); linked to sympathetic arousal.

stem: Saliva samples were collected from 12 students 30 minutes before and 30 minutes after a mock exam. The mean cortisol level was 12.4 nmol/L before the exam and 18.6 nmol/L after.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean cortisol. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark: increase of 6.2 nmol/L. 1 mark: 50.0% (divide by the before mean).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one conclusion from these data, and explain why the study cannot show that the exam caused the increase.
parts.answer: Cortisol rose after the mock exam, suggesting that the students' stress response increased. However, there was no control group, so other factors such as the time of day or the anticipation of the test could explain the rise.
parts.working: 1 mark: conclusion (cortisol increased, so stress may have increased). 2 marks: explanation (no control group; other extraneous factors such as time of day or anticipation).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of using physiological measures as the dependent variable in a study of stress.
parts.answer: Strength: the measure is objective and recorded continuously, so it is less affected by demand characteristics or social desirability than self-report. Weakness: physiological arousal does not equal stress, because heart rate and cortisol can also rise with exercise, caffeine or excitement, so the measure may not be valid for stress alone.
parts.working: 2 marks for the strength (objective, less bias, with explanation). 2 marks for the weakness (arousal is not specific to stress, with explanation).

stem: A researcher records the heart rate (beats per minute) of one participant at five points during a task: 78, 82, 75, 90, 85.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean heart rate. Show your working.
parts.working: 1 mark for the total of 410. 1 mark for 82 bpm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this mean cannot be generalised to the population.
parts.answer: It comes from only one participant, and heart rate differs between people because of factors such as fitness and general health, so one person's mean is not representative.
parts.working: 2 marks: one participant is not representative; individual differences in heart rate.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an increase in heart rate during a task might not be a reliable indicator of stress.
parts.answer: Heart rate rises with many types of arousal, including physical exercise, caffeine, excitement or positive emotions, so it is not specific to stress. The measure therefore lacks validity as a stress indicator unless these other factors are controlled, for example by measuring heart rate at rest and asking participants not to exercise or drink caffeine beforehand.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: heart rate is non-specific arousal (1); named other causes such as exercise, caffeine or excitement (1); the validity problem stated (1); a control suggested (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how fMRI measures brain activity, and give one limitation of using fMRI to study emotion.
parts.answer: fMRI detects changes in blood oxygenation (the BOLD signal). Brain regions that are more active use more oxygen, so blood flow to them increases and the magnetic signal changes. Limitation: fMRI is correlational, so an active region does not prove that it causes an emotion. Also, the BOLD response is slow, so fMRI cannot track rapid emotional changes in the way that EEG can.
parts.working: 2 marks: explanation of the BOLD signal (blood oxygenation linked to activity). 2 marks: one limitation developed (correlational, poor temporal resolution or expensive equipment limiting use).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a researcher could use EEG to compare brain activity when participants watch a frightening video compared with a neutral video.
parts.answer: Place electrodes on the scalp and record EEG while each participant watches each video. Use a repeated measures design with counterbalancing of video order. Compare the frequency and amplitude of brain waves (for example alpha and beta activity) between the two conditions. Obtain informed consent and tell participants they can withdraw at any time.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: a suitable procedure for EEG recording (2); a sensible design with counterbalancing (2); what is compared and how (1); a relevant ethical safeguard (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the use of EEG in this study, referring to one strength and one weakness.
parts.answer: Strength: EEG is non-invasive and has good temporal resolution, so it can show rapid changes in brain activity as the video unfolds. Weakness: EEG has poor spatial resolution, so it cannot show exactly which emotional brain structures are active, and muscle movement can add electrical noise.
