parts.working: 2 marks per evaluated point: strength (non-invasive, good time resolution, explained); weakness (poor spatial resolution or electrical noise, explained).

stem: A researcher measures the resting heart rate of one participant before and after a 5-minute caffeine drink. Before: 72 bpm. After: 84 bpm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in heart rate. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark: increase of 12 bpm. 1 mark: 16.7%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this result alone cannot show that caffeine caused the increase.
parts.answer: There was no control group, so other factors, such as the time of day, anticipation of the drink, or exercise, could explain the increase. A single measure before and after cannot separate these effects from the caffeine.
parts.working: 2 marks: no control group / other extraneous variables named and explained.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A study of 60 participants finds a correlation of +0.71 between salivary cortisol levels and self-reported anxiety scores.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what this correlation shows and what it does not show, referring to both the physiological measure and the self-report measure.
parts.answer: It shows a strong positive relationship: participants with higher cortisol also tend to report higher anxiety. It does not show that cortisol causes anxiety, since the direction is unknown and a third variable could cause both. Cortisol varies with the time of day and with individual differences, and self-report can be affected by social desirability, so neither measure is perfectly valid.
parts.working: 1 mark: strong positive relationship shown. 1 mark: not causal (direction unknown or third variable). 2 marks: a limitation of the cortisol measure and a limitation of the self-report measure, each developed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to make the cortisol measurement more valid.
parts.answer: Collect all saliva samples at the same time of day, so that natural daily variation in cortisol does not affect the comparison.
parts.working: 2 marks: one suggestion with a reason linked to daily variation in cortisol or standardised sampling time.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two features of the physical environment of a shop that could influence a consumer's behaviour.
parts.answer: For example: background music (tempo or volume), lighting, scent, colour, the layout of aisles, temperature or the level of crowding.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid feature named (any two). Do not accept "the shop" or "the staff".

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define "scent congruence" and explain why a retailer might use it.
parts.answer: Scent congruence means that the smell in the store matches the product being sold, for example a bakery smell in a bakery. Retailers use it because a matching scent can make the product seem more appealing and attractive to buy.
parts.working: 2 marks: the scent matches the product (congruence defined); linked to making the product more appealing. 1 mark for a vague definition.

stem: A hypothetical study: 40 shoppers are randomly allocated to a supermarket aisle playing either slow music (about 60 beats per minute) or fast music (about 120 beats per minute). The time each shopper spends in the store is recorded. Mean time: slow music 28.4 minutes; fast music 21.9 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in mean time spent in the store between the two groups.
parts.working: 1 mark for 6.5 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one conclusion that could be drawn from this hypothetical study.
parts.answer: Slower background music is associated with shoppers spending longer in the store, suggesting that tempo affects how long shoppers stay.
parts.working: 2 marks: a conclusion that links tempo to time in store, worded tentatively (for example "suggests"). 1 mark for a conclusion with no link to the data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why random allocation of shoppers to the two music conditions was used, and what it controls.
parts.answer: Random allocation spreads individual differences, such as shopping habits, mood and how much time shoppers have, equally across the two groups. This means that any difference in time spent is more likely to be due to the tempo of the music.
parts.working: 1 mark: spreads individual differences across groups. 1 mark: reduces confounding variables. 1 mark: difference can be attributed to music tempo.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a supermarket study, eye-tracking equipment records how long shoppers look at a shelf display before they move on.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest one other measure of consumer behaviour that could be used in a supermarket study of shelf displays, and explain how it could be operationalised.
parts.answer: For example: the number of items picked up from a display, counted each time a shopper lifts an item and places it in their trolley. Operationalised as a specific, observable action that can be recorded in a tally during set time periods.
parts.working: 2 marks for a valid measure of consumer behaviour (for example, items taken, dwell time, purchases). 2 marks for a precise operational definition that is observable and can be recorded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why sales data might be a better measure than eye-tracking data for deciding whether a display changes buying.
parts.answer: Sales data record actual purchases, not just whether shoppers looked at a display, so they show the behaviour that matters to the retailer and are more valid for this question.
parts.working: 2 marks: sales data measure purchasing (behaviour that matters) rather than attention; linked to validity.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the nature–nurture debate in relation to consumer buying.
parts.answer: Nature: some preferences, such as a liking for sweet tastes, may be innate. Nurture: many buying preferences are learned from culture, family and advertising, so they vary between societies.
parts.working: 2 marks: one side of the debate (nature or nurture) linked to consumer preferences; both sides for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why research on the physical environment is reductionist.
parts.answer: It explains buying behaviour in terms of one or two physical stimuli, such as music tempo, and ignores thoughts, mood, budget and social influences that also affect what people buy.
parts.working: 2 marks: reduces behaviour to physical stimuli, with an explanation of what is ignored.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment to test whether the smell of baking bread in a bakery increases sales of bread. Identify the IV, the DV, a suitable sample and two controls.
parts.answer: IV: the presence of the bread scent (scent present or absent, for example on alternate days or in matched bakeries). DV: number of loaves sold in a set period. Sample: all customers in the chosen bakeries over the same time periods. Controls: same staff, same products, same prices and opening hours; the scent is applied in the same way in each condition.
parts.working: 1 mark for the IV. 1 mark for the DV (measurable). 1 mark for a sample described. 1 mark for each of two named controls (2 marks). 1 mark for a sensible design choice (alternate days or matched sites). Maximum 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define "brand loyalty" and give one example from a consumer's purchases.
parts.answer: A consistent preference for, and repeated purchase of, one brand over its competitors. Example: buying the same brand of tea every week even when cheaper brands are on the shelf.
parts.working: 2 marks: consistent repeated purchase of one brand over competitors. 1 mark: a valid example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two features of product packaging that can influence a consumer's perception of the product.
parts.answer: For example: colour, shape, size, the logo or font, the amount of information shown, or a premium-looking material.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid feature (any two).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the door-in-the-face technique used in sales.
parts.answer: The salesperson first makes a very large request, which the customer refuses. The salesperson then makes a smaller request, which the customer is more likely to accept because it seems reasonable by comparison.
parts.working: 1 mark: a large request is made first. 1 mark: the customer refuses. 1 mark: the smaller request is more likely to be accepted by contrast (or through a sense of obligation). Accept a valid example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the price–quality heuristic in relation to a £50 jacket sold in a city shop.
parts.answer: Consumers may use price as a cue for quality: an expensive jacket is assumed to be better made, even without direct evidence. This is a quick mental shortcut that makes the decision easier, and it can shape how valuable the jacket seems to the shopper.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: the heuristic named and defined (1); price used as an indicator of quality (1); applied to the £50 jacket (1); the effect on the decision or perceived value (1).

stem: In a hypothetical study, 60 participants taste the same yogurt. Half are given it in a plain white pot and half in a bright, illustrated pot. They rate its taste on a 1–10 scale. Mean taste rating: plain pot 6.2; illustrated pot 7.1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: IV: type of packaging (plain white pot or bright illustrated pot). DV: taste rating on a 1–10 scale.
parts.working: 1 mark for the IV. 1 mark for the DV, which must be measurable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage difference between the two means, relative to the plain pot's mean. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark: difference of 0.9. 1 mark: 14.5%.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how repeated exposure to a brand's logo could increase a consumer's liking of the brand.
parts.answer: This is the mere exposure effect: repeated exposure to a stimulus makes it familiar, and familiarity tends to increase liking. Familiar brands feel safer, so consumers are more likely to choose them without thinking carefully about alternatives.
parts.working: 1 mark: named as the mere exposure effect (or repeated exposure → familiarity). 2 marks: explanation that familiarity increases liking and makes the brand feel safer or easier to choose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one debate about whether research on sales techniques can be generalised to all consumers.
parts.answer: Techniques such as the foot-in-the-door effect have been studied mainly with samples from Western countries, so their effects on consumers in other cultures may differ. Individual differences in how people respond to pressure also limit generalisation.
parts.working: 2 marks: a clear debate (generalisability, cultural bias, individual differences) with a supporting point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why research on sales techniques is reductionist.
parts.answer: It explains a purchase in terms of one technique, such as the order of requests, and ignores the customer's need for the product, their budget, emotional state and social context.
parts.working: 2 marks: reduces buying to one technique, with an explanation of what is ignored.

stem: A shop sells a shampoo at £18.50 a bottle. A 2-for-£30 offer is available this week.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the saving per bottle when two bottles are bought under the offer, and express it as a percentage of the normal price. Give the percentage to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Normal price for two = 2 × £18.50 = £37.00. Offer price = £30.00. Saving = £7.00, or £3.50 per bottle. 7 ÷ 37 × 100 = 18.9%
parts.working: 1 mark: normal price for two bottles = £37.00. 1 mark: saving = £7.00 (£3.50 per bottle). 1 mark: 18.9% of the normal price.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one psychological reason why a shopper might buy two bottles under this offer when they only need one.
parts.answer: Shoppers may feel that they are getting a bargain, and the normal price acts as an anchor so the saving seems large, or they may fear losing the saving if they do not take it up.
parts.working: 2 marks: one psychological reason (anchoring, perceived bargain, loss aversion) explained.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a study to test whether larger pack sizes encourage shoppers to buy more rice. State the IV, the DV, the sample, and two ways to control extraneous variables.
parts.answer: IV: pack size (1 kg or 500 g pack of the same rice, same price per kg). DV: the amount of rice (kg) bought per customer, from till data. Sample: customers in several supermarkets in one city over the same weeks. Controls: same shelf position and price per kg, the same store layout, and the same time period for each condition.
parts.working: 1 mark IV. 1 mark DV (measurable). 1 mark sample. 1 mark design (repeated or matched stores). 2 marks for two controls. Maximum 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term "heuristic" and give one example of a heuristic that could affect a consumer's choice.
parts.answer: A heuristic is a mental shortcut that simplifies a decision and reduces the effort needed to choose. Example: the availability heuristic, where a shopper chooses the brand they can recall most easily, or the price–quality heuristic.
parts.working: 2 marks: definition as a mental shortcut that reduces effort. 1 mark: a valid heuristic named as an example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between impulse buying and planned buying.
parts.answer: Impulse buying is sudden, unplanned and emotional, often triggered by cues in the store. Planned buying is deliberate, based on a shopping list or prior research.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid difference (any two): unplanned vs planned; emotional or quick vs deliberate; in-store cues vs prior decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define "cognitive dissonance" and describe how it could occur after a consumer buys an expensive phone.
parts.answer: Cognitive dissonance is the discomfort felt when a person holds conflicting thoughts, such as after making a choice. After buying the phone, the consumer may notice its drawbacks or the cheaper alternatives, and then reduce the discomfort by focusing on its good features.
parts.working: 2 marks: definition (discomfort from conflicting thoughts or after a decision). 2 marks: description linked to the expensive phone (noticing drawbacks or alternatives, reducing discomfort by justification).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the availability heuristic could lead a shopper to choose a brand that is advertised most often.
parts.answer: The availability heuristic means judging how popular or good something is by how easily examples come to mind. A brand that is advertised often is easier to recall, so the shopper may judge it to be more popular or better, and choose it without comparing other brands.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: definition of the availability heuristic (1); frequent adverts make the brand easy to recall (1); the recall is judged as popularity or quality (1); the shopper skips comparison or chooses quickly (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the rational choice model of consumer decision-making.
parts.answer: Consumers consider all the available options and weigh up the costs and benefits of each. They then choose the option that gives them the greatest satisfaction, or utility. The model assumes the consumer has complete information and reasons logically.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: consumers consider all available options (1); evaluate costs and benefits logically (1); choose the option that maximises utility or satisfaction (1); assumes full information and logical reasoning (1).

stem: In a hypothetical study, a supermarket display of 24 jams and a display of 6 jams are compared. At the 24-jam display, 60 shoppers stopped and 3 bought a jam. At the 6-jam display, 30 shoppers stopped and 9 bought a jam.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of shoppers who stopped and bought a jam in each display. Give each answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for the 24-jam display (5.0%). 1 mark for the 6-jam display (30.0%).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Conclude what the data suggest about choice overload, and explain one limitation of this hypothetical study.
parts.answer: The larger display attracted more shoppers to stop, but far fewer of them went on to buy, which suggests that too much choice may reduce buying. Limitation: the two displays may have been in different parts of the store or on different days, so location or customer numbers could account for the difference rather than the number of jams.
parts.working: 2 marks: conclusion about choice overload, linked to the percentages (more stop but fewer buy). 2 marks: one limitation explained, such as confounding by location or time.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the rational choice model of consumer decision-making. Refer to at least one issue or debate in your answer, such as reductionism or the nature–nurture debate.
parts.answer: Strengths: the model gives a clear, testable account of how consumers should choose, and it has practical use in pricing and marketing. Weaknesses: consumers rarely have complete information or the time to weigh every option, so they use heuristics (bounded rationality). The model is reductionist because it treats choice as purely cost-benefit and ignores emotion, social pressure and habits. The nature–nurture debate also applies: the model assumes an innate capacity to calculate, whereas learned habits and culture shape choices. Overall, the model is useful as an idealised standard, but it does not describe most real decisions.
parts.working: Up to 10 marks: description and at least two evaluative points each with a strength or weakness and an example (up to 6); a named issue or debate discussed with reasons (up to 2); a balanced conclusion (up to 2). Credit use of bounded rationality, heuristics or emotion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a shopper in Lahore could be influenced by social proof when choosing a mobile phone.
parts.answer: Social proof: people look at others' choices as evidence of the best option. A shopper may choose a phone because many friends or family members use it, or because an online review site labels it a "best seller" and so assumes it must be good.
parts.working: 2 marks per way: a named mechanism (friends' choices, bestseller label, online reviews) with an explanation of how it guides the decision.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline the debate about whether consumers are rational when making purchases.
parts.answer: Economic models assume that consumers are rational and maximise utility, but research shows that people use heuristics and biases, so many decisions are not fully rational.
parts.working: 2 marks: outline of both sides (rational model versus evidence of heuristics and biases).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a questionnaire study to find out whether shoppers feel regret after choosing from a large range of products. Identify the sample, the design, one closed and one open question, and one ethical consideration.
parts.answer: Sample: adults who bought a product in the last month, recruited from a shopping centre (opportunity sample) with consent. Design: a self-report questionnaire completed shortly after purchase. Closed question: "On a scale of 1 (no regret) to 5 (strong regret), how much do you regret your purchase?" Open question: "What, if anything, made you unsure about your choice?" Ethics: participants can refuse or withdraw, and their answers are anonymous.
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable sample. 1 mark: design (questionnaire, timing after purchase). 1 mark: a closed question. 1 mark: an open question. 2 marks: one ethical consideration explained (consent, anonymity, withdrawal). Maximum 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two features of an advertisement that use an emotional appeal.
parts.answer: For example: music that creates a warm or exciting mood, close-up images of happy people, a story that tugs at the heartstrings, humour, or images of fear.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid feature (any two).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define "celebrity endorsement" and give one reason it might persuade consumers.
parts.answer: A well-known person who appears in an advert to promote a product. Consumers may transfer their positive feelings about the celebrity to the product, so they become more likely to buy it.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition (well-known person promoting a product). 2 marks: a reason explained, such as transfer of liking or trust in the celebrity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define "fear appeal" and give one example of a fear appeal in an advertisement in Pakistan.
parts.answer: An advert that warns of harmful consequences if people do not act, in order to motivate a change in behaviour. Example: a road-safety advert showing the consequences of not wearing a helmet on a motorbike.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition (warning of harm to motivate change). 1 mark: linked to behaviour change. 1 mark: a valid example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how repetition of an advert can increase brand recognition.
parts.answer: Repeated exposure strengthens memory for the advert, so the brand becomes easier to recall at the point of purchase. Familiarity also builds, and familiar stimuli tend to be liked more (the mere exposure effect), which makes a consumer more likely to choose that brand.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: repetition strengthens memory (1); recall at the point of purchase (1); familiarity (1); increased liking leads to choice (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how a mobile phone company in Lahore could use humour in an advert to persuade young consumers.
parts.answer: For example, a short comic sketch in which a student's old phone repeatedly fails at a crucial moment, and the new phone saves the day. Humour captures attention and creates a positive mood, so the brand becomes associated with enjoyment and reliability.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: a specific suggestion suited to the young audience (1); how humour gains attention (1); a positive mood or emotional association with the brand (1); a sensible reason for the local audience (1).

stem: In a hypothetical study, 50 participants watch an advert for the same drink, either with a celebrity endorser or without one. Purchase intention is rated on a 1–7 scale. Mean with celebrity: 5.2. Mean without celebrity: 4.1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the two means, and the percentage by which the mean with the celebrity is higher than the mean without. Give the percentage to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Difference = 1.1 points; 1.1 ÷ 4.1 × 100 = 26.8%
parts.working: 1 mark: difference of 1.1. 1 mark: divide by the without-celebrity mean (4.1). 1 mark: 26.8%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the IV and the DV, and state whether this is a true experiment.
parts.answer: IV: presence of a celebrity endorser (with or without). DV: purchase intention rating on a 1–7 scale. It is a true experiment if participants are randomly allocated to the two conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark for IV and DV correctly identified. 1 mark: true experiment only with random allocation of participants.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the debate about whether adverts can influence buying without the consumer being aware of it.
parts.answer: Some researchers argue that repeated and emotional exposure shapes preferences below conscious awareness. Others argue that evidence for subliminal persuasion is weak, and most advertising works through conscious processing of the message.
parts.working: 2 marks: outline of both sides of the debate (unconscious influence versus conscious processing).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why research on advertising is reductionist.
parts.answer: It reduces the decision to one feature of the advert, such as a celebrity or a slogan, and ignores personal values, past experience and the wider social and cultural context.
parts.working: 2 marks: reduces buying to one feature, with an explanation of what is ignored.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of fear appeals in anti-smoking adverts. Include a discussion of one ethical issue in your answer.
parts.answer: Strengths: fear appeals can capture attention and prompt people to think about the consequences of smoking, and evidence suggests that strong, specific threats can change intentions. Weaknesses: fear that is too strong may lead to avoidance, denial or fatalism, so the message does not change behaviour; the effect may depend on whether the viewer believes they can act (self-efficacy). Ethical issue: adverts shown to children or to people already anxious may cause distress without giving them a way to act, so there is a responsibility to balance the threat with clear advice on quitting. Overall, fear appeals work best when they combine a credible threat with a specific, achievable action.
parts.working: Up to 10 marks: at least two evaluative points (strength or weakness) each developed with evidence or example (up to 6); a discussion of one ethical issue (up to 2); a balanced conclusion (up to 2). Credit the role of self-efficacy and avoidance responses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a study to test whether humour increases recall of a brand name in an advert. Identify the IV, the DV, the design, the sample, and one ethical safeguard.
parts.answer: IV: advert with humour versus the same advert without humour. DV: number of brand names recalled after a 10-minute filler task (or a memory test). Design: independent groups with random allocation, so participants see only one version. Sample: adults recruited from a university or shopping centre, matched for age and gender where possible. Ethics: informed consent, the right to withdraw, and debriefing after the study.
parts.working: 1 mark: IV. 1 mark: DV (measurable). 1 mark: design with random allocation. 1 mark: sample described. 2 marks: one ethical safeguard explained. Maximum 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define "personal space" and identify one factor that affects how much personal space people need.
parts.answer: The invisible zone around a person that they feel is their own, and into which others should not come without permission. Factors: culture, familiarity with the other person, gender, age, or the setting (for example a crowded lift or an empty bank counter).
parts.working: 2 marks: definition (invisible zone around a person that others should respect). 1 mark: a valid factor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define "crowding" and identify one way it can affect a shopper's behaviour.
parts.answer: Crowding is the feeling of having too many people in a space, which causes stress or discomfort. As a result, shoppers may leave early or buy less.
parts.working: 2 marks: definition (feeling of too many people or of lack of space, causing discomfort). 1 mark: a valid effect on behaviour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define "perceived control" and explain why a queue with no clear information about waiting times can increase frustration.
parts.answer: Perceived control is the belief that one can influence or predict what happens. Without information, a customer does not know how long they will wait and feels powerless, so frustration rises.
parts.working: 2 marks: definition (belief that one can influence or predict outcomes). 2 marks: explained link to queues (no information about waiting time, feeling powerless, frustration rises).

stem: Five customers at a bank in Karachi record their waiting times in minutes: 4, 6, 9, 12, 14.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the median waiting time for these five customers.
parts.answer: Mean = (4 + 6 + 9 + 12 + 14) ÷ 5 = 45 ÷ 5 = 9.0 minutes. Median = 9 minutes (the middle value when ordered).
parts.working: 1 mark: total of 45. 1 mark: mean 9.0 minutes. 1 mark: median 9 minutes.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a long wait in a crowded queue could affect a shopper's decision to buy an impulse item placed at the till.
parts.answer: Frustration and stress can reduce self-control, so the shopper is more likely to respond to items that are easy to grab. A small item at the till also offers a quick reward and a way to pass the time, so it is more likely to be bought on impulse.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: frustration or stress reduces self-control (1); impulse items offer a quick reward or distraction (1); the till position makes items easy to grab (1); clear link to the decision (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why crowding in a shop can reduce shoppers' satisfaction, referring to personal space.
parts.answer: Crowding invades personal space, which causes discomfort and physiological arousal. Shoppers feel less in control of their movement and are more likely to leave early, so their satisfaction with the shopping trip falls.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: crowding intrudes into personal space (1); discomfort and arousal (1); reduced sense of control (1); lower satisfaction or early exit (1).

stem: A hypothetical study randomly assigns shoppers to be approached by a staff member who stands either 0.5 m (close) or 1.5 m (far) from the shelf. Mean time spent browsing: close 2.1 minutes; far 4.6 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in browsing time when the staff member stood close, relative to the far condition. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark: difference of 2.5 minutes. 1 mark: 54.3%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the IV, the DV and one extraneous variable that should be controlled.
parts.answer: IV: distance of the staff member (0.5 m or 1.5 m). DV: time spent browsing (minutes). Extraneous variable: the shopper's reason for visiting the store, controlled by random allocation of shoppers to conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark for IV. 1 mark for DV. 1 mark for a valid extraneous variable with a control.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the debate about whether consumer behaviour is shaped by the environment or by the individual.
parts.answer: Environmental explanations say that the layout, crowding and noise of a store determine how people behave. Individual explanations say that personality, mood and past experience influence how consumers respond to the same environment.
parts.working: 2 marks: both sides outlined (environment-led explanation versus individual differences).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why research on personal space is nomothetic.
parts.answer: It aims to find general laws about how people in general respond to crowding or closeness, rather than describing one shopper in detail.
parts.working: 2 marks: aims for general laws applying to many people; contrast with idiographic detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the psychological environment as an explanation of consumer behaviour. Refer to research on crowding or queuing in your answer, and include one issue or debate.
parts.answer: Strengths: research on crowding and queuing shows clear, practical effects, such as shoppers leaving earlier when space is limited, and the explanation is supported by evidence about stress and perceived control. Weaknesses: the effects depend on the individual, since some people enjoy busy environments, so a general explanation is limited. Most studies are laboratory or survey-based, which may not reflect real shopping, and the explanation ignores the product and budget. Issue: nature versus nurture; personal space norms are partly learned, so they vary across cultures, as a study in a Pakistani market might show. Overall, the psychological environment explains some behaviour, but it should be combined with individual and product factors.
parts.working: Up to 10 marks: at least two evaluative points (strength or weakness) each developed with evidence (up to 6); a named issue or debate, such as individual differences or cultural variation (up to 2); a balanced conclusion (up to 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two ways that a supermarket could reduce queue frustration for customers. Explain why each would work.
parts.answer: For example: display a visible queue-length or expected waiting-time sign, so customers feel more in control; or provide a separate express lane for small purchases, so the wait feels shorter. Each works by giving customers information or a sense of control, which reduces frustration.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: two suitable suggestions (1 each); a correct explanation for each linked to perceived control, information or unoccupied time (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a queue that is perceived as moving slowly can increase frustration, even when the actual wait is the same.
parts.answer: Unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time, and an empty-feeling wait makes a customer focus on the delay, so the same real waiting time is experienced as longer and more frustrating.
parts.working: 2 marks: perceived versus actual waiting time; unoccupied time or attention on delay makes the wait feel longer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a study to test whether a longer queue reduces customers' mood. Identify the design, the sample, the IV, the DV, and one ethical issue with a suitable safeguard.
parts.answer: Design: a field experiment in which the queue length is varied across days or matched tills, with customers allocated to the condition by the time they arrive. IV: queue length (short: 3 customers ahead; long: 10 ahead). DV: mood rated on a 1–7 scale after the customer leaves the till, using a short questionnaire. Sample: adult customers at one supermarket during matched time slots, approached after payment. Ethics: the study involves a short, non-harmful questionnaire, so customers must be informed afterwards, may refuse to take part, and their answers are anonymous and kept confidential.
parts.working: Up to 10 marks: a suitable design (2); an operationalised IV (2); an operationalised DV (2); a suitable sample and sampling method (2); one ethical issue with a justified safeguard (2).

stem: A survey of 75 customers at one Karachi supermarket finds that 45 of them report feeling stressed when queueing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of customers who reported stress when queueing (give your answer to 1 decimal place).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a sample of 75 customers from one store limits how far the finding can be generalised.
parts.answer: The sample comes from one store, in one city, at one time, so customers in other shops, areas or times may differ in income, queue length and expectations. The customers who agreed to answer may also be unrepresentative, for example if the more stressed people were less likely to stop.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: one store, city or time limits the sample (1); customers elsewhere may differ (1); volunteer or self-selection bias (1); link to the finding (1).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study investigates 'politeness' of shoppers in a bazaar in Lahore. Suggest two ways the researcher could operationalise politeness so that it can be observed and recorded.
parts.answer: Any two observable, countable behaviours, e.g. number of times a shopper says 'please' or 'thank you' per visit; whether the shopper greets the shopkeeper within 10 seconds of arriving.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a clear, observable behaviour that could be counted or rated (not a vague trait such as 'nice').

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher wants to know whether people feel happier on Fridays than on Mondays. Explain why 'happiness' must be operationalised before data are collected.
parts.answer: Happiness is an abstract concept that cannot be observed directly; operationalising it (e.g. a 0–10 self-rating) makes it measurable so that the two days can be compared and the study can be replicated.
parts.working: 1 mark: happiness is not directly observable or measurable as it stands. 1 mark: operationalising it as a specified measure allows reliable, comparable data and replication.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an operationalised measure of happiness for this study, giving the scale and anchors.
parts.answer: e.g. 'On a scale from 0 (very unhappy) to 10 (very happy), how happy did you feel today?' with the scale anchors shown.
parts.working: 1 mark for a specified scale with numeric range; 1 mark for clear labelled anchors at each end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher compares the reading speed of 30 adults in Karachi and 30 adults in Dubai. State whether the variable 'country of residence' is a participant variable or a situational variable, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: It is a participant variable: it is a characteristic of the individuals, not of the testing conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct classification. 1 mark for a reason linked to the characteristic belonging to each participant (not to the environment or procedure).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one situational variable that the researcher should control in this study.
parts.answer: e.g. the same reading material, the same time of day, the same lighting or quiet room for testing.
parts.working: 1 mark for a situational variable that is standardised across both groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two independent groups of participants were tested. Group A had a mean age of 21.4 years and Group B had a mean age of 25.0 years. Calculate the difference in mean age in years, then explain why this difference could affect the results of a memory experiment.
parts.answer: Difference = 25.0 − 21.4 = 3.6 years. Older participants may have different memory performance, so age (a participant variable) could be confounded with the IV rather than the IV itself causing any difference.
parts.working: 1 mark for 3.6 years. 1 mark for stating that age is a participant variable. 1 mark for explaining that it could produce differences in memory unrelated to the IV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a researcher could use stratified allocation to reduce the influence of participant variables in an independent measures experiment on learning vocabulary. Refer to one participant variable used to form the strata.
parts.answer: Participants are first sorted into subgroups (strata) according to a key participant variable, such as prior vocabulary test score or age band. Within each stratum, participants are randomly allocated to the conditions, so each condition contains a similar mix of the variable. The variable is then spread across conditions rather than concentrated in one, reducing its influence on the DV.
parts.working: 1 mark for sorting participants into strata by a named participant variable; 1 mark for random allocation within each stratum; 1 mark for explaining that the variable is spread evenly across conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of random allocation as a way of controlling participant variables.
parts.answer: With small samples, chance may still produce unequal groups, so some participant variables remain unbalanced.
parts.working: 1 mark for the limitation; 1 mark for explaining why (small samples or chance imbalances).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher in Pakistan wants to test whether a mindfulness session reduces test anxiety in students. She recruits 60 students and measures each student's anxiety before and after the session. Describe two participant variables that could affect the 'before and after' difference, and explain how the researcher could measure one of them so that it can be used as a covariate in analysis.
parts.answer: e.g. baseline anxiety level, prior experience of meditation, general health or sleep, and the student's general worry tendency. Measure baseline anxiety or prior experience with a questionnaire at the start, then include it in the analysis as a covariate so its effect on the change score can be statistically removed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two appropriate participant variables (max 2). 1 mark for naming a measurable form. 1 mark for stating that it is recorded before the intervention. 1 mark for explaining its role as a covariate. 1 mark for a clear link to controlling its influence on the change score.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment tests whether background music affects typing speed in office workers in Islamabad. Write a directional (one-tailed) hypothesis for this experiment.
parts.answer: Office workers who type with background music will type more words per minute than those who type in silence.
parts.working: 1 mark for a comparison of the two conditions with the IV and DV named; 1 mark for a clear direction of the difference stated (more/fewer, higher/lower).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher investigates whether there is a relationship between hours of sleep and exam score in 16-year-olds. Write a null hypothesis for this correlational study.
parts.answer: There is no relationship between hours of sleep and exam score in 16-year-olds.
parts.working: 1 mark for stating 'no relationship' or 'no correlation'; 1 mark for naming both co-variables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a one-tailed (directional) hypothesis and a two-tailed (non-directional) hypothesis.
parts.answer: A one-tailed hypothesis predicts the direction of the difference or relationship; a two-tailed hypothesis states that there will be a difference or relationship without specifying its direction.
parts.working: 1 mark for directional prediction in a one-tailed hypothesis; 1 mark for no direction stated in a two-tailed hypothesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a hypothesis should be stated before data are collected. Use an example about the effect of exercise on mood.
parts.answer: A hypothesis is a precise, testable prediction about the IV and DV, for example: 'Adults who exercise for 30 minutes a day will report higher mood scores after two weeks than adults who do not.' Stating it before the data are collected means the prediction cannot be changed to fit the results, so the test is fair and the findings can be checked against the prediction.
parts.working: 1 mark for a precise, testable prediction about the IV and DV with an example; 1 mark for explaining that stating it in advance prevents the prediction being fitted to the results.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a hypothesis must be falsifiable. Give an example of a hypothesis that is not falsifiable.
parts.answer: A falsifiable hypothesis can be shown to be wrong by evidence; without this, a theory cannot be tested scientifically. Example of a non-falsifiable hypothesis: 'Some people are destined to be happy whatever happens', which no data could disprove.
parts.working: 1 mark for explaining falsifiability (could be proved wrong by evidence). 1 mark for a valid non-falsifiable example or contrast.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical field experiment in Dhaka records whether drivers stop at a zebra crossing when a pedestrian with a white cane is waiting, compared with a pedestrian without one. Write a directional hypothesis for this experiment, naming the IV and DV.
parts.answer: Drivers are more likely to stop at a zebra crossing when a pedestrian with a white cane is waiting than when no such pedestrian is waiting. IV: presence of a white cane (or pedestrian type); DV: whether the driver stops.
parts.working: 1 mark for directional prediction; 1 mark for IV named; 1 mark for DV named as an operationalised measure (stop or not stop).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a researcher might choose a non-directional hypothesis when two previous studies have found opposite results on the same question.
parts.answer: The earlier studies disagree about the direction of the effect, so there is no reliable basis for predicting a direction. A non-directional hypothesis avoids making a prediction that may be wrong and allows the new data to show either an increase or a decrease.
parts.working: 1 mark for explaining that conflicting evidence gives no reliable direction; 1 mark for explaining that a non-directional hypothesis avoids a possibly wrong prediction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher found in previous research that longer commuting time is linked to lower job satisfaction. A new hypothetical study in Lahore plans to test this with 120 office workers. Evaluate whether the new study should use a directional or a non-directional hypothesis.
parts.answer: A directional hypothesis is appropriate: earlier research supports a predicted direction (negative correlation), so the researcher can state that longer commuting is associated with lower satisfaction. However, a non-directional hypothesis is safer if the previous findings are inconsistent or weak. Strength of the earlier evidence and consistency should be judged; a directional hypothesis takes a risk but is more informative if correct.
parts.working: 1 mark for stating the directional option; 1 mark for linking to the existing evidence; 1 mark for a discussion of consistency or weakness of earlier evidence; 1 mark for a reasoned weighing of risk; 1 mark for a justified conclusion; 1 mark for accurate use of terms (e.g. negative correlation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of the following, state whether it is an aim or a hypothesis: (i) 'To find out whether people in Quetta sleep worse during the summer than during the winter.' (ii) 'People in Quetta will report fewer hours of sleep per night in summer than in winter.' (iii) 'To examine the effect of caffeine on reaction time.' (iv) 'Caffeine will shorten reaction time compared with a placebo drink.'
parts.answer: (i) aim; (ii) hypothesis; (iii) aim; (iv) hypothesis.
parts.working: 1 mark each: aims are general intentions without a predicted outcome; hypotheses are specific, testable predictions with a direction or a clear comparison.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A correlational study in Karachi is planned to investigate whether time spent on household chores is related to self-esteem in teenage girls. Write a directional hypothesis for this study and explain why the researcher should not write that chores cause higher self-esteem.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: Teenage girls who spend more hours per week on household chores will report higher self-esteem scores. Causal language should be avoided because a correlation shows only that two variables are related; a third variable (e.g. family support) could explain both, or self-esteem could cause the chores.
parts.working: 1 mark for a directional hypothesis with both co-variables operationalised; 1 mark for stating that it is correlational; 1 mark for the third variable or reverse-causality explanation; 1 mark for clear language about relationship not causation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment in Peshawar compares two groups of students: one watches a 5-minute video about revision, and the other reads a 5-minute text about revision. Afterwards, all students take a 10-question quiz. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: IV: type of material (video or text). DV: score on the 10-question quiz.
parts.working: 1 mark for the IV; 1 mark for the DV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher records the number of hours per week that students spend on their phones and their grade point average (GPA). Identify the two co-variables in this study.
parts.answer: Hours per week on the phone and GPA.
parts.working: 1 mark for each co-variable named accurately.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A study examines how light affects the growth of seedlings. Half of the seedlings are kept in a bright room and half in a dark cupboard. After 14 days, the height of each seedling is measured in centimetres. Identify the independent variable and state its two levels.
parts.answer: IV: light condition; levels: bright room (light) and dark cupboard (no light).
parts.working: 1 mark for the IV; 1 mark for both levels stated clearly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study in Hyderabad tests whether drinking a sugary drink affects how long children can sit still in class. Children are given either a sugary drink or a plain drink and then timed sitting still. Identify two extraneous variables that the researcher should control.
parts.answer: e.g. time since the children last ate, the child's usual sugar intake, the temperature of the classroom, the age of the children, the length of the lesson.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a valid extraneous variable that could affect the DV in the same way across conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher in Nairobi finds that the students in her 'study group' condition also had higher attendance rates than students in her 'self study' condition. Explain why 'attendance' is a confounding variable in this study.
parts.answer: Attendance differs systematically between the groups and may affect the DV (test score) in addition to the IV (study method), so the effect of study method cannot be separated from the effect of attendance.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying that it varies with the IV; 1 mark for explaining that it may also affect the DV, so the results are confounded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment investigates whether the time of day affects reaction time. Participants are tested at 9:00 am, 1:00 pm and 6:00 pm. Identify the independent variable and state how many levels it has.
parts.answer: IV: time of day; 3 levels (9:00 am, 1:00 pm, 6:00 pm).
parts.working: 1 mark for IV; 1 mark for 3 levels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an independent variable and an extraneous variable, using a study of the effect of caffeine on concentration.
parts.answer: The independent variable is deliberately changed by the researcher (e.g. caffeine dose or caffeinated versus decaf drink); an extraneous variable is any other factor that might affect the DV and is not deliberately manipulated (e.g. the time of day or amount of sleep).
parts.working: 1 mark for IV as deliberately manipulated; 1 mark for extraneous variable as an unwanted factor that could affect the DV, with an example from the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher measures how many words 20 participants in Lahore recall from a list after either (i) hearing the list read aloud or (ii) reading the list silently. Identify the dependent variable and explain how it is operationalised.
parts.answer: DV: number of words recalled from the list of 20, counted by the researcher when participants write down all words they remember.
parts.working: 1 mark for DV named; 1 mark for an operational definition (counted words, time limit, or method of recall).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher in Karachi studies whether a 10-minute walk affects mood. Participants who walk are all volunteers who already exercise three times a week, while the comparison group is made up of people who do not exercise. Identify the independent variable and the confounding variable, and explain how the confound could affect the conclusion.
parts.answer: IV: 10-minute walk (walk vs no walk). Confound: prior exercise habits (the groups differ on this). Explanation: regular exercisers may have better mood anyway, so any difference could come from prior habits rather than the walk; the researcher cannot conclude that the walk improved mood.
parts.working: 1 mark for IV; 1 mark for confound named; 1 mark for explaining that the confound varies with the IV; 1 mark for explaining it could affect the DV (mood); 1 mark for stating the conclusion is not valid; 1 mark for suggestion or precise use of terms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A study uses 60 secondary-school pupils in Mumbai. The researcher records hours of homework per week and the score on an end-of-term test. Explain why the researcher cannot identify either variable as an independent variable in this correlational study, and identify the appropriate terms.
parts.answer: The variables are not manipulated by the researcher; both are measured as they naturally occur. They are co-variables (or correlated variables), not IV and DV; the correlational design cannot establish which variable, if either, causes change in the other.
parts.working: 1 mark for stating that no variable is manipulated; 1 mark for the term co-variable; 1 mark for explaining that causality cannot be determined; 1 mark for a clear conclusion about direction of influence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment at a sports centre in Islamabad allocates 45 participants to sit still, walk slowly or jog for 15 minutes. Afterwards, each person takes a 20-question memory test. Identify the independent variable and its three levels, the dependent variable, and two variables that should be controlled. Justify one of your choices of control.
parts.answer: IV: type of activity (3 levels: sitting still, walking slowly, jogging). DV: number of correct answers on the 20-question memory test. Controls: e.g. time of day, time since last meal, the test given in the same room, the same instructions, the same test. Justification (one control): e.g. time since last meal could affect concentration and so affect memory test score, so it is standardised across all participants.
parts.working: 1 mark IV; 1 mark for three levels; 1 mark DV; 1 mark DV operationalised; 1 mark for each of two controls (max 2); 1 mark for justification of control; 1 mark for linking control to DV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher in Karachi tests participants on a mirror-drawing task. One of the two testers is friendly and smiles throughout, while the other is brisk and does not smile. Explain why the tester's manner is a situational variable, and explain how the researcher could standardise it.
parts.answer: It is a feature of the testing situation, not a characteristic of the participant. Standardisation: the same script and manner for every participant, or the same tester for all participants, or a recorded set of instructions.
parts.working: 1 mark for classifying it as a situational variable; 1 mark for a reason based on the testing environment or procedure; 1 mark for a suitable standardisation method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A theory predicts that a loud environment reduces the accuracy of reading comprehension. Explain why a researcher testing this theory is more likely to write a directional hypothesis than a non-directional hypothesis.
parts.answer: The theory gives a predicted direction (less accurate in loud conditions), so a directional hypothesis matches the theory and tests it more precisely.
parts.working: 1 mark for the theory providing a predicted direction; 1 mark for explaining that the directional hypothesis tests the theory more precisely.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher measures reaction time to a red light by recording the time in milliseconds between the light turning red and a button being pressed. Identify the dependent variable and state its units, and explain why it is suitable for this study.
parts.answer: DV: reaction time, measured in milliseconds. It is suitable because it is an objective, quantitative measure that can be recorded precisely for each trial.
parts.working: 1 mark for DV named; 1 mark for ms as units; 1 mark for a valid reason about objectivity, precision or quantitative measurement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: a teacher in Multan wants to test whether background music helps Grade 7 pupils finish a maths worksheet faster. She plays the music to Section A (24 pupils) and gives silence to Section B (21 pupils), and times each pupil with a stopwatch she holds herself. Identify one weakness of this design.
parts.answer: The two sections are different groups of pupils, so differences in maths ability or motivation between the sections could explain any difference in time, not the music. Alternatively, one person timing all pupils with one stopwatch may time some pupils inconsistently.
parts.working: 1 mark for a correctly identified weakness (participant variables/confounding, or inconsistent timing by one person). 1 mark for explaining how it affects the conclusion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one change to the design that would overcome this weakness.
parts.answer: Randomly allocate the 45 pupils from the same classes to the two conditions (independent measures with random allocation), or use a repeated measures design with counterbalancing so the same pupils do both conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark for a specific, appropriate change; 1 mark for explaining how it controls participant variables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: a school counsellor in Multan asks 40 Year 10 pupils one question: 'How stressed do you feel about exams: a lot or a little?' She will ask the same question after a mock exam to measure change. Explain one weakness of this measure.
parts.answer: The terms 'a lot' and 'a little' are vague and undefined, so each pupil may interpret them differently. The answers are therefore not directly comparable between pupils, and a small real change after the mock exam may not be detected.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying the weakness (vague, undefined response terms); 1 mark for explaining the consequence for comparing pupils or measuring change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improved measure of exam stress that she could use.
parts.answer: A rating scale from 1 (not at all stressed) to 7 (extremely stressed), or a validated questionnaire with several items, averaged to give a score.
parts.working: 1 mark for a suitable measure (rating scale or multi-item questionnaire); 1 mark for explaining how it gives more precise or sensitive data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: a researcher observes shoppers at a supermarket in Karachi to see whether they buy more when music is playing. She sits near the till and records purchases from the till receipt for 30 minutes, on one day each week, for four weeks. Evaluate this design in terms of reliability and validity.
parts.answer: Reliability: a single observer is used and receipts are objective records, so the data should be consistent; however, only 30 minutes on one day each week may not represent the store and days differ. Validity: till receipts show purchases but not whether music caused them; other factors (day, promotions, customers) may affect purchasing; the researcher's presence may change behaviour. Credit for a suggested improvement.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a reliability strength and weakness with reference to the design (max 2); 1 mark each for a validity strength and weakness (max 2); 1 mark for linking to the aim (causation vs correlation/confounding); 1 mark for a suggested improvement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A psychologist tests reaction times and recruits only psychology undergraduates from one university. She then claims the results show the effect of caffeine on reaction time in the general population. Explain one sampling problem with this design.
parts.answer: The sample is biased and not representative: psychology students may have different ages, alertness, caffeine habits, or test familiarity from the general population, so generalisability is limited.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying the sampling problem (unrepresentative/biased sample); 1 mark for explaining the effect on generalisation to the population.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a sampling method that would improve the generalisability of the findings, and explain how it would work.
parts.answer: Random sampling from a list of adults of different ages and backgrounds in the population (e.g. a regional census list of households), so every member has an equal chance of being selected.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming a suitable method (random, stratified or opportunity sampling with justification); 1 mark for describing how it is done; 1 mark for explaining why it improves representativeness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: a researcher tells participants that a short study is about 'food tastes'. Participants are then given a tray of snacks alone in a room, and secretly counted through a one-way mirror to see how many snacks they eat while they believe they are unobserved. Identify one ethical issue in this plan and explain how debriefing could address it.
parts.answer: Issue: deception and lack of informed consent, plus invasion of privacy (covert observation without knowing). Debriefing could explain the real purpose, reveal the observation, allow participants to withdraw their data, and reassure them about confidentiality.
parts.working: 1 mark for an ethical issue identified; 1 mark for explaining why it is a problem; 1 mark for a relevant feature of debriefing; 1 mark for explaining how debriefing addresses the issue (e.g. right to withdraw data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: Dr Naveed plans to test whether a one-hour hand-hygiene training session reduces errors in nurses in a Lahore hospital. He observes 20 nurses for two weeks before training and two weeks after, counting hand-hygiene errors on a clipboard. The nurses know he is observing them. Evaluate this design, referring to at least two of: validity, reliability, demand characteristics and ethics.
parts.answer: Strengths: pre/post design allows change over time to be measured; observation gives direct behavioural data; counts are objective if categories are clear. Weaknesses: no control group, so improvements could be due to time, seasonal changes, or hospital-wide campaigns (poor internal validity); awareness of observation may change behaviour (demand characteristics and reactivity; low ecological validity); nurses' consent is needed and 'watched' nurses may feel pressured; reliability depends on clear categories and a single observer, so inter-observer reliability should be checked; the sample of 20 from one hospital limits generalisation.
parts.working: Mark bands: 1–3 descriptive points on the design with limited evaluation; 4–6 valid evaluation of at least two named concepts with reasons (validity/reliability/demand characteristics/ethics); 7–10 detailed, balanced evaluation with specific links to the study, including a justified improvement such as a control group, covert or blind observation, inter-observer checks or a consent process that avoids deception.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher studies whether online reviews affect purchase decisions. All participants are female students aged 18–22 from one college. Each reads either a five-star or a two-star review of a set of headphones costing Rs 3,500, then rates how likely they would be to buy it on a scale of 1 to 10. The researcher then concludes that 'negative reviews reduce buying among shoppers in Pakistan'. Evaluate the design and the conclusion.
parts.answer: Points: the sample is unrepresentative (one gender, narrow age, one college) so the conclusion cannot be generalised to shoppers in Pakistan; the rating is a single hypothetical question, so it measures intention not actual purchasing (low ecological validity, social desirability in hypothetical choices); the experimental design allocates conditions (IV = review type) which supports cause, but if participants were not randomly allocated, participant variables might differ; price and brand are controlled only if the same headphones are used; the conclusion overreaches the data.
parts.working: Mark bands: 1–3 limited, descriptive comments; 4–7 evaluation of design (sample, measure, validity) with links to conclusion; 8–10 balanced evaluation that identifies the overgeneralisation, the nature of the DV (intention vs behaviour), and suggests improvements (a representative sample, a behavioural measure such as a real choice, random allocation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: Ayesha tests whether a three-minute breathing exercise lowers pulse rate. She records the pulse rate of 20 students before and after the exercise. Identify the experimental design used.
parts.answer: Repeated measures (within participants) design.
parts.working: 1 mark for repeated measures (or within-subjects).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way that participant variables could affect the results of this study.
parts.answer: Students' fitness or anxiety levels before the test could affect resting pulse, and the 'before' reading could be affected by excitement or walking to the room, so the change may not be caused by the exercise alone.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming a participant variable (fitness, anxiety, prior caffeine); 1 mark for explaining how it could affect pulse readings or the difference.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'control condition' in an experiment. Give one example for a study on whether coffee improves reaction time.
parts.answer: A control condition is a condition in which the IV is not applied (or a neutral condition) to provide a baseline for comparison. Example: participants given decaffeinated coffee or water.
parts.working: 1 mark for a definition (condition without the IV, or baseline comparison); 1 mark for an appropriate example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a control condition makes the results of the experiment more valid.
parts.answer: Without a control condition, any change in reaction time could be due to time, practice or expectation; comparing with the control shows the change is specifically due to the IV.
parts.working: 1 mark for linking the control to isolating the effect of the IV; 1 mark for explaining that other causes are ruled out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'demand characteristics' in an experiment.
parts.answer: Cues in the experimental situation that lead participants to guess the aim of the study and change their behaviour to fit what they believe the researcher wants.
parts.working: 1 mark for indicating that participants are influenced by cues; 1 mark for linking to changing behaviour to fit expectations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing demand characteristics in an experiment on memory for a list of words.
parts.answer: Use a single-blind design where participants are not told the aim, or use a cover story so the real purpose is hidden until debriefing.
parts.working: 1 mark for an appropriate method (single blind, cover story, filler tasks).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A repeated measures experiment compares three conditions (quiet, background music, traffic noise) using 24 participants. Counterbalancing is used to control order effects. Calculate the number of different orders in which the three conditions can be presented.
parts.answer: 3! = 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 different orders.
parts.working: 1 mark for 6 (accept working 3 × 2 × 1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the 24 participants could be counterbalanced so that each order is used equally often.
parts.answer: Each of the 6 orders is used with 24 ÷ 6 = 4 participants, allocated randomly to orders.
parts.working: 1 mark for dividing 24 by 6 to get 4 per order; 1 mark for explaining that each order is used equally and allocation is random.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why counterbalancing is needed in this study.
parts.answer: Order effects such as practice or fatigue could otherwise make later conditions appear better or worse, which would confound the effect of the IV.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming an order effect (practice, fatigue, boredom); 1 mark for explaining how it would confound the results.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher wants to test whether a revision app improves exam scores of students in Islamabad. Explain how a matched pairs design could be used to control participant variables in this experiment.
parts.answer: Participants are matched in pairs on a key characteristic (e.g. pre-test score or prior GPA). One member of each pair is randomly allocated to the app condition and the other to the control condition, so the groups are equivalent on the matching variable.
parts.working: 1 mark for pairing participants on a relevant variable; 1 mark for random allocation of one per pair to each condition; 1 mark for explaining that this balances participant variables across conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one disadvantage of a matched pairs design in this study.
parts.answer: It is time-consuming to find matched pairs; only the matched variable is controlled, and other participant variables can still differ; if a participant drops out, the partner's data must also be removed.
parts.working: 1 mark for a disadvantage; 1 mark for an explanation specific to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an independent measures design avoids order effects, and give one disadvantage of an independent measures design in an experiment on the effect of colour on mood.
parts.answer: Each participant takes part in only one condition, so practice, fatigue or familiarity cannot affect their performance across conditions. Disadvantage: participant variables may differ between the groups, so more participants are needed and random allocation is required.
parts.working: 1 mark for different participants in each condition; 1 mark for explaining that order effects are therefore avoided; 1 mark for a disadvantage; 1 mark for an explanation linked to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a laboratory experiment to test whether watching a short stress-inducing video (a timed, unfamiliar maths quiz) affects the accuracy of short-term memory in university students in Karachi. Describe the design, the IV and DV with how each is operationalised, the controls you would use, and how you would allocate participants to conditions.
parts.answer: Design: independent measures or matched pairs with two conditions (stress video vs neutral video of similar length), or repeated measures with counterbalancing. IV: type of video (stress or neutral); operationalised as the video shown. DV: number of items recalled correctly from a list of 15 words after a 2-minute delay. Controls: same room, same lighting, same time of day, same instructions, same word list, same delay, filler task, participants without caffeine or sleep deprivation, standardised debriefing. Allocation: random allocation (or matching on baseline memory score) to avoid participant variables.
parts.working: Mark bands: 1–3 limited plan with few specific details; 4–7 a clear design with IV, DV and some controls; 8–10 full, operational plan with a sound allocation method and justified controls (e.g. standardising the time of day, order effects, demand characteristics).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher in Lahore wants to know whether noise from a generator affects the speed of simple addition. She tests participants in a room next to a generator and claims the noise caused slower work. Identify two situational variables that she has not controlled and explain how each could have affected the results, and suggest how a laboratory experiment could be designed to control them.
parts.answer: e.g. heat from the generator, room distractions or other people nearby, time of day, familiarity with the task, tester behaviour. Each variable is an alternative explanation for slower work (for example, heat may slow participants whatever the noise level). A better design: a quiet laboratory room with the noise played through headphones at a fixed volume; standardised instructions; random allocation; the same tester for all participants; counterbalanced order if repeated measures.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two appropriate situational variables (max 2); 1 mark each for explaining the effect on the DV (max 2); 1 mark for stating that the claim is not valid; 1 mark for a suitable design improvement; 2 marks for justifying how the improved design controls a named variable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A psychologist designs a repeated measures experiment in which participants recall a list of 20 nouns after either a 0-minute, 5-minute or 15-minute delay, with a filler task. Describe two ways she could control order effects and one way she could reduce demand characteristics, and explain why each is needed.
parts.answer: Order effects: counterbalancing all six orders of the three conditions (or a Latin square), using different word lists per condition. Demand characteristics: a single-blind procedure or a cover story. Explanations: order effects such as practice or fatigue could make later recall better or worse; demand characteristics could make participants recall more or less to match what they think is expected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid order-effect controls (max 2); 1 mark for a valid demand characteristic control; 1 mark for an explanation of why order effects arise; 1 mark for an explanation of how demand characteristics bias results.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical survey: a researcher in Karachi records the number of hours per week that adults spend watching television and their body mass index (BMI). Identify the two co-variables.
parts.answer: Hours of television watched per week and BMI.
parts.working: 1 mark for each co-variable named correctly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the likely direction of the correlation between these variables if people who watch more television tend to have higher BMI, and state what this means in words.
parts.answer: Positive correlation: as television hours increase, BMI tends to increase.
parts.working: 1 mark for a positive correlation with a correct verbal description.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'scattergram' (scatter plot) and describe what a correlation of zero would look like in one.
parts.answer: A scattergram plots each participant's pair of scores as a point. A correlation of zero shows no pattern: points are spread randomly with no upward or downward trend.
parts.working: 1 mark for a scattergram showing paired scores as points; 1 mark for describing a random, patternless spread for zero correlation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher finds that children who read more books have higher vocabulary scores. Explain why this correlation does not show that reading more books causes a larger vocabulary, referring to reverse causation.
parts.answer: Correlation shows only that two variables are associated. Reverse causation is possible: children with larger vocabularies may enjoy reading and so choose to read more books, so the direction of cause is unknown.
parts.working: 1 mark for stating that correlation shows association only; 1 mark for explaining reverse causation with an example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one third variable that might affect both reading habits and vocabulary in this study.
parts.answer: e.g. parents' education level, household income, or the number of conversations with adults at home.
parts.working: 1 mark for a plausible third variable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a researcher could operationalise 'daily screen time' and 'sleep duration' in a correlational study of 15-year-olds in Karachi.
parts.answer: Screen time: a diary of minutes spent on phones, tablets and computers each day for seven days, or a parent-checked app log; averaged over the week. Sleep duration: time in bed each night recorded in a sleep diary or measured by a wrist actigraphy device, averaged over the week.
parts.working: 1 mark for an observable, quantified measure of screen time; 1 mark for a suitable timeframe; 1 mark for an operational sleep duration measure; 1 mark for a clear method of recording (diary, log, device).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher records the hours of practice per week on a maths app (x) and the score out of 40 on a maths test (y) for 8 students in Peshawar. Hours: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Scores: 14, 17, 19, 23, 24, 28, 29, 30. Calculate the mean number of practice hours and the mean test score.
parts.working: 1 mark for sum 36 and mean 4.5 hours; 1 mark for sum 184 and mean 23.0; 1 mark for both answers with correct units (hours; marks out of 40).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of a correlational design compared with an experiment for studying the link between smoking and lung disease.
parts.answer: Strength: it can study a naturally occurring behaviour that cannot ethically be manipulated (e.g. researchers cannot force people to smoke) and it can be done with existing data; it can show a relationship and so suggest hypotheses. Weakness: it cannot show causation, as third variables (e.g. diet, air pollution, genetics) may explain the link.
parts.working: 1 mark for a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining why; 1 mark for a relevant weakness; 1 mark for linking the weakness to the inability to show cause.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write one directional hypothesis (1 mark) and one null hypothesis (1 mark) for a correlational study of the relationship between hours of sleep and reaction time in adults in Lahore.
parts.answer: Directional: The fewer hours of sleep adults in Lahore get, the slower their reaction time. Null: There is no relationship between hours of sleep and reaction time in adults in Lahore.
parts.working: 1 mark for a directional hypothesis with both variables named and a direction; 1 mark for a null hypothesis stating no relationship.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A psychologist wants to investigate whether there is a correlation between the amount of time 13-year-old pupils in Islamabad spend on household chores each week and their academic motivation. Describe how she could conduct this correlational study, including how each variable would be measured, the sample, the procedure, and how she would analyse the data.
parts.answer: Design: correlational; co-variables: weekly hours of chores (diary or parent report) and academic motivation (validated self-report questionnaire, Likert scale). Sample: e.g. 60 pupils from four schools, randomly chosen from class lists, with parental consent; stratify by gender or school. Procedure: pupils complete a chores diary for two weeks, then questionnaire in a quiet classroom; anonymity, right to withdraw. Analysis: plot a scattergram; calculate a correlation coefficient (e.g. Spearman's if ordinal); consider third variables such as family income and parental support.
parts.working: Mark bands: 1–3 limited description, one variable only; 4–7 clear description of both measures and a sample/procedure; 8–10 full, operational plan with a justified sample, ethical points, analysis (scattergram, coefficient) and a discussion of causation/third variables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher in Karachi finds that households with more electrical appliances have children who score higher on maths tests. She concludes that owning appliances improves children's maths. Explain how a third variable could account for this relationship, and describe how she could design a study that tests whether the third variable explains the relationship.
parts.answer: Third variable: household income or parental education, which affects both the number of appliances and access to resources and educational support. A better design: measure household income and parental education, then examine the relationship between appliances and maths scores within income bands (or use multiple regression / partial correlation); or use a longitudinal study with a change in appliance ownership.
