parts.working: 1 mark for a plausible third variable; 1 mark for explaining how it affects both co-variables; 1 mark for identifying that the conclusion is causal and is invalid; 1 mark for measuring the third variable; 1 mark for a suitable analysis that controls it; 1 mark for an appropriate longitudinal or statistical method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher in Lahore finds a correlation of +0.62 between the number of books in the home and the scores of 11-year-old pupils on a reading test. A colleague says this proves that children's reading ability is inherited. Evaluate the colleague's claim, referring to the nature–nurture debate.
parts.answer: The correlation shows an association but not inheritance: books in the home are an environmental factor, and books could be linked to parental reading habits, which are both genetic and environmental (genes and environment are confounded in natural families). The claim is not supported; a design such as adoption or twin studies would be needed to separate genetic and environmental effects. Also the coefficient reflects one sample and one measure.
parts.working: 1–2 marks for a basic statement that correlation does not show cause; 3–4 marks for identifying the environmental and genetic confound (parental reading habits); 5–6 marks for evaluation of the nature–nurture debate and the design needed to separate them; 7–8 marks for a balanced, specific evaluation including alternative explanations and reference to the limitation of one sample.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'naturalistic observation' and give one advantage of it for studying shoppers in a Lahore market.
parts.answer: Observing behaviour in its natural setting without manipulating the environment. Advantage: behaviour is more likely to be natural and realistic (higher ecological validity) because shoppers are unaware of the study.
parts.working: 1 mark for a definition (natural setting, no manipulation); 1 mark for an advantage with reference to natural behaviour or validity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an 'overt' observation and identify one ethical issue that arises when observations are overt.
parts.answer: Overt observation: participants know they are being observed. Ethical issue: they may change their behaviour (reactivity) or may not have given full consent to be observed; or they may feel uncomfortable.
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct definition; 1 mark for an appropriate ethical issue with explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'observer bias' and suggest one way to reduce it in an observation of children's play in a school in Hyderabad.
parts.answer: Observer bias: the observer's expectations or prior beliefs influence what they notice or how they record behaviour. Reduce it by using clear, operationalised behavioural categories, training observers, or using two observers who record independently.
parts.working: 1 mark for defining observer bias (expectations affecting recording); 1 mark for a valid method of reducing it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An observer records a child's behaviour at 10-second intervals for 15 minutes. Calculate the number of intervals in the observation. The observer records 'pushing' in 18 of these intervals. Calculate the percentage of intervals in which pushing was recorded.
parts.answer: 15 minutes = 900 seconds; 900 ÷ 10 = 90 intervals. Percentage = 18 ÷ 90 × 100 = 20%.
parts.working: 1 mark for 90 intervals; 1 mark for 18 ÷ 90; 1 mark for 20%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two observers independently code the same 60 behavioural categories of children's aggression on a video. They agree on 45 of the 60 categories. Calculate the percentage agreement between the two observers.
parts.working: 1 mark for 45 ÷ 60; 1 mark for 75%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what a 75% agreement suggests about inter-observer reliability, and explain one step the researcher could take to improve it.
parts.answer: Reasonable but not high reliability; the researcher should refine the behavioural categories with examples, retrain the observers, and then re-check agreement on a new sample.
parts.working: 1 mark for a judgement about reliability; 1 mark for a valid improvement with explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between time sampling and event sampling, using an example of an observation of passengers boarding a bus in Karachi.
parts.answer: Time sampling: the observer records behaviour at fixed intervals (e.g. every 30 seconds) whatever happens, for example noting whether each passenger pushes ahead at each 30-second mark. Event sampling: the observer records every occurrence of a specific behaviour during the observation, for example each time a passenger pushes ahead to board.
parts.working: 1 mark for time sampling defined; 1 mark for a bus example of time sampling; 1 mark for event sampling defined; 1 mark for a bus example of event sampling with the difference drawn.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher plans to observe aggression in a school playground in Quetta. Suggest two behavioural categories for 'aggression' that are clearly operationalised, and explain why operationalised categories are needed before observations begin.
parts.answer: e.g. 'hitting: making contact with another child's body with a hand or object'; 'verbal threat: saying words such as "I will hurt you" aloud'. Operationalised categories allow each observer to record the same behaviour in the same way, making the data reliable and replicable.
parts.working: 1 mark for each clear, observable category (max 2); 1 mark for explaining that operationalisation allows consistent recording and reliability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would conduct a covert naturalistic observation of cyclists in Lahore to find out whether they ride in a bicycle lane or on the pavement when the lane is blocked by parked vans. Include the sampling method, the behavioural categories, the recording method, how you would reduce observer bias, and the ethical considerations.
parts.answer: Sampling: observe at several times of day over a fixed period, using time sampling to record every cyclist who reaches the blocked section. Behavioural categories: 'rode in lane', 'moved onto pavement', 'dismounted and walked'. Recording: tally sheet with time-stamps, from a distance such as a nearby shop entrance. Observer bias: clear category definitions, training with video examples, two observers with an inter-observer reliability check. Ethics: covert observation of public behaviour is acceptable when no identifiable data are recorded; data anonymised; no interaction; consider whether consent is needed if filming.
parts.working: Mark bands: 1–3 limited description with few details; 4–7 description of method and some categories and bias controls; 8–10 full, specific design with operational categories, sampling, reliability checks and a reasoned ethics section.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher observes children's behaviour in a playroom in Dhaka, with a one-way mirror, and records how often they share toys. The researcher claims that children share more in a playroom than they do at home. Evaluate this claim, referring to ecological validity and demand characteristics.
parts.answer: The playroom is a controlled setting, so it lacks ecological validity: children may behave differently from home, where family rules and siblings matter. Demand characteristics: children may behave differently because they know they are in a study or a new room. The claim cannot be made without observations in the home setting too. Credit for a suggestion such as observing at home, or using a covert approach in a familiar setting.
parts.working: 1 mark for a basic comment; 2 marks for ecological validity with reasons; 1 mark for demand characteristics or reactivity with reasons; 1 mark for linking to the comparison claim; 1 mark for a suggested improvement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher plans a non-participant observation of teachers' use of praise in a secondary school in Karachi. Explain two ways in which the observer could limit bias and one ethical issue the researcher must consider.
parts.answer: Bias reduction: operational definitions of praise (e.g. 'says well done, good work, or that is correct'); training with example videos; recording every instance using time sampling; two observers with inter-observer checks; observer positioned to avoid intervention. Ethics: teachers and pupils should be informed and consent obtained; pupils' identity protected; anonymous coding; right to withdraw.
parts.working: 2 marks for each of two valid bias controls, each explained (max 4); 2 marks for identifying an ethical issue and explaining why it matters; 2 marks for explaining how the researcher addresses it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write one closed question and one open question for a questionnaire about how often families in Multan eat meals at restaurants each week.
parts.answer: Closed: 'How many meals did your family eat at a restaurant last week? None / 1 / 2–3 / 4 or more.' Open: 'Describe the main reasons your family chooses to eat out or to cook at home.'
parts.working: 1 mark for a closed question with fixed response options; 1 mark for an open question inviting a free-text answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'social desirability bias' and give one example of it in a questionnaire about how often people exercise.
parts.answer: Social desirability bias: participants answer in a way that they think is socially approved rather than honestly. Example: participants over-report how often they exercise because they believe it is a healthy behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark for the definition (answers to appear acceptable); 1 mark for an appropriate example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a structured interview compared with an unstructured interview.
parts.answer: Advantage: the same questions in the same order allow reliable comparison between participants and easier analysis. Disadvantage: little flexibility to follow up unexpected answers, so less depth and possible loss of detail.
parts.working: 1 mark for a relevant advantage; 1 mark for explaining it; 1 mark for a relevant disadvantage; 1 mark for explaining it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A questionnaire about use of public transport is posted to 250 commuters in Lahore. 146 completed questionnaires are returned. Calculate the response rate as a percentage, giving your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for 146 ÷ 250 (or × 100); 1 mark for 58.4% correct to 1 dp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write one five-point Likert-scale item measuring job satisfaction for call-centre workers in Karachi, including labelled anchors for each end and the middle point.
parts.answer: e.g. 'I feel satisfied with my job. 1 = Strongly disagree, 2 = Disagree, 3 = Neither agree nor disagree, 4 = Agree, 5 = Strongly agree.'
parts.working: 1 mark for a statement that measures one attitude; 1 mark for five numbered points; 1 mark for labelled anchors including a neutral midpoint.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why some items on the questionnaire should be reverse-scored.
parts.answer: Some items are worded negatively (e.g. 'I often think about leaving my job'), so agreeing means lower satisfaction. Reverse-scoring makes all items point in the same direction so that the total score is meaningful and avoids response sets such as always agreeing.
parts.working: 1 mark for explaining the wording direction issue; 1 mark for explaining that reverse-scoring keeps scores consistent or prevents response bias.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of a pilot study for a questionnaire about internet use among university students in Pakistan.
parts.answer: A pilot tests the questionnaire with a small group to find confusing questions, check the timing and response options, and check whether responses vary as expected, so the final questionnaire can be improved before the main study.
parts.working: 1 mark for a small trial with similar participants; 1 mark for identifying a problem it finds; 1 mark for improving the final design.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A questionnaire item reads: 'Don't you agree that using a phone while driving is very dangerous?' Rewrite the item in a neutral form, and explain why the original wording could bias the answers.
parts.answer: e.g. 'How dangerous do you think using a phone while driving is? Not at all / A little / Moderately / Very dangerous.' The original is leading: the wording suggests the answer participants should give, which increases agreement.
parts.working: 1 mark for a neutral rewrite; 1 mark for a suitable response scale; 1 mark for identifying the leading wording; 1 mark for explaining how it biases answers (demand/agreement).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A psychologist wants to find out why patients in Hyderabad choose a private clinic rather than a government hospital. Describe how she could conduct a semi-structured interview study to investigate this. Include the sample, how she would write the interview questions, how she would record and analyse the responses, and two ethical considerations.
parts.answer: Sample: e.g. 20 patients from three private clinics, selected by opportunity or stratified sampling (for example by age and income). Questions: a schedule of open questions (e.g. 'What influenced your choice of clinic?') with prompts (e.g. 'Tell me more about that'), piloted first. Recording: audio recording with consent, then transcription. Analysis: thematic analysis, coding themes (cost, travel distance, recommendations, waiting times) and checking inter-rater agreement. Ethics: informed consent, confidentiality with pseudonyms, right to withdraw, no pressure to disclose.
parts.working: Mark bands: 1–3 limited plan; 4–7 plan includes sample, questions and recording with some ethics; 8–10 full, specific plan with justified sample, schedule design, analysis method and two developed ethical considerations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of a semi-structured interview to find out why patients in a Karachi dialysis unit miss their sessions. Refer to the validity and reliability of the data collected.
parts.answer: Strengths: open questions allow patients to explain their reasons in depth, giving rich data and valid insight into lived experience; prompts allow follow-up. Weaknesses: the interviewer's behaviour may vary (low reliability, investigator effects); patients may give socially desirable answers (e.g. blaming transport rather than emotional reasons); small sample; analysis is subjective. Improvements: standardised schedule, interviewer training, triangulation with records, member checking.
parts.working: 1–2 marks for a description of semi-structured interviews; 3–4 marks for one strength and one weakness each explained (validity, reliability, social desirability); 5–6 marks for a balanced evaluation with reference to the study; 7–8 marks for a justified improvement and clear conclusion about data quality.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how investigator effects could influence the responses given in an interview study of attitudes to recycling in Rawalpindi, and explain how standardisation of procedures reduces this problem.
parts.answer: Investigator effects: the interviewer's tone, facial expressions, or wording may encourage certain answers (e.g. nodding when a respondent agrees), so the responses reflect the interviewer as well as the participant. Standardisation: same script, same wording, same tone and same order of questions for every participant, and training so interviewers do not add comments.
parts.working: 1 mark for defining investigator effects; 1 mark for an example of interviewer behaviour; 1 mark for explaining the bias it creates; 1 mark for a standardisation method; 1 mark for linking standardisation to reduced bias; 1 mark for consistency of data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher gives 40 participants a 5-point Likert questionnaire on attitudes to online learning. Ten participants' scores on one item (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree) are: 4, 3, 5, 2, 4, 3, 4, 5, 2, 4. Calculate the mean score for this item, giving your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for sum 36 (or method); 1 mark for 3.60.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a 'cohort effect' in a longitudinal study.
parts.answer: A cohort effect is when differences between participants' results are caused by the generation or time period in which they were born or grew up, rather than by the variable being studied or by ageing itself.
parts.working: 1 mark for a link to a shared generation or birth period; 1 mark for the idea that results reflect the group's background, not development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one practice effect that could occur when the same children take the same reading test at ages 7, 8 and 9.
parts.answer: Children become familiar with the test items and format, so their scores improve because of practice rather than real development in reading ability.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming practice effect; 1 mark for explaining that scores rise due to familiarity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A longitudinal study is planned to follow the language development of children in Karachi from age 2 to age 6. Identify one weakness of this design in terms of cost or time.
parts.answer: It takes several years and is expensive because the same participants must be tracked and tested repeatedly; funding and staff may change during the study.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying time or cost; 1 mark for explaining why (multiple testing points over years, tracking costs).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A longitudinal study of 520 primary-school children in Quetta begins. After two years, 418 children remain in the study. Calculate the percentage of the original sample that was lost (attrition), giving your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for 102 lost; 1 mark for 19.6%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one way a researcher could reduce attrition in a longitudinal study, and explain one ethical concern about keeping in contact with participants over several years.
parts.answer: Reduction: keep contact details up to date, send reminders, offer small incentives, or make the schedule convenient. Ethical concern: data must be kept secure and confidential over many years; participants must be told that they may withdraw at any time and how their data will be stored.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid method of reducing attrition; 1 mark for explaining how it works; 1 mark for an ethical concern; 1 mark for explaining why it matters over time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a longitudinal study and a cross-sectional study. Use an example about vocabulary development in children.
parts.answer: Longitudinal: the same children are tested repeatedly over time to measure change within individuals. Cross-sectional: different groups of children at different ages are tested once at the same time, so differences between ages are measured.
parts.working: 1 mark for defining longitudinal; 1 mark for defining cross-sectional; 1 mark for a vocabulary example of each; 1 mark for stating what each reveals about change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A longitudinal study tests the anxiety levels of the same teenagers in Lahore at ages 12, 14 and 16. Describe how the researcher could measure anxiety reliably at each stage.
parts.answer: Use the same validated questionnaire at each age, with age-appropriate wording; standardise administration (same time, same setting, same instructions); record scores in the same way; check inter-rater or test-retest reliability where relevant.
parts.working: 1 mark for a suitable anxiety measure; 1 mark for consistency across ages; 1 mark for standardised procedure; 1 mark for a reliability check.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher in Lahore wants to study how adults' sleep habits change between the ages of 25 and 35. Plan a longitudinal study: describe the sample, the measures, how often participants would be tested, and how you would deal with attrition and practice effects.
parts.answer: Sample: e.g. 150 adults aged 25 recruited from workplaces across Lahore, with informed consent and a range of jobs and genders. Measures: a sleep diary kept for seven nights, plus a wrist actigraphy device and a validated sleep-quality questionnaire. Testing: every two years (five waves). Attrition: keep contact details up to date, send reminders, offer small incentives, and compare those who drop out with those who stay. Practice effects: vary the diary format slightly, avoid repeating identical questionnaires, and allow enough time between waves. Analysis: compare the same individuals over time.
parts.working: Mark bands: 1–3 limited plan with one or two details; 4–7 clear design with measures and timing and some attrition/practice points; 8–10 detailed, feasible plan with justified sample, measures and timings, and specific, well-explained controls for attrition and practice effects.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of a longitudinal design, rather than a cross-sectional design, to investigate the effect of a six-month training programme on the job performance of hospital staff in Lahore. Refer to validity and cost.
parts.answer: A longitudinal design tracks each person before and after training, so changes are measured within individuals, which reduces participant variables; it is valid for showing change, but attrition may lower validity and practice effects may affect the measures. It is costly and slow. A cross-sectional design is cheaper but cannot show change within individuals and is affected by cohort differences.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to four valid strengths or weaknesses of the longitudinal design (max 4); 1 mark for a cross-sectional comparison; 1 mark for a justified judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a longitudinal study that uses retrospective school records of pupils' exam results from 2005 to 2015 may be limited, referring to the type of data, the sample and the possibility of confounding.
parts.answer: Records were not collected for research, so the variables may be inconsistent or missing; the sample is limited to those who stayed in the school system (attrition by selection); records may not include variables such as family income or motivation (confounders); changes in exam difficulty or grading across years may make scores not comparable (cohort or time-of-measurement effects).
parts.working: 1–2 marks for identifying a limitation; 3–4 marks for explaining one limitation about data (not collected for research); 5–6 marks for the sample or confounding limitation with explanation; 7–8 marks for two well-developed limitations, linked to validity or reliability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher follows 150 adults in Karachi for four waves of testing (Wave 1: 150; Wave 2: 132; Wave 3: 120; Wave 4: 96). Calculate the percentage of participants retained at Wave 4, giving your answer to 1 decimal place. Explain why the researcher should compare the characteristics of those who left with those who stayed.
parts.answer: Retention = 96 ÷ 150 × 100 = 64.0%. Comparing leavers with stayers checks whether attrition was random or systematic; if drop-outs differ (e.g. are less healthy or less educated), the remaining sample is biased and the results may not generalise.
parts.working: 1 mark for 64.0%; 1 mark for a suitable explanation of why comparison matters; 1 mark for explaining that systematic attrition biases the sample; 1 mark for linking to generalisation or validity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher wants to know how often students at a college in Multan use a library. Write a closed question with an appropriate response scale for this, and explain one advantage of using a closed rather than an open question for this measure.
parts.answer: e.g. 'How often do you use the college library in a typical week? Never / 1–2 times / 3–4 times / 5 or more times.' Advantage: answers are easy to compare and quantify, and quick to answer, which suits a large sample.
parts.working: 1 mark for a closed question with mutually exclusive, exhaustive categories; 1 mark for a suitable scale; 1 mark for a correct advantage with a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A longitudinal study follows 80 newly qualified nurses in Karachi for three years, testing their stress every six months. Identify one advantage and one disadvantage of testing participants every six months rather than only at the end of the study.
parts.answer: Advantage: frequent measurement gives a detailed picture of how stress changes over time and can identify when changes happen. Disadvantage: repeated testing increases the burden on participants, which may increase attrition, and repeated testing may cause practice effects on the questionnaire.
parts.working: 1 mark for a relevant advantage; 1 mark for explaining it; 1 mark for a relevant disadvantage; 1 mark for explaining it with reference to attrition or practice effects.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what is meant by 'perceived susceptibility' in the health belief model.
parts.answer: Perceived susceptibility is a person's belief about how likely they are to get a particular health problem; a higher belief in personal risk is expected to motivate health-protective behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark for a belief about personal risk of a condition; 1 mark for the expected effect on behaviour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a teenager in Multan might not wear sunscreen even though she knows that sun exposure causes skin cancer. Refer to perceived barriers.
parts.answer: She may believe sunscreen is sticky, expensive, or makes her skin look oily, so the perceived costs outweigh the benefits of protection.
parts.working: 1 mark for a perceived barrier (cost, inconvenience, appearance); 1 mark for explaining how the barrier outweighs perceived benefits or risk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'self-efficacy' and give one example of how it could be used to encourage people to stop smoking.
parts.answer: Self-efficacy is a person's belief in their own ability to carry out a behaviour successfully. Example: giving smokers practice in refusing cigarettes in social situations to build their confidence.
parts.working: 1 mark for a definition (belief in own ability to perform the behaviour); 1 mark for an appropriate example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ms Sadia runs a health campaign in Peshawar to reduce the amount of salt that families add to their food. Using the health belief model, suggest two ways she could design the campaign to increase the chances that families change their behaviour.
parts.answer: e.g. make risk personal and relevant (perceived susceptibility and severity: high blood pressure and stroke, with local examples); show that cutting salt is easy and low-cost (reduce perceived barriers, e.g. using herbs and spices); give cues to action such as posters in shops and mosques; build self-efficacy through a simple reduction plan.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid suggestions, each linked to a named HBM component (max 4 marks, 2 per suggestion: 1 for suggestion, 1 for linking it to the model).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how implementation intentions could be used to increase the uptake of seasonal flu vaccination among older adults.
parts.answer: Implementation intentions are 'if–then' plans that link a situation to a specific action (e.g. 'If I get my pension collection letter, then I will book my flu jab at the clinic on the same day'). They reduce the gap between intention and action by making the plan automatic when the cue occurs.
parts.working: 1 mark for defining implementation intentions as if–then plans; 1 mark for an example linked to flu vaccination; 1 mark for explaining how they bridge the intention–behaviour gap; 1 mark for linking the cue to an automatic response.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using fear arousal in health promotion campaigns.
parts.answer: Very high fear can cause people to deny the risk or avoid the message, so the campaign may have less effect; Janis and Feshbach (1953) found that a high-fear dental message produced less behaviour change than a milder one.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying a weakness (defensive avoidance or reduced effect at high fear); 1 mark for a supporting explanation or reference.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way in which fear arousal messages could be made more effective.
parts.answer: Pair the fear message with clear, specific actions the audience can take and reassure them that the actions are achievable (high self-efficacy and response efficacy).
parts.working: 1 mark for a method; 1 mark for explaining why it increases effectiveness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the health belief model as an explanation of why people take up health-protective behaviour, such as vaccination, in a community in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Strengths: the model identifies clear components (susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers, cues to action, self-efficacy) that can be measured; it has been used to design campaigns and explain screening attendance; it highlights barriers that campaigns can address. Weaknesses: it is mainly based on rational decision-making and ignores emotion, habit and social norms; it does not predict behaviour well on its own (the intention–behaviour gap); cultural and religious beliefs (e.g. about vaccines) may be more important than the model's components; it is mostly tested with correlational or self-report data, so causal claims are limited. Application: a campaign in Pakistan would need to address local beliefs and trusted messengers as well as the model's components.
parts.working: Mark bands: 1–3 description of the model only; 4–6 some strengths and weaknesses with limited evidence; 7–8 balanced evaluation with specific research or application; 9–10 well-supported evaluation that links the model to the cultural context and considers the limits of rational decision models.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a government should focus health promotion on individual behaviour change or on changing the environment, using the example of food labelling in shops in Karachi.
parts.answer: Individual approach: education and labelling help individuals choose healthier food; it respects choice, but relies on people understanding and acting on labels and may increase inequality (people with low literacy or limited income may be less able to act). Situational approach: changing the environment (e.g. reducing sugar in shop products, placing healthy options at eye level, or taxing sugary drinks) affects everyone without relying on individual decisions; but it may be seen as restricting choice. Balanced conclusion: a combined approach is likely to be the most effective.
parts.working: 1–2 marks for description of one approach; 3–4 marks for each approach evaluated with a reason (max 4); 5–6 marks for application to food labelling in Karachi; 7–8 marks for a reasoned, balanced discussion with a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A health campaign in Karachi reached 5,000 adults. Of these, 1,250 said they intended to reduce their use of sugary drinks, and 300 were later found to have actually reduced their use. Calculate (i) the percentage of people reached who intended to change, (ii) the percentage of those who intended to change who actually changed, and (iii) the intention–behaviour gap in percentage points (the difference between the percentage who intended to change and the percentage of all people reached who actually changed). Give each answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: (i) 1250 ÷ 5000 × 100 = 25.0%. (ii) 300 ÷ 1250 × 100 = 24.0%. (iii) Percentage of all people who changed = 300 ÷ 5000 × 100 = 6.0%; gap = 25.0 − 6.0 = 19.0 percentage points.
parts.working: 1 mark for (i) 25.0%; 1 mark for (ii) 24.0%; 1 mark for 6.0% actual change of all reached; 1 mark for 19.0 percentage points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the role of the hypothalamus, the sympathetic nervous system and the adrenal medulla in the initial stress response.
parts.answer: The hypothalamus detects a threat and activates the sympathetic nervous system. The sympathetic branch stimulates the adrenal medulla to release adrenaline, which raises heart rate and breathing rate and sends more blood to the muscles, preparing the body to fight or flee.
parts.working: 1 mark for the hypothalamus detecting the threat and activating the sympathetic nervous system; 1 mark for the adrenal medulla releasing adrenaline; 1 mark for one physiological effect of adrenaline on the body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'stressor' and give one example of a daily hassle.
parts.answer: A stressor is an event or situation that triggers a stress response. Example: missing a bus or being stuck in heavy traffic on the way to work.
parts.working: 1 mark for a definition; 1 mark for an appropriate example of a daily hassle (minor, frequent event).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two physiological effects of stress that result from the release of adrenaline and cortisol.
parts.answer: e.g. increased heart rate, raised blood pressure, faster breathing, increased blood glucose, muscle tension.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct physiological effect (max 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the three phases of stress inoculation training (Meichenbaum), giving one coping skill that might be taught in one of the phases.
parts.answer: Conceptualisation: the person identifies their stressors and how they interpret them, e.g. by recording triggers and automatic thoughts. Skills acquisition: the person learns coping skills such as breathing control, relaxation, self-talk or problem-solving; e.g. learning slow breathing. Application and follow-through: the skills are practised in real situations, starting with less stressful ones, and progress is reviewed.
parts.working: 1 mark for each phase named and outlined (max 3); 1 mark for a relevant coping skill linked to a phase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of using a daily stress diary to measure stress in nurses.
parts.answer: Strength: stress is recorded close to the time it is experienced, so it is less affected by memory and gives a detailed picture of change over time. Weakness: keeping a diary is time-consuming for busy nurses, so they may stop or fill it in carelessly, and the act of recording may change how stressed they feel (reactivity).
parts.working: 1 mark for a strength; 1 mark for explaining it; 1 mark for a weakness; 1 mark for explaining it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of life-events scales, such as the Social Readjustment Rating Scale (Holmes and Rahe), to predict stress-related illness.
parts.answer: Strengths: the scale is quick to use and gives a numerical score; it has been used in many studies showing an association between life events and illness, so it has practical use in clinical settings; it is a standardised, objective measure of many events. Weaknesses: it does not measure how each person appraises an event (a wedding may be stressful or not); it includes positive events, which may not be stressful; it ignores daily hassles and coping resources (Kanner et al. showed hassles can be strong predictors); the correlations with illness are modest, so prediction is limited; the scores were developed in a particular cultural setting and may not apply to all cultures (e.g. in Pakistan, family events may carry different weight). Usefulness: good as a screening tool, but should be combined with measures of appraisal and coping.
parts.working: Mark bands: 1–3 description of scale only; 4–6 some evaluation with limited evidence; 7–8 balanced evaluation with specific points on validity and cultural applicability; 9–10 well-supported evaluation that weighs strengths and weaknesses and makes a justified recommendation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how cognitive appraisal (Lazarus) affects the stress response, referring to primary appraisal, secondary appraisal and coping.
parts.answer: Primary appraisal: the person judges whether an event is a threat, a harm or a challenge. Secondary appraisal: the person assesses their resources to cope (skills, support, time). The stress response depends on these appraisals: if the person perceives threat and few resources, stress is high. Coping: problem-focused or emotion-focused strategies are then chosen; effective coping reduces the stress response, while poor coping maintains it.
parts.working: 1 mark for primary appraisal defined; 1 mark for secondary appraisal defined; 1 mark for explaining that appraisal determines the intensity of stress; 1 mark for describing coping strategies; 1 mark for explaining the effect of coping on the stress response; 1 mark for a clear link across the model.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three patients in a Lahore clinic each had the following life events in the last year, scored with the life-change units (LCU) of the Social Readjustment Rating Scale. Patient A: death of a close family member (63) and change in financial state (38). Patient B: personal injury or illness (53), trouble with boss (23) and change in sleeping habits (16). Patient C: Christmas (12) and change in sleeping habits (16). Calculate the mean total LCU for the three patients, giving your answer to 1 decimal place. Then explain one reason why an LCU total cannot tell a clinician whether a patient will become ill.
parts.answer: Totals: A = 101, B = 92, C = 28; total 221; mean = 221 ÷ 3 = 73.7 LCU. Reason: the scale does not measure how each patient appraises an event or what coping resources and social support they have, so a high total may not lead to illness.
parts.working: 1 mark for the three totals (101, 92, 28) or the total 221; 1 mark for 73.7 LCU; 1 mark for a reason based on appraisal, coping or protective factors not being measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what is meant by 'nociception'.
parts.answer: Nociception is the detection of potentially damaging stimuli by sensory receptors (nociceptors) that send signals to the spinal cord and brain.
parts.working: 1 mark for detection of harmful stimuli by receptors; 1 mark for signals sent to the nervous system.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way that psychological factors such as anxiety can increase the pain a person feels.
parts.answer: Anxiety raises arousal and focuses attention on the pain, so the person perceives it as more intense; it may also increase muscle tension, which can add to the pain.
parts.working: 1 mark for a psychological mechanism (attention or arousal); 1 mark for explaining how it increases perceived pain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the role of endorphins in the experience of pain.
parts.answer: Endorphins are natural opioid-like chemicals released in the brain and spinal cord that reduce the transmission of pain signals and may produce feelings of relief.
parts.working: 1 mark for endorphins as natural pain-reducing chemicals; 1 mark for their effect on transmission or perception of pain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what is meant by the 'affective' dimension of pain, using one example.
parts.answer: The affective dimension is the emotional component of pain, such as feeling fear, distress or misery about it. Example: a patient describing a toothache as 'miserable' or 'frightening'.
parts.working: 1 mark for an emotional/feeling-based definition; 1 mark for an appropriate example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using gate control theory (Melzack and Wall), explain why rubbing a bruised elbow can reduce the pain felt.
parts.answer: Rubbing activates large-diameter nerve fibres, which send signals that close the 'gate' in the spinal cord, reducing the signals from small pain fibres. This reduces the pain signals reaching the brain.
parts.working: 1 mark for large-diameter fibres activated by rubbing; 1 mark for closing the gate in the dorsal horn; 1 mark for reduced pain signals passing to the brain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mr Tariq, a 45-year-old office worker in Quetta, has a broken wrist that must be set while the doctor works on it. Explain how attention diversion could reduce Mr Tariq's experience of pain during the procedure, and suggest one task the nurse could ask him to do.
parts.answer: Attention diversion means directing attention to something other than the pain, so fewer attentional resources are given to the pain signals and the pain feels less intense. The nurse could ask Mr Tariq to count backwards in sevens, or to describe a favourite place in detail, during the procedure.
parts.working: 1 mark for defining attention diversion; 1 mark for explaining reduced attention to pain signals; 1 mark for an appropriate task; 1 mark for linking this to reduced perceived pain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Patients in a clinic rated their pain on a 100 mm visual analogue scale (0 = no pain, 100 = worst possible pain) before and after a relaxation programme. Their ratings before were 72, 65, 80, 58, 90 and 70 mm; after the programme they were 40, 52, 60, 35, 71 and 48 mm. Calculate the percentage of patients whose pain rating fell by at least 20 mm, giving your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Reductions: 32, 13, 20, 23, 19, 22 mm. Patients with a reduction of at least 20 mm: 32, 20, 23 and 22 mm, so 4 of the 6 patients. 4 ÷ 6 × 100 = 66.7%.
parts.working: 1 mark for listing the reductions; 1 mark for identifying 4 patients (including the 20 mm reduction); 1 mark for 66.7%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Farmer Riaz in Sindh has chronic back pain. He believes that the pain means his back is permanently damaged and that he can never work again. Explain how cognitive redefinition could help him, and identify one limitation of this technique for Riaz.
parts.answer: Cognitive redefinition involves changing how the person thinks about the pain, for example seeing it as a sign of muscle strain that can recover rather than permanent damage. Riaz would learn to replace 'my back is ruined' with 'this pain is a signal that I need to rest and build strength'. Limitation: changing beliefs takes time and requires a trained therapist; if the pain is caused by an underlying medical condition, redefining it does not treat it, and Riaz may feel that his experience is being dismissed.
parts.working: 1 mark for defining cognitive redefinition; 1 mark for relevant example for Riaz; 1 mark for explaining how the new belief reduces pain perception; 1 mark for a limitation; 1 mark for explaining the limitation; 1 mark for linking to the case.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the visual analogue scale (VAS) and the Wong-Baker FACES scale (six cartoon faces, from no hurt to hurts worst) as measures of pain in children.
parts.answer: VAS: quick, simple and sensitive to small changes, so it suits repeated measurement; but it gives a single number, and a child must understand a line or numbers to rate pain on an abstract scale. Wong-Baker FACES: children can simply point to a face, so it suits young children who cannot read or describe pain in words; but it gives only one dimension (intensity), has fewer response options than a 100 mm line so it is less sensitive to small changes, and the choice of face may be influenced by the order of the faces or by a wish to please. Evaluation should consider validity, reliability, the child's age and practicality; a combined approach with behavioural observation is suggested.
parts.working: Mark bands: 1–3 description of one or both measures; 4–6 some strengths and weaknesses with limited justification; 7–8 balanced evaluation with specific points on validity, reliability and practicality; 9–10 well-reasoned evaluation for children, with a justified recommendation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how individual differences in pain thresholds, such as cultural background and levels of anxiety, could affect the pain that patients report for the same injury.
parts.answer: Cultural background shapes how pain is expressed and what is considered acceptable to report, so people from some cultures may report less or more pain for the same injury. High anxiety increases attention to pain and perceived intensity, so the same stimulus is experienced as more painful.
parts.working: 1 mark for an individual difference; 1 mark for explaining how it affects pain expression or perception; 1 mark for a second individual difference; 1 mark for linking to differences in reported pain for the same injury.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'non-adherence' and give one example of it for a patient on a 30-day antibiotic course.
parts.answer: Non-adherence is when a patient does not follow the treatment or advice given by a health professional, for example by stopping the course early or missing doses. Example: taking the antibiotic for 10 days and then stopping when symptoms improve.
parts.working: 1 mark for a definition; 1 mark for an appropriate example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one treatment-related factor and one patient-related factor that could reduce adherence to medical advice.
parts.answer: Treatment-related: a complex regimen with many doses or side effects. Patient-related: forgetfulness, or beliefs that the treatment is unnecessary.
parts.working: 1 mark for a treatment-related factor; 1 mark for a patient-related factor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why patients may forget medical instructions they have been given by a doctor.
parts.answer: The consultation may be short and filled with unfamiliar terms; patients are anxious and cannot absorb a lot of information at once, so key details are lost.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reason; 1 mark for explaining how it leads to forgetting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Over a 120-day follow-up period, a pharmacy record shows that a patient collected three refills, each covering 30 days of medicine, with no overlaps. Calculate the proportion of days covered (PDC) as a percentage, giving your answer to 1 decimal place. Explain why PDC may give a more accurate picture of adherence than a self-report question.
parts.answer: Days covered = 3 × 30 = 90; PDC = 90 ÷ 120 × 100 = 75.0%. Self-report may be affected by social desirability or poor recall; refill records are an objective measure of the medicine supplied, though they do not prove the patient took the tablets.
parts.working: 1 mark for 90 days covered; 1 mark for 75.0%; 1 mark for an advantage of PDC (objective, record-based); 1 mark for noting its limitation (supply does not prove consumption).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of electronic monitoring (such as a pill bottle cap that records when it is opened) as a measure of adherence.
parts.answer: Strength: it gives an objective, time-stamped record of when the container is opened, so it is less affected by social desirability than self-report. Weakness: it records that the container was opened, not that the patient took the tablet; it is expensive and may be ignored or disabled by the patient.
parts.working: 1 mark for a strength; 1 mark for explaining it; 1 mark for a weakness; 1 mark for explaining it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hakim, aged 70, lives in Quetta. He has been prescribed four different tablets each day for heart disease and diabetes. He often forgets some of his tablets and is confused about which tablet to take at which time. Suggest two ways a doctor could improve Hakim's adherence.
parts.answer: e.g. simplify the regimen (fewer tablets, combined tablets or a single daily time); use a pill organiser or reminder alarms; give a written schedule in Urdu with pictures; involve a family member who can help; check the regimen at each visit.
parts.working: 1 mark for each suggestion (max 2); 1 mark for explaining how each would reduce the problem (max 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the health belief model, explain why a patient with high cholesterol might not take prescribed statins.
parts.answer: The patient may not perceive themselves as susceptible or the condition as severe because they feel well; they may believe the perceived barriers (side effects, cost, inconvenience) outweigh the benefits; without a cue to action, such as a reminder, they forget; low self-efficacy may mean they doubt they can keep to a daily routine.
parts.working: 1 mark for a component of the model (susceptibility or severity) explained; 1 mark for perceived barriers outweighing benefits; 1 mark for cues to action or self-efficacy; 1 mark for a clear link to adherence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of pill counts and electronic monitoring as measures of adherence in children with asthma attending a clinic in Hyderabad.
parts.answer: Pill counts: cheap and simple; count remaining medication; but children may take doses out of sight, parents may top up tablets, and counts do not show when or how doses were taken. Electronic monitoring: gives time-stamped records of use, giving more detail; but it records when the device was used, not whether the medicine was inhaled correctly; it is expensive, the child may be aware of monitoring (reactivity), and devices can fail. Evaluation should consider validity, practicality and ethics (e.g. parental consent and privacy) and suggest that a combination is more accurate.
parts.working: 1–2 marks for a description of one measure; 3–4 marks for a clear evaluation of pill counts with limitations; 5–6 marks for electronic monitoring evaluated; 7–8 marks for a balanced comparison with a justified conclusion, reference to children and clinical context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient is prescribed one tablet twice a day for 20 days. A diary kept by the patient shows that on 15 of the 20 days both tablets were taken. Calculate the percentage of days on which all prescribed doses were taken, giving your answer to 1 decimal place. Explain one reason why this figure may still overestimate the patient's true adherence.
parts.answer: 15 ÷ 20 × 100 = 75.0% of days. The diary is self-report, so the patient may over-report doses taken (social desirability) or record doses from memory inaccurately; a day marked as fully taken may also include a dose taken at the wrong time or not swallowed.
parts.working: 1 mark for 15 fully adhered days; 1 mark for 75.0%; 1 mark for explaining that a diary is self-report that may be inaccurate; 1 mark for a second reason (e.g. wrong timing or not swallowed) linked to overestimation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss individual and situational explanations for non-adherence in people with type 2 diabetes who are prescribed a daily medicine and advised to change their diet.
parts.answer: Individual explanations: beliefs about the need for treatment (low perceived severity), poor self-efficacy, forgetfulness, emotional state (depression), low health literacy, preference for food over diet. Situational explanations: complex or costly medicine supply, side effects, long waiting times, lack of support from family, poor communication from clinicians, cultural food habits and shared meals, rural distance from clinics. Discussion: individual explanations can lead to victim-blaming and focus on changing patients, whereas situational explanations suggest practical changes (cheaper supplies, simpler regimens, community support). Interaction: both usually operate together; the most useful explanation depends on the evidence and the aim (e.g. intervention design). A balanced conclusion is expected.
parts.working: Mark bands: 1–3 description of one explanation; 4–6 individual and situational explanations described with examples; 7–8 applied to the case with a comparison; 9–10 a critical, balanced discussion including the interaction of the two and the implications for intervention.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a practitioner's use of closed questions can limit the information a patient gives during a consultation.
parts.answer: Closed questions have a fixed or yes/no answer, so the patient gives a short reply and may not mention concerns or background that the doctor has not asked about. Open questions invite fuller answers that show the patient's own view.
parts.working: 1 mark for closed questions restricting the patient to short or fixed replies; 1 mark for explaining that relevant concerns may then go unmentioned.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'empathy' in the context of a doctor–patient consultation and give one example of an empathic response.
parts.answer: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the patient's feelings and perspective, communicated to the patient. Example: 'That sounds like a very frightening time for you; tell me what worries you most.'
parts.working: 1 mark for a definition (understanding the patient's feelings); 1 mark for an appropriate example of a response.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why a doctor may use medical jargon with patients, and suggest one way to avoid this problem.
parts.answer: Jargon can be a habit from training or a way of sounding professional, but it can confuse patients who do not understand the terms. Suggest using plain language and checking understanding by asking the patient to repeat the key points.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reason for jargon; 1 mark for a suggestion to avoid it with explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a consultation in a Karachi clinic, the doctor spoke for 14 minutes and the patient spoke for 6 minutes. Calculate the percentage of the total talking time that was spoken by the doctor. Explain what this figure suggests about the style of the consultation.
parts.answer: Total = 20 minutes; doctor's share = 14 ÷ 20 × 100 = 70%. This suggests a doctor-centred consultation, in which the patient has limited opportunity to express concerns.
parts.working: 1 mark for total 20 minutes; 1 mark for 70%; 1 mark for linking the figure to a doctor-centred style.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why a patient may not disclose important symptoms to a doctor.
parts.answer: The patient may feel embarrassed or fear judgement (e.g. about sexual health or alcohol use), or may think the symptom is unimportant.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reason; 1 mark for explaining how it prevents disclosure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way a practitioner could encourage a patient to disclose symptoms.
parts.answer: Use open questions and show empathy, reassure the patient about confidentiality, and ask directly about sensitive topics in a non-judgemental way.
parts.working: 1 mark for a suggestion; 1 mark for explaining how it reduces the barrier to disclosure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dr Zoya works in a clinic in Islamabad. Many of her patients forget what she has told them about their medicines. Using research on recall of medical information, suggest two ways Dr Zoya could improve her patients' recall.
parts.answer: e.g. give no more than two or three key points at a time; use simple language and explain terms; provide written information or a summary card; ask the patient to repeat the instructions back; arrange follow-up. Research on recall of medical advice shows patients forget a large part of what they are told, and that recall improves with simpler, shorter and written information.
parts.working: 1 mark for each suggestion (max 2); 1 mark for explaining how it improves recall (max 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of patient satisfaction questionnaires to measure the quality of doctor–patient consultations.
parts.answer: Strengths: quick to complete; allows large samples; gives a standardised score that can be compared across clinics; it reflects patients' views of care. Weaknesses: satisfaction may be high even when care is poor (patients may not know what good care is, or be grateful and reluctant to criticise); social desirability; questionnaires may not capture the detail of the communication; response rates may be low and biased; satisfaction is not the same as adherence or health outcomes; questions may not be tailored to the patient's language or culture. Improvement: combine with observation of consultations or outcome measures.
parts.working: 1–2 marks for a description of questionnaires; 3–4 marks for one strength and one weakness explained; 5–6 marks for a balanced evaluation with specific issues; 7–8 marks for a conclusion with suggested improvements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether patient-centred consultations are more effective than doctor-centred consultations at improving attendance at follow-up appointments after a diagnosis of hypertension. Refer to research evidence and to the limitations of that evidence.
parts.answer: Patient-centred consultations may improve understanding, satisfaction and trust, which can make patients more likely to attend follow-ups. Evidence: studies often compare styles using observation and patient questionnaires, and show links between patient-centred communication and satisfaction or recall. Limitations: much of this evidence is correlational, so the style may reflect other differences (e.g. more motivated patients or longer consultations); attendance is often taken from clinic records, which may be incomplete; findings may not transfer across cultures or healthcare systems; doctor-centred consultations may be efficient in short appointments. Conclusion: patient-centred consultations are probably helpful, but the evidence does not show with certainty that they are more effective; a controlled study with random allocation of consultation style would be needed.
parts.working: Mark bands: 1–3 limited description of the two styles; 4–6 evidence and at least one limitation with reasons; 7–8 balanced evaluation of effectiveness, quality of evidence and generalisation; 9–10 well-supported conclusion with a justified suggestion for a stronger study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A clinic audits 60 consultations. After each consultation, patients were asked to recall in their own words two or more instructions given by the doctor. 42 patients recalled at least two instructions correctly; 18 did not. Calculate the percentage of patients who recalled at least two instructions, and the percentage who did not.
parts.answer: Recalled at least two = 42 ÷ 60 × 100 = 70.0%; did not recall = 18 ÷ 60 × 100 = 30.0%.
parts.working: 1 mark for 70.0%; 1 mark for 30.0%; 1 mark for a suitable note that the two sum to 100% (or a correct interpretation of the finding).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dr Kamal's patients often look away or check their phones during consultations. Explain how a practitioner's body language, such as eye contact and posture, can affect the patient's trust and willingness to share information.
parts.answer: Eye contact and an open posture communicate attention and warmth, which increases patient trust and willingness to disclose. Distraction (checking a screen) or turning away signals low interest, which can make patients withhold information or feel dismissed. Body language also affects how patients interpret the words used.
parts.working: 1 mark for a specific non-verbal behaviour; 1 mark for the message it sends; 1 mark for the effect on trust; 1 mark for the effect on disclosure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Baron-Cohen et al. included an IQ-matched group as well as the group from the general population.
parts.answer: To check whether low Eyes Test scores in the Asperger syndrome/high-functioning autism group could be explained simply by lower general intelligence. The IQ-matched group had similar IQ but scored much higher, so intelligence alone does not explain the difference.
parts.working: 1 mark for controlling intelligence (IQ as a possible confounding variable); 1 mark for explaining that the IQ-matched group scored higher, so the low score is not just due to intelligence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the Eyes Test is designed to measure.
parts.answer: Theory of mind: the ability to recognise another person's thoughts or feelings from the eye region of a face.
parts.working: B1: theory of mind / recognising mental states from the eyes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one reason why a low score on the Eyes Test might not reflect poor theory of mind.
parts.answer: A participant may not know the meaning of one of the four target words, so they choose the wrong word for a language reason rather than a social one; or they may be tired or not paying attention.
parts.working: 1 mark for a vocabulary or word-meaning reason; 1 mark for an attention, fatigue or motivation reason. Accept other sensible non-mentalising reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way researchers could test whether the Eyes Test measures theory of mind rather than general vocabulary.
parts.answer: Give participants a vocabulary test with similarly difficult words and compare the scores with the Eyes Test. If the Eyes Test still separates the groups, and the vocabulary test does not, the test is more likely to measure theory of mind.
parts.working: 1 mark for a suggested comparison (a vocabulary task, a control task, or a second theory of mind measure); 1 mark for explaining what the result would show (validity).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Eyes Test was scored, including the range of possible scores.
parts.answer: Each of the 36 photographs scored one point if the participant chose the correct word out of four options. Scores therefore range from 0 to 36.
parts.working: 1 mark for one point per correct answer; 1 mark for the four-option choice; 1 mark for the range 0 to 36.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A clinician in Karachi wants to use the Revised Eyes Test in the assessment of an adult referred for possible Asperger syndrome. Explain how she could use the test alongside other information, and give one reason why the test should not be used on its own.
parts.answer: She could combine the score with a clinical interview, the person's developmental history and a questionnaire such as the AQ, comparing the score with the norms for the general population. The test should not be used alone because many adults with low scores do not have autism, and it measures only one aspect of social cognition, so it cannot confirm a diagnosis.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for describing how the test is combined with other information (interview, history, AQ, comparison with norms); 1 mark for a reason it should not be used alone (only one aspect; low scores occur in people without autism; not diagnostic); 1 mark for applying the answer to this adult.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Baron-Cohen et al.'s study in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your points must be about the construct validity of the Eyes Test as a measure of theory of mind.
parts.answer: Strengths: the same 36 photographs and four-word forced choice were used for every group, so scores are standardised and can be compared; the IQ-matched group makes it more likely that the low scores reflect social cognition rather than general intelligence. Weaknesses: a low score may reflect a vocabulary problem or lack of attention rather than poor theory of mind, so the test may not measure only the construct it claims to measure (weak construct validity); the Asperger syndrome/high-functioning autism group was small (15 men), so results may not generalise to women or to all autistic adults.
parts.working: Level-based. 9–10 marks: two strengths and two weaknesses, each developed and linked to the study, with at least one point on construct validity and a balanced judgement. 5–8 marks: points present but less developed, or no clear construct validity point. 1–4 marks: descriptive or unlinked points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why Andrade used a monotonous (boring) mock telephone message rather than an interesting story.
parts.answer: A boring message makes daydreaming more likely; the researcher wanted to see whether doodling could keep attention on the message when attention would normally drift, so any effect on memory could be seen.
parts.working: 1 mark for linking a boring task to daydreaming or mind-wandering; 1 mark for linking doodling to keeping attention on the message (the hypothesis).

stem: In a hypothetical follow-up study, 24 participants in a doodling group recalled a mean of 9.0 items from a message, and 24 participants in a non-doodling group recalled a mean of 7.2 items. The study is hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the doodling group's mean recall was higher. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 subtract the means (1.8) and divide by the control mean (7.2); A1 25.0%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a researcher should be careful about using this result to recommend doodling in school lessons.
parts.answer: Only 24 people per group took part, so a chance difference could explain the result. A list of names and places is also much simpler than a real lesson, so the result may not apply to learning complex material.
parts.working: 1 mark for a sample or chance point (small groups, one study); 1 mark for an ecological validity or generalisation point about the simple task.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one ethical consideration in asking participants to sit through a boring task, and say how it could be reduced.
parts.answer: Protection from harm: participants may become bored, irritated or tired. This could be reduced by letting them leave at any time and by debriefing them afterwards.
parts.working: 1 mark for the ethical issue (protection from harm or distress, or right to withdraw); 1 mark for a way to reduce it (right to withdraw, debriefing, keeping the task short).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a researcher might measure daydreaming directly, rather than only testing recall, when testing Andrade's explanation.
parts.answer: Recall alone cannot show that doodling reduced daydreaming; measuring daydreaming (for example with a self-report scale) would show whether the mechanism proposed in the explanation really happened.
parts.working: 1 mark for explaining that recall does not test the proposed mechanism; 1 mark for explaining that measuring daydreaming tests the explanation directly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way daydreaming could be measured during the task.
parts.answer: Ask participants to rate on a scale how much their thoughts drifted away from the message, or to say at intervals whether they were thinking about something else.
parts.working: 1 mark for a method (self-report rating, thought-sampling at intervals); 1 mark for the detail of how it would work.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teacher in Lahore asks whether pupils should be allowed to doodle during a lesson to help them remember. Using Andrade's study, explain two reasons why the answer might be yes and one reason why it might be no.
parts.answer: Yes: doodling may stop pupils daydreaming during dull parts, so more of the lesson is attended to; doodling may improve recall of spoken information. No: Andrade's task was simple and not a real lesson, so doodling may distract from complex material; the study has not shown that doodling helps in real classrooms.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons why yes (reduces daydreaming or keeps attention; improves recall of spoken material); 1 mark for a reason why no (complex material, distraction, lack of classroom evidence); 1 mark for explanation of the reason to the teacher's setting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Andrade's study is taken to show that doodling improves memory. Explain one alternative explanation for a difference in recall between the two groups that does not depend on doodling improving attention.
parts.answer: Individual differences: even after random allocation, the doodling group might contain participants who were naturally better at remembering lists, so the difference could be chance or differences between people rather than the doodling itself. A participant who enjoyed the task may also have been more motivated to listen.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming an alternative (chance, individual differences, motivation, or demand characteristics); up to 3 marks for explaining how it could produce the difference without doodling improving attention.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms 'correct rejection' and 'hit' as used in line-up research.
parts.answer: Correct rejection: in a target-absent line-up, correctly saying that the culprit is not present. Hit: in a target-present line-up, correctly identifying the person who was the culprit.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct definition (in the right type of line-up).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline two instructions a police officer should give a witness before showing a line-up.
parts.answer: The culprit may or may not be in the line-up; the witness does not have to choose anyone and may say the person is not there; the witness should take as long as they need.
parts.working: 1 mark for each relevant instruction (culprit may be absent; no obligation to choose; "not there" is acceptable; no time pressure). Accept any two.

stem: A hypothetical study showed target-absent line-ups to 50 children and 50 adults. Children made a false positive identification on 22 of the 50 trials; adults made a false positive on 9 of the 50 trials. The study is hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of target-absent trials on which (i) children and (ii) adults made a false positive identification.
parts.working: 1 mark for 44%; 1 mark for 18%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why this difference does not prove that children's memory is poorer than adults' memory.
parts.answer: Children may want to please the adult or may think they must choose someone, so their false positives may reflect social compliance or response bias rather than memory. They may also misunderstand the procedure.
parts.working: 1 mark for a social or response-bias explanation (compliance, wanting to please); 1 mark for a procedural explanation (misunderstanding the instructions or the task).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why each line-up needs several foils (other people who are not the culprit) as well as the suspect.
parts.answer: If the suspect were the only person who matched the description, he would stand out, and the witness could pick him for that reason rather than from memory. Several foils make the choice depend on memory and reduce false identifications.
parts.working: 1 mark for the suspect should not stand out; 1 mark for the choice then depends on memory; 1 mark for linking foils to reducing false positives or bias.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one extraneous variable that a line-up study should control, and suggest how the researcher could control it.
parts.answer: The time the witness is allowed to view the culprit at the crime, which should be the same for all participants; the researcher can use a standard recording or a fixed viewing time.
parts.working: 1 mark for a suitable extraneous variable (viewing time, lighting, delay before the line-up); 1 mark for a control (standard viewing time, same recording, same delay).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a line-up procedure that is fair for adults might be unfair for a seven-year-old witness.
parts.answer: A seven-year-old may not understand that the culprit may be absent, may be unable to hold the faces in memory during a long line-up, may find it hard to say that they are not sure, and may want to please the adult conducting the procedure, so the procedure is not equally fair.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark each for two different reasons related to understanding, memory load, language or compliance; 1 mark for a clear link to why the procedure is unfair (e.g. more false positives).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how using both target-present and target-absent line-ups allows a researcher to measure two different kinds of error in a witness's identification.
parts.answer: In a target-absent line-up, any identification is a false positive, so this measures the tendency to pick an innocent person. In a target-present line-up, a witness who does not identify the culprit has made a miss (false negative), so this measures the failure to recognise the person who was really there.
parts.working: 1 mark for explaining a false positive measured in target-absent line-ups; 1 mark for explaining a miss or false negative measured in target-present line-ups; 1 mark each for explaining why one type of line-up cannot measure the other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one ethical issue in using children as witnesses in a line-up study, and explain one way the issue could be reduced.
parts.answer: Protection from harm: a child may feel distressed or upset at being asked to pick out a person, or may feel they have failed. This could be reduced by making the task clear, telling children they can say "not there", and debriefing them.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming the ethical issue (protection from harm or distress, or informed consent for a child); 1 mark for explaining why it is an issue; 1 mark for a reduction (right to withdraw, clear instructions, debriefing with parents).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of laboratory line-up studies to explain the accuracy of real eyewitnesses, in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses.
parts.answer: Strengths: the researcher controls the target, the procedure and the time, so cause and effect can be tested; quantitative counts of hits and false positives allow objective comparison between children and adults. Weaknesses: participants know the situation is not real, so they may not take it as seriously as a real witness, reducing ecological validity; real crimes involve stress, delays and suggestive questioning that are not present in the lab, so results may not generalise to real eyewitnesses.
parts.working: Level-based. 9–10 marks: two strengths and two weaknesses, each explained and linked to line-up research, with a balanced judgement. 5–8 marks: some explanation but less developed or unbalanced. 1–4 marks: descriptive, unlinked points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Laney et al. hid the true aim of their study from participants.
parts.answer: To reduce demand characteristics: if participants knew the study was about asparagus and childhood memories, they might guess what was expected and change their answers about how much they liked it.
parts.working: 1 mark for demand characteristics or guessing the aim; 1 mark for the effect on participants' answers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a 'false memory', and give one example from Laney et al.'s study.
parts.answer: A false memory is a memory of an event that did not happen, or a distorted version of a real event, which the person believes to be accurate. In the study, a false memory was the belief that the participant had loved asparagus as a child.
parts.working: 1 mark for the definition (memory of something that did not happen or is distorted, believed to be true); 1 mark for a correct example from the study.

stem: In a hypothetical follow-up study, 18 of 24 participants in the love group were classed as believers, compared with 4 of 24 participants in a control group. The study is hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of each group who were believers. Give each answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 divide each number of believers by 24 and multiply by 100; A1 both answers correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one conclusion and one limitation of these hypothetical results.
parts.answer: Conclusion: the false feedback was associated with many more believers than in the control group, so it may have helped create false memories. Limitation: the groups are small (24 each), so chance could explain some of the difference, and believers may simply be going along with the feedback.
parts.working: 1 mark for a conclusion linked to the false feedback; 1 mark for a limitation (small groups, chance, self-report, compliance).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it is difficult to know whether a participant's report of a childhood memory is accurate.
parts.answer: Memory is reconstructive, so it can change over time as new information is added; there is no independent record of the childhood event to check against, so the participant may be confabulating or guessing.
parts.working: 1 mark for memory being reconstructive or changing over time; 1 mark for the lack of an independent record or the risk of guessing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest one way the researchers could check whether believers were genuinely influenced by the feedback, rather than only going along with it.
parts.answer: Measure behaviour as well as self-reported attitudes, for example how much asparagus participants chose to eat or how much they were willing to pay, since behaviour is harder to fake than a questionnaire answer. Repeating the measure later would also show whether the change lasted.
parts.working: 1 mark for a behavioural measure; 1 mark for explaining why behaviour is a better check than self-report; 1 mark for a second check (repeat measure later, comparison with control).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one extraneous variable that could affect believers' liking for asparagus and suggest how it could be controlled.
parts.answer: Participants' existing liking of vegetables in general (or how hungry they were when answering). It could be controlled by measuring baseline food preferences before the feedback and allocating participants to groups at random.
parts.working: 1 mark for a suitable extraneous variable; 1 mark for a suitable control (baseline measure, random allocation, standard conditions).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher argues that Laney et al.'s findings show that all childhood memories can easily be changed. Explain two reasons why this conclusion goes beyond the evidence.
parts.answer: The false memory concerned a low-stakes food preference, not a significant emotional event, so it cannot show that all memories change. The study used a small sample of volunteers in one setting, so it cannot show how common false memories are. Also, only some participants became believers, showing that the effect is not universal.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason, 1 for stating it and 1 for explaining why it limits the conclusion (trivial memory; small or unrepresentative sample; only some believed the feedback).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline two reasons why a researcher should debrief participants after a study that gave them false feedback.
parts.answer: To tell them the true aim and the feedback was false, so that they are not left believing something untrue about their own childhood; to allow them to withdraw their data; and to check they are not distressed.
parts.working: 1 mark for each relevant reason (correct the false belief; right to withdraw data; check for distress), up to 3 marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the cognitive approach, explain how Laney et al.'s finding could be explained by the reconstructive nature of memory.
parts.answer: Memory is not a copy of events but is built from existing schemas and new information.
