The feedback provided new information that was combined with the participant's existing schema about asparagus and their childhood, so the participant reconstructed a memory of liking it, which then influenced their current attitude and behaviour.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for stating that memory is reconstructive; 1 mark for schemas or existing knowledge; 1 mark for the feedback as new information; 1 mark for how the reconstructed memory affects attitudes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Laney et al.'s study in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your points must be about the use of questionnaire data.
parts.answer: Strengths: a cover story and filler items reduced demand characteristics; questionnaires gave quantitative data on liking and willingness to pay that could be compared between believers and non-believers. Weaknesses: attitudes were self-reported, so participants might have said what they thought the researchers wanted; the sample of volunteers may not represent the wider public, and the study used a trivial food memory, which limits generalisation.
parts.working: Level-based. 9–10 marks: two strengths and two weaknesses, developed and linked, at least one about questionnaire data, with a balanced judgement. 5–8 marks: less developed or unbalanced. 1–4 marks: descriptive or unlinked.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the cognitive approach assumes about the processes between a stimulus and a response.
parts.answer: Internal mental processes (for example attention, perception, memory and thinking) mediate between a stimulus and the response, so behaviour cannot be fully understood without them.
parts.working: 1 mark for internal mental processes mediating between stimulus and response; 1 mark for explaining that behaviour depends on these processes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what is meant by a 'schema' in the cognitive approach.
parts.answer: A schema is an organised mental framework of knowledge, built from experience, which helps a person interpret new information, predict events and direct attention and memory.
parts.working: 1 mark for a mental framework or organised knowledge built from experience; 1 mark for its function (interpreting or predicting, guiding attention or memory).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the computer analogy of human cognition.
parts.answer: The mind is compared with a computer: sensory information is input, mental processes such as encoding, storage and retrieval transform it, and behaviour is the output, just as a computer processes data and produces a result.
parts.working: 1 mark for input (information received by the senses); 1 mark for processing (encoding, storage, retrieval, thinking); 1 mark for output as behaviour or response.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why cognitive psychologists have to infer mental processes rather than observe them directly. Refer to one study from the cognitive approach.
parts.answer: Mental processes such as memory or attention cannot be seen directly, so psychologists infer them from behaviour, such as the number of correct answers or the choices people make. For example, in Pozzulo et al.'s study, the difference in false positives was used to infer differences in how children process faces.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for mental processes cannot be observed directly; 1 mark for inference from behaviour or performance; 1 mark for an example from a named study; 1 mark for linking the example to inference.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Andrade's study supports the assumption that attention is a limited cognitive resource.
parts.answer: Participants listening to a dull message were more likely to daydream, so their attention drifted from the message. Doodling kept attention on the message (or reduced the drift into daydreaming) and so more names were recalled. This suggests attention has to be directed to one task and that a drift in attention reduces what is processed.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for attention drifting in the boring condition; 1 mark for doodling directing attention; 1 mark for linking attention to memory performance; 1 mark for the idea of limited attention.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the cognitive approach's assumption that internal mental processes cause behaviour is a strength or a weakness of the approach. Refer to one study in your answer.
parts.answer: Strength: the assumption explains why people in the same situation can differ, for example in Baron-Cohen et al.'s Eyes Test, where adults with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism scored lower than controls, which points to differences in internal social processing rather than just the photographs. Weakness: mental processes can be inferred but not measured directly, so the assumption relies on indirect evidence, and it may underplay the role of the environment and learning.
parts.working: Level-based. 5–6 marks: a clear judgement with an explained strength and weakness, supported by a named study. 3–4 marks: one side developed or not linked to a study. 1–2 marks: descriptive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one way evidence from cognitive neuroscience supports the cognitive approach.
parts.answer: Brain-imaging techniques such as fMRI show increased activity in specific brain areas during memory or attention tasks, which suggests that mental processes have a physical basis and can be studied scientifically.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming a technique or type of evidence (brain imaging, fMRI, PET, brain damage studies); 1 mark for explaining what it shows about mental processes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two cognitive processes and give one everyday example of each.
parts.answer: Attention: noticing a bus number while walking past a bus stop. Memory: recalling a friend's phone number when you need to call them. (Accept any clear example of perception, language, decision-making or thinking.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correctly identified process with a clear everyday example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the computer analogy as a model of human cognition, in terms of one strength and one weakness.
parts.answer: Strength: the analogy gives a clear model of stages (input, processing, output) that can be tested and that led to the study of memory stores and processes. Weakness: computers process information in a fixed, logical way, whereas human cognition is influenced by emotions, motivation and context, so the analogy oversimplifies how people think.
parts.working: Level-based. 5–6 marks: a strength and a weakness, both explained and evaluated, with a judgement. 3–4 marks: one side developed. 1–2 marks: descriptive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the cognitive approach would account for two people with the same experience remembering it differently.
parts.answer: Each person has different schemas and attended to different features of the event, so they encoded and stored different information. Later reconstruction of the memory is also influenced by each person's existing knowledge and expectations.
parts.working: 1 mark for different schemas or knowledge; 1 mark for different attention or encoding; 1 mark for reconstruction of the memory later.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how the cognitive approach differs from the learning approach in explaining behaviour.
parts.answer: The cognitive approach focuses on internal mental processes such as memory and attention that mediate behaviour, whereas the learning approach focuses on observable behaviour and how the environment (reinforcement, conditioning, modelling) shapes it.
parts.working: 1 mark for the cognitive approach focusing on internal processes; 1 mark for the learning approach focusing on observable behaviour and environment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one limitation of using the computer analogy to study thinking in real people.
parts.answer: People's thinking is affected by emotions, motivation and the social situation, which a computer does not have, so experiments on isolated tasks may not reflect everyday thinking. Also, computers follow precise rules, whereas people often use shortcuts and make errors.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying the limitation; 1 mark for explaining why it matters for real thinking; 1 mark for a human factor (emotion, motivation, heuristics or errors); 1 mark for applying it to the study of real people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the researchers used a forced-choice format (four words to choose from) rather than asking participants to describe what the person in each photograph was feeling.
parts.answer: Choosing from four words makes scoring quick and objective, so every participant's answers can be compared in the same way across the four groups; free description would need subjective judgements of whether an answer was correct.
parts.working: 1 mark for objective or standardised scoring; 1 mark for comparability across participants or groups. Accept that it limits the richness of answers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest one way a line-up study could record a witness's confidence, and explain why this information is useful to researchers.
parts.answer: Ask the witness to rate how confident they are in their choice on a scale (for example 0 to 100) immediately after the decision. Confidence is useful because researchers can check whether high-confidence identifications are more often correct, which matters for how far a witness's certainty should be trusted.
parts.working: 1 mark for a method of recording confidence (rating scale immediately after the choice); 1 mark for explaining that confidence can be compared with accuracy; 1 mark for why this helps assess the reliability of identifications.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'mental representation', and give one example from memory research.
parts.answer: A mental representation is an internal model or image of an object, event or idea that stands in for it when it is not present. For example, a memory of a face lets a witness recognise the same person in a line-up even when the person is not in view.
parts.working: 1 mark for an internal model or representation of something absent; 1 mark for linking it to stored information; 1 mark for a clear example from memory research.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the dependent variable in Bandura et al.'s study of the imitation of aggression, and give one example of a behaviour that was recorded.
parts.answer: The dependent variable was the number of imitative acts (for example physical aggression, verbal aggression or non-aggressive responses) shown by each child in the test room. Example: hitting the Bobo doll with a mallet.
parts.working: 1 mark for the dependent variable (number or type of imitative behaviour recorded); 1 mark for a correct example (e.g. punching or hitting the Bobo doll, shouting "Sock him").

stem: In a hypothetical replication, 24 children who watched an aggressive adult model produced 84 imitative physical aggressive acts in the test room in total. A separate group of 24 children who saw no model produced 12 such acts in total. The study is hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of imitative physical aggressive acts per child in each condition.
parts.answer: Aggressive model: 84 ÷ 24 = 3.5 acts per child. No-model control: 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5 acts per child.
parts.working: M1 divide each total by 24 children; A1 both means correct (3.5 and 0.5).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the study needed a control group in which children saw no model.
parts.answer: The control group shows how often children behave aggressively without seeing any aggression, so any higher rate in the aggressive-model group can be attributed to the model.
parts.working: 1 mark for a baseline or comparison point; 1 mark for showing that the difference can be attributed to the model.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Bandura et al.'s findings do not show that children will always imitate the aggression they see.
parts.answer: Not all children imitated the aggression; there were individual differences in how far children imitated the model. Imitation also depends on the situation: children who see the model punished are less likely to copy the behaviour. The study was a short lab observation, so it does not show what happens over long periods or in everyday life.
parts.working: 1 mark for individual differences in imitation; 1 mark for the effect of situational factors (such as seeing the model punished); 1 mark for the limits of a short laboratory observation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between learning and performance of a behaviour in social learning theory. Explain why Bandura et al.'s study measured performance rather than learning.
parts.answer: Learning is acquiring a new behaviour, which may not be shown at once; performance is actually carrying out the behaviour. Bandura et al. could only observe what children did in the test room, so they measured performance (imitation) and inferred that learning had occurred, for example from the children's imitation of behaviour they had not been rewarded for.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for defining learning as acquisition; 1 mark for defining performance as carrying out the behaviour; 1 mark for the observable measure being performance; 1 mark for explaining why learning is inferred from it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the learning approach's explanation of aggression, with reference to Bandura et al.'s study and one other study from the learning approach. Give at least one strength and one weakness.
parts.answer: Strengths: Bandura et al. showed that children imitate aggression they observe, and the controlled procedure allowed cause and effect to be inferred; social learning theory also explains why children imitate same-sex models. Weaknesses: the explanation ignores biological factors such as testosterone or brain development, so it is reductionist; the lab study used a Bobo doll, which is a special case that may not represent aggression between people, so it has low ecological validity. Balanced judgement needed.
parts.working: Level-based. 9–10 marks: a developed evaluation with at least one strength and one weakness, referring to Bandura et al. and a second learning study, with a balanced judgement. 5–8 marks: less developed or only one side. 1–4 marks: description of the study or unlinked points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of phobia the boy had, and explain why it is classed as a specific phobia rather than a social phobia.
parts.answer: He had a specific phobia of buttons: a strong, persistent fear of one particular object. A social phobia is a fear of being judged or embarrassed in social situations, which was not the main problem here.
parts.working: 1 mark for specific phobia (fear of a particular object); 1 mark for contrast with social phobia (fear of social situations or evaluation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the difference between in vivo exposure and imaginal exposure, and give one example of each for a person with a fear of spiders.
parts.answer: In vivo exposure means facing the real feared object or situation, for example sitting in the same room as a real spider. Imaginal exposure means imagining the feared situation in detail, for example imagining a spider crawling on the arm while sitting quietly.
parts.working: 1 mark for in vivo as real exposure; 1 mark for imaginal as imagined exposure; 1 mark for a suitable example of each.

stem: Hypothetical: a boy with a button phobia rates his distress on a 0 to 10 feelings thermometer. His rating falls from 8 at the start of treatment to 3 at the end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the boy's distress rating from the start to the end of treatment, to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 find the fall (5 points) and divide by the starting rating (8); A1 62.5%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of relying on a single 0–10 distress rating to judge whether treatment has worked.
parts.answer: A single rating is a self-report that can be affected by mood on that day, and it does not show whether the improvement will last or whether the boy's avoidance of buttons has changed.
parts.working: 1 mark for a limitation of self-report or momentary mood; 1 mark for explaining that it does not measure behaviour or long-term change.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how negative reinforcement could maintain the boy's avoidance of buttons after the phobia had developed.
parts.answer: Each time the boy avoids buttons, the anxiety he feels is reduced, so the avoidance is reinforced because it removes an unpleasant feeling. This makes the avoidance more likely to happen again, so the phobia is maintained even though the original fear was learned by classical conditioning.
parts.working: 1 mark for avoidance removes or reduces an unpleasant state (anxiety); 1 mark for the avoidance being reinforced and therefore likely to recur; 1 mark for explaining that this maintains the phobia.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school psychologist in Lahore wants to treat a seven-year-old boy who is terrified of sewing needles. Using Saavedra and Silverman's study, outline a two-step treatment plan.
parts.answer: Step 1: build a fear hierarchy of needle-related situations, from least to most distressing (for example a picture of a needle, then a sealed packet, then a needle in a sewing kit). Step 2: work up the hierarchy in vivo, rewarding each completed step with praise or an agreed reward, and use imagery if the child's main reaction is disgust rather than fear.
parts.working: 1 mark for a sensible hierarchy with a description; 1 mark for graded in vivo exposure; 1 mark for positive reinforcement of each step; 1 mark for targeting disgust imagery if appropriate, or linking to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss two ethical issues in using a single child as the participant of a case study of phobia treatment.
parts.answer: Informed consent: a child cannot fully understand the treatment and consent may need to come from parents, who may pressure the child; the child cannot easily withdraw. Protection from harm: exposing a child to the feared object could cause distress, so the study must be stopped if distress is too great. Confidentiality: the child's identity and history must be protected in any published report.
parts.working: Level-based. 5–6 marks: two issues each described and explained in relation to a child case study, with discussion of how they could be managed. 3–4 marks: one issue developed or both described. 1–2 marks: names only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one advantage of a case study, compared with a group design, for studying a rare phobia.
parts.answer: A case study gives a detailed, in-depth account of one individual's history, treatment and progress, which a group design cannot. This is valuable for a rare condition, where few people are available for a larger group.
parts.working: 1 mark for the in-depth detail of the individual; 1 mark for suitability for rare conditions or small populations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a food reward, rather than punishment, is a more suitable way to train an elephant, referring to the learning approach.
parts.answer: Food is a pleasant consequence, so it is positive reinforcement and makes the trained behaviour more likely to be repeated. Punishment may cause fear or stress, which can reduce welfare and may suppress the behaviour without teaching the correct one.
parts.working: 1 mark for food as a pleasant consequence that increases the behaviour (positive reinforcement); 1 mark for punishment causing fear or stress or only suppressing behaviour.

stem: Hypothetical: a trainer recorded the number of food rewards given for successful steps of a trunk wash over five training sessions with one elephant. The totals were 14, 18, 22, 26 and 30 rewards. The data are hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of rewards per session.
parts.answer: (14 + 18 + 22 + 26 + 30) ÷ 5 = 22 rewards per session.
parts.working: M1 add the five totals (110); A1 divide by 5 to give 22.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rewards from session 1 to session 5. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 find the difference (16) and divide by the session 1 total (14); A1 114.3%.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the timing of reinforcement is important in operant conditioning. Use Fagen et al.'s study as an example.
parts.answer: Reinforcement must follow the desired behaviour immediately, so the elephant connects the food with the action. In Fagen et al., a bridging stimulus marked the exact moment the behaviour was correct, so the food could be delivered in the right moment even when it was not yet possible to give food immediately.
parts.working: 1 mark for reinforcement must follow the behaviour closely; 1 mark for explaining that the animal links the reward with the behaviour; 1 mark for the bridging stimulus in the study marking the correct moment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why five elephants trained in the same way could still learn at different rates. Use the learning approach in your answer.
parts.answer: Each elephant has a different learning history, age and temperament, so the same reinforcement may be more or less rewarding for each one; the food may be a stronger reward for one animal than another. Previous experience of reinforcement or punishment will also shape how quickly a new behaviour is learned.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark each for two individual differences (history of reinforcement, age, motivation or temperament, value of the reward); 1 mark for the link to the reinforcement process; 1 mark for the effect on the speed of learning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one way the findings of Fagen et al.'s study could be used to improve the welfare of working elephants.
parts.answer: Trainers could use positive reinforcement with food rewards instead of punishment or fear, which reduces distress for the animal and the risk to handlers. Training with a bridging stimulus and small steps can make learning quicker and less stressful.
parts.working: 1 mark for the application; 1 mark for explaining how reinforcement replaces punitive methods; 1 mark for the welfare benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the learning approach's explanation of behaviour, using Fagen et al.'s study as one example, in terms of reductionism and determinism.
parts.answer: Reductionism: Fagen et al. explain elephant behaviour only in terms of reinforcement, ignoring the animal's cognitive processes, emotions and social relationships with its handlers, which may also affect learning; this simplifies complex behaviour. Determinism: the approach suggests behaviour is controlled by past reinforcement, so elephants have no free will; but the study showed individual differences in learning, which suggests the environment does not control behaviour completely. Balanced judgement needed.
parts.working: Level-based. 9–10 marks: both reductionism and determinism evaluated with reference to Fagen et al., a balanced judgement, and practical or theoretical consequences. 5–8 marks: one issue developed or both briefly. 1–4 marks: description or unlinked points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the learning approach assumes about the origin of behaviour.
parts.answer: Behaviour is learned from experience and interaction with the environment (nurture), rather than being innate or determined by biology.
parts.working: 1 mark for behaviour being learned from the environment or experience; 1 mark for contrast with innate or biological explanations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the difference between classical conditioning and operant conditioning.
parts.answer: Classical conditioning is learning by association: a neutral stimulus becomes paired with an unconditioned stimulus and comes to trigger a conditioned response, as in a reflex. Operant conditioning is learning from consequences: a behaviour becomes more or less likely depending on whether it is reinforced or punished.
parts.working: 1 mark for classical conditioning as association of stimuli (reflexive response); 1 mark for operant conditioning as learning from consequences (reinforcement or punishment); 1 mark for a clear contrast.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline two principles of social learning theory.
parts.answer: Attention: the observer must notice the model's behaviour. Retention: the observer must remember the behaviour. Reproduction: the observer must be physically able to copy it. Motivation: the observer must want to copy it, often because of vicarious reinforcement, which is seeing the model rewarded. (Any two, fully outlined.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each of two principles named and outlined (e.g. attention: the observer must notice the model; retention: the observer must remember it; reproduction: the observer must be able to copy it; motivation: the observer must want to copy it, often because the model was rewarded).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the assumption that behaviour is learned from the environment could explain a child who develops a fear of dogs after being bitten.
parts.answer: A neutral stimulus (a dog) is paired with an unconditioned stimulus (the bite) that naturally causes fear; after this pairing, the dog alone becomes a conditioned stimulus that triggers fear, so the child learns the fear from the experience.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying the pairing of dog and bite; 1 mark for the conditioned fear response; 1 mark for linking to the learned (environmental) origin of the fear.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the learning approach studies observable behaviour rather than inner thoughts, and why this is seen as a scientific strength.
parts.answer: Observable behaviour can be measured and repeated, so experiments can be replicated and findings checked objectively; inner thoughts cannot be observed directly, so they would make the research less scientific.
parts.working: 1 mark for observable behaviour can be measured objectively; 1 mark for replication or reliability; 1 mark for contrast with inner thoughts being hard to measure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the learning approach, explain why two siblings raised in the same home may behave differently.
parts.answer: Each sibling experiences different reinforcement and punishment, because parents respond differently to each child, and each sibling has different models to observe outside the home, such as friends or relatives. Their different reinforcement histories lead to different behaviours being learned.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for different reinforcement or punishment histories; 1 mark for different models or observation; 1 mark for the link to conditioning or social learning; 1 mark for explaining why the differences persist.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the learning approach means by 'reinforcement', and give one example.
parts.answer: Reinforcement is any consequence that increases the likelihood that a behaviour will be repeated, such as praise or a reward (positive reinforcement) or removal of something unpleasant (negative reinforcement).
parts.working: 1 mark for definition (consequence increasing the likelihood of a behaviour); 1 mark for a correct example of positive or negative reinforcement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the learning approach can fully explain human behaviour. Refer to one study in your answer.
parts.answer: The approach explains how behaviour is shaped by reinforcement and modelling, as in Bandura et al.'s study, where children copied aggression they saw; but it does not explain biological influences or thinking, and it underplays the role of innate predispositions. A fuller explanation may need to combine learning with cognitive and biological approaches.
parts.working: Level-based. 5–6 marks: a balanced discussion with a named study, a judgement, and at least one strength and one limitation. 3–4 marks: one side developed. 1–2 marks: descriptive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of learning shown when a child is praised for sharing toys and then shares more often.
parts.answer: Operant conditioning (positive reinforcement).
parts.working: B1: operant conditioning, positive reinforcement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how extinction could be used to reduce a learned behaviour, and give an example.
parts.answer: Extinction is when a learned behaviour is no longer reinforced, so it gradually decreases in frequency. For example, if a child no longer gets attention for tantrums, the tantrums are likely to reduce over time.
parts.working: 1 mark for the definition (no reinforcement); 1 mark for the behaviour decreasing; 1 mark for a suitable example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why the assumption that all behaviour is learned might be criticised.
parts.answer: The assumption ignores innate biological factors, such as inherited temperament or brain development, which affect how easily something can be learned. Some behaviours, such as the rapid learning of language, appear to be prepared by biology, which the approach cannot fully explain.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying the criticism (ignores biology); 1 mark for an example of innate influence; 1 mark for explaining why this limits the approach; 1 mark for evidence or a link to a named study or biological approach.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the reinforcement schedule in which a reward is given after an unpredictable number of responses, and explain why it usually produces a high response rate.
parts.answer: Variable ratio schedule. Because the reward cannot be predicted, the animal or person keeps responding, hoping the next response will be rewarded, so responding is high and resistant to extinction.
parts.working: 1 mark for variable ratio; 1 mark for explaining that unpredictability keeps responding high.

stem: A school has 480 pupils: 180 in Year 10, 150 in Year 11, 90 in Year 12 and 60 in Year 13. A researcher wants a stratified sample of 48 pupils, with each year group represented in proportion to its size.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of pupils to be sampled from each year group.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method (each group's share of 480 multiplied by 48); 1 mark for 18 and 15; 1 mark for 9 and 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a stratified sample is more suitable than a simple random sample in this study.
parts.answer: A stratified sample guarantees that every year group is represented in proportion to its size, so the sample reflects the school's structure. A simple random sample could by chance include too few pupils from one year group, which would bias the results.
parts.working: 1 mark for ensuring each year group is represented in proportion; 1 mark for explaining that a random sample could by chance under-represent a group; 1 mark for linking this to reducing bias or improving representativeness.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'sampling frame', and give one example of a sampling frame for a study of nurses in Pakistan.
parts.answer: A sampling frame is the list of people in the target population from which the sample is actually drawn. Example: a staff list or register of nurses held by a hospital or a nursing council.
parts.working: 1 mark for the definition (list from which the sample is drawn); 1 mark for a suitable example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'generalisation', and identify one reason why generalising from a sample of 20 students is limited.
parts.answer: Generalisation means applying the findings from the sample to the whole target population. A sample of 20 students is small and may not represent people of other ages or backgrounds, so the findings may not apply to them.
parts.working: 1 mark for the definition (applying findings to the target population); 1 mark for a limit (small and unrepresentative sample, e.g. only students).

stem: A survey of 400 students at a Peshawar university found that 208 of the respondents were women. The university has 5,000 students, of whom 2,900 are women. The data are hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of women in (i) the sample and (ii) the university population.
parts.working: 1 mark for 52.0%; 1 mark for 58.0%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this sample may not be representative of the university's students, and suggest one way to improve it.
parts.answer: Women make up a smaller share of the sample (52.0%) than of the population (58.0%), so women are under-represented and the sample is biased in favour of men. Improvement: use a stratified sample by gender, drawing the number of women and men in proportion to the population.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying the under-representation of women; 1 mark for explaining the bias; 1 mark for a suitable improvement (stratified sampling by gender, or weighting).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher says her findings on 'teenagers' apply to all teenagers in Pakistan, although she studied 30 Grade 9 pupils from one private school in Karachi. Explain two reasons why her claim is not justified.
parts.answer: The sample covers only one age group and one type of school, so it does not represent all teenagers, such as those in rural areas or in state schools. It also covers only one city, so cultural and regional differences are not included. Thirty pupils is also a small number.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons (one age group; one school type or social background; one city or region; small size); 1 mark for explaining each reason in terms of the target population.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a researcher should define the target population more narrowly than "people" in a study.
parts.answer: A narrow definition, such as "adults aged 18 to 30 who use social media every day", makes it clear who the findings apply to and allows a sample to be drawn from that group. A vague definition makes it impossible to judge whether the sample represents the population.
parts.working: 1 mark for a precise definition is needed to identify the group; 1 mark for it allowing a sample to be drawn from the group; 1 mark for it allowing the representativeness of the sample to be judged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a sampling frame that is incomplete can bias a sample, even if the sample is then drawn at random.
parts.answer: If the sampling frame leaves out some members of the target population, those people have no chance of being selected, so the sample cannot represent them. For example, a list of registered mobile phone owners leaves out people without phones, who may be poorer or older, so the random sample is biased even though it was drawn at random.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for explaining that excluded members have no chance of selection; 1 mark for linking this to a sample being biased; 1 mark for a clear example; 1 mark for explaining why the random draw does not correct the problem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'bias' in a sample, and give two examples of how a sample can be biased.
parts.answer: Bias means that some members of the target population are more or less likely to be included than others, so the sample does not reflect the population. Examples: a sample drawn only from people who visit a particular clinic; a sample where most volunteers are highly motivated people.
parts.working: 1 mark for the definition (unequal chance of selection); 1 mark for each of two examples (e.g. one location, volunteers only, a gender imbalance).

stem: A radio phone-in show asked listeners whether they supported a new law. The show received 812 calls, and 530 callers said they supported the law. The data are hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of callers who supported the law. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 divide 530 by 812 and multiply by 100; A1 65.3%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this result cannot be taken as the views of Lahore residents.
parts.answer: Callers are self-selected, so people with strong opinions, or those who listen to the programme, are more likely to call; the sample is not random and does not represent all residents. The poll also covered only callers to one programme, and many residents may not have heard of the law or been able to call.
parts.working: 1 mark for self-selection or volunteer bias; 1 mark for the sample not representing all residents (only programme listeners); 1 mark for the effect on the conclusion (cannot generalise to all Lahore residents).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why researchers do not usually study the whole target population.
parts.answer: It is usually too time-consuming, expensive or impractical to study everyone in the target population, so a sample is drawn that is intended to represent it.
parts.working: 1 mark for time, cost or practicality; 1 mark for the idea that a sample stands in for the population.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of university students as samples in psychology research on the general population, in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses.
parts.answer: Strengths: students are easy and cheap to recruit, and the sample is usually homogeneous, so the variables under study are less affected by individual differences; they are often willing to take part and can be tested in a controlled setting. Weaknesses: students are mostly young and well-educated, so findings may not apply to older adults or people in other cultures; their results may reflect the social environment of university rather than the general population.
parts.working: Level-based. 5–6 marks: two strengths and two weaknesses, each explained and linked to generalisation, with a judgement. 3–4 marks: one side developed or points less explained. 1–2 marks: description or unlinked points.

stem: A study of sleep used a sample of 240 adults from a town of 12,000 adults. Of the 240 sample members, 12 were aged 65 or over. The town has 1,800 adults aged 65 or over. The data are hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of people aged 65 or over in (i) the sample and (ii) the town.
parts.working: 1 mark for 5.0%; 1 mark for 15.0%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this sample may not represent older adults in the town, and how this affects the findings on sleep.
parts.answer: Older adults make up only 5.0% of the sample, against 15.0% of the town, so their views and sleep patterns are under-represented. The findings on sleep may therefore not apply to older residents.
parts.working: 1 mark for under-representation of older adults with figures; 1 mark for the effect on the generalisability of the findings.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A health survey was conducted using a sampling frame of telephone numbers in a district. Explain two ways in which this sampling frame could bias the findings on health.
parts.answer: People without a telephone, often poorer or rural households, have no chance of being selected, so their health needs are not represented. People who own phones may also differ in age or income. These gaps mean the findings may overstate the health of the district as a whole.
parts.working: 2 marks for each of two ways (excludes households without phones; over-represents some groups; rural or poorer groups under-represented; age or income imbalance), with 1 mark for explaining the effect on the findings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one reason why a researcher should aim for a representative sample.
parts.answer: A representative sample reflects the important characteristics of the population, so the results can be generalised to that population rather than applying only to the people studied.
parts.working: 1 mark for a representative sample reflecting the population; 1 mark for allowing generalisation of the findings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a larger sample usually gives more reliable results.
parts.answer: Individual differences and unusual participants have less effect on the overall results when there are more people, so the findings are more likely to show the true effect.
parts.working: 1 mark for individual differences or unusual participants having less effect; 1 mark for the results being more reliable or closer to the true effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a very large sample is not always better.
parts.answer: A very large sample takes more time, money and effort to recruit and test, and more people are exposed to any risks; a large study with poor procedures or a biased sample is still unreliable.
parts.working: 1 mark for time, cost or practical burden (or extra exposure to risk); 1 mark for the point that a large sample cannot fix poor design or bias.

stem: A psychologist needs 60 participants who have a particular condition. In the population, 1 in 4 adults has the condition. The figures are hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of adults who must be screened to find 60 people with the condition, if 1 in 4 adults has it.
parts.working: M1 divide 60 by 1/4 (or multiply by 4); A1 240 adults.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one practical problem of screening 240 adults to find a sample for a study.
parts.answer: Screening 240 adults takes a lot of time and money, which may exceed the research budget, and the staff needed for the screening may not be available.
parts.working: 1 mark for a practical problem (time, cost, staff); 1 mark for linking it to the study's budget or timescale.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hypothetical reaction times (ms) for a group of six participants: 412, 398, 405, 421, 410 and 620.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean of all six reaction times. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 add the six scores (2666) and divide by 6; A1 444.3 ms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean with the 620 ms score removed. Explain what this shows about small samples.
parts.answer: (412 + 398 + 405 + 421 + 410) ÷ 5 = 2046 ÷ 5 = 409.2 ms. A single unusual score in a small sample has a large effect on the mean (it moves it by about 35 ms), so small samples are more affected by outliers.
parts.working: M1 remove 620 and divide the remaining total (2046) by 5; A1 409.2 ms; 1 mark for explaining the effect of an outlier on a small sample mean.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher has a budget for 40 questionnaires. She could survey 40 pupils from one school, or 20 pupils from each of two schools in different parts of a city. Explain which option is preferable for studying pupils' attitudes across the city, referring to sample size and representativeness.
parts.answer: Two schools are preferable: 20 pupils from each of two schools gives a sample from more than one area and school type, so it is more representative of the city. The total sample size is the same, so one school does not give more reliable results. However, two schools with only 20 each may still be too few to represent a whole city, so the findings should be treated cautiously.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for choosing the two-school option; 1 mark for the same total sample size; 1 mark for representativeness across areas; 1 mark for a caution about the small number per school.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'sampling error', and why it is larger in a smaller sample.
parts.answer: Sampling error is the difference between the sample result and the true population value that arises because only some people were studied. In a small sample, a few unusual people have a bigger effect on the result, so the difference from the population is more likely to be large.
parts.working: 1 mark for the definition (difference between sample and population due to chance); 1 mark for only some people being studied; 1 mark for smaller samples being more affected by unusual individuals.

stem: Hypothetical study: 20% of people in a population are left-handed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a population, 20% of people are left-handed. Sample A has 15 people, of whom 5 are left-handed. Sample B has 150 people, of whom 27 are left-handed. Calculate the percentage left-handed in each sample to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for 33.3%; 1 mark for 18.0%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the result from Sample A is less accurate than the result from Sample B.
parts.answer: In a small sample, one or two individuals change the percentage a lot (here, one person changes it by 6.7 percentage points), so Sample A is more affected by chance; Sample B is larger, so its percentage is closer to the true 20%.
parts.working: 1 mark for the small-sample effect (a single person has a large effect); 1 mark for Sample B being closer to the population value of 20%.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways a researcher could decide on an appropriate sample size before starting a study.
parts.answer: Use the sample sizes of similar published studies as a guide; consider the minimum number needed to show the effect of interest (for example, how many participants are needed in each group for a reliable comparison); take account of the budget, time and access to participants.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two sensible methods (previous studies, minimum needed for the analysis, budget or time constraints); 1 mark for explaining how each method helps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the trade-off between sample size and the time, cost and ethics of a study, using one example.
parts.answer: A larger sample gives more reliable and generalisable results, but needs more time and money to recruit and test, and more participants are exposed to any risks, which raises ethical issues. A smaller sample is cheaper and quicker and imposes less burden, but its results are less reliable and less generalisable. For example, a study of a rare condition may have to accept a small sample, and should explain the limits this places on the conclusions.
parts.working: Level-based. 5–6 marks: both sides of the trade-off discussed with an example, reaching a justified judgement. 3–4 marks: one side developed or example missing. 1–2 marks: descriptive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a researcher might choose a small sample for a pilot study.
parts.answer: A pilot study tests whether the procedures, materials and timings work, which needs only a few participants and saves time and money before the main study.
parts.working: 1 mark for a pilot testing procedures, materials or timing; 1 mark for why a small sample is enough (cheap, quick, not for the final conclusions).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a sample of 150 can still be unrepresentative. Give one example of how the sample size would not solve the problem.
parts.answer: A large sample drawn in a biased way, for example only from one school or only volunteers, can still be unrepresentative because more people from the same biased group are included, so the bias remains.
parts.working: 1 mark for the sample being drawn from a biased group; 1 mark for explaining that size does not remove bias; 1 mark for a clear example (volunteers only, one location).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a researcher who has only 8 participants might choose to report the median rather than the mean for a set of scores that includes one very high score.
parts.answer: The mean is pulled towards the very high score, so it is not typical of most participants when the sample is small. The median is the middle score when the scores are ordered, so it is not affected by one extreme value and gives a better description of the typical participant.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for the mean being affected by the extreme score; 1 mark for the median being the middle value; 1 mark for the median being unaffected by outliers; 1 mark for the median being a better typical value in a small sample.

stem: A school has 1,200 pupils, and 40 of them have a disability. A researcher wants to survey a 10% random sample of all pupils. The figures are hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sample size for a 10% sample of the school, and state how many pupils with a disability in the sample could be expected if the school has 40 such pupils.
parts.answer: 10% of 1,200 pupils = 120 pupils in the sample. If 40 of the 1,200 pupils (1 in 30) have a disability, the sample would contain 40 ÷ 1,200 × 120 = 4 such pupils. Four pupils is too few for any reliable conclusion about this group.
parts.working: 1 mark for 120; 1 mark for 4 pupils with a disability; 1 mark for stating that this is too few to draw reliable conclusions about the subgroup.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline why a researcher studying a varied population, such as all pupils in a district, may need a larger sample than one studying a uniform group.
parts.answer: A varied population contains many different types of people, so a small sample may miss some types and the results may vary more between samples; a larger sample is more likely to include all the important sub-groups.
parts.working: 1 mark for more variety needing more participants to capture it; 1 mark for a larger sample being more likely to include all sub-groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how increasing each group from 10 to 40 participants would change the reliability of a comparison between the means of two groups.
parts.answer: With 40 per group, the mean of each group is less affected by individual differences or unusual scores, so the difference between the means is more likely to reflect a real difference. The standard error of each mean falls as sample size rises, so the comparison is more reliable.
parts.working: 1 mark for individual differences having less effect on each mean; 1 mark for the difference being more likely to reflect a real effect; 1 mark for a reference to the estimate becoming more precise or reliable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether a sample of 2,000 people who volunteered online is always better than a random sample of 200 people from the same population. Refer to sample size and sampling method in your answer.
parts.answer: Not always. A larger sample reduces sampling error, but if the 2,000 are volunteers, they may differ systematically from the population, so the bias does not shrink with size. The random sample of 200 has no such bias, and its results may be more trustworthy for the population, although its sampling error is larger.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for the larger sample reducing random error; 1 mark for volunteer bias not reducing with size; 1 mark for the random sample being free of systematic bias; 1 mark for the trade-off with larger sampling error.

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main characteristics of trichotillomania.
parts.answer: Recurrent pulling out of one's own hair, leading to noticeable hair loss. The person feels increasing tension before pulling and relief or gratification afterwards. The behaviour is not due to another condition, such as a skin problem.
parts.working: 1 mark each for recurrent hair pulling; the tension before and relief after; hair loss or distress and not better explained by another condition (up to 3 marks).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline two features that a clinician would look for when diagnosing intermittent explosive disorder.
parts.answer: Recurrent outbursts of verbal aggression or physical aggression towards people or property that are out of proportion to the provocation; the outbursts are not better explained by another mental disorder, and they cause distress or problems at work or home.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct feature (recurrent outbursts; disproportionate to the trigger; not better explained by another condition; causes distress or impairment).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the cognitive explanation of gambling disorder, including the role of the gambler's fallacy.
parts.answer: Gamblers hold irrational beliefs, such as the belief that a win is due after a run of losses. This is the gambler's fallacy: the assumption that past random outcomes affect future ones. Gamblers also overestimate their skill or control, and remember wins more than losses, which encourages them to keep playing and chase losses.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for irrational beliefs or cognitive distortions; 1 mark for defining the gambler's fallacy; 1 mark for overestimating control or selective memory; 1 mark for linking these to continued gambling.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction
stem: The data in this question are hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical trial of imaginal desensitisation, 18 of 30 gamblers reduced their gambling frequency after 12 weeks. Calculate the percentage who improved.
parts.working: M1 divide 18 by 30 and multiply by 100; A1 60.0%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this result alone would not show that imaginal desensitisation caused the improvement.
parts.answer: There was no control group, so the improvement could be due to other factors, such as natural change over time, support from family or a wish to stop. The sample of 30 is also small, so chance could affect the result.
parts.working: 1 mark for lack of a control group or other causes of improvement; 1 mark for the small sample (chance) or another limitation of the design.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss two ethical issues in using aversion-based treatments, such as covert sensitisation, to reduce urges in people with impulse control disorders.
parts.answer: Protection from harm: the treatment pairs an urge with an unpleasant stimulus, which may cause distress and, if used repeatedly, may harm the person's wellbeing. Informed consent: participants may not fully understand the treatment or may feel pressured to accept it, especially if they are seeking help. Right to withdraw: the person may find it hard to stop. Credit is given for any two issues described and discussed with reference to the treatment.
parts.working: Level-based. 5–6 marks: two issues each described and discussed with reference to aversion-based treatment, with some balance (e.g. benefit weighed against harm). 3–4 marks: one issue developed or two briefly described. 1–2 marks: names only.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a clinician might use a diagnostic interview as well as a symptom checklist when assessing a person for kleptomania.
parts.answer: A checklist can be completed quickly but may miss details, so an interview allows the clinician to explore the context of the urges, their intensity and their effect on daily life, which a checklist cannot show.
parts.working: 1 mark for the limit of a checklist (misses detail or context); 1 mark for what the interview adds (context, severity, impact).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the role of dopamine in the biological explanation of gambling disorder.
parts.answer: Dopamine is involved in the brain's reward pathway. Winning, or the anticipation of winning, triggers dopamine release, which reinforces the gambling behaviour. Repeated gambling may change the reward system so that the person needs more gambling to feel the same reward. Unpredictable wins may produce particularly strong dopamine responses.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for dopamine in the reward pathway; 1 mark for winning or anticipation triggering dopamine; 1 mark for reinforcement of the gambling; 1 mark for tolerance or changes in the reward system.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 26-year-old man spends each evening on sports-betting apps, has borrowed money from relatives without telling them, and has missed work to gamble. Using the DSM-5 criteria for gambling disorder as a guide, explain two features that support a diagnosis.
parts.answer: He has borrowed money to gamble (relying on others for money); he has lied about his gambling to his relatives (lying); he has gambled to chase losses; and his gambling has put his job at risk (jeopardising a job). The DSM-5 criteria require four or more of nine features in the last 12 months, and these show a pattern of repeated loss of control.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks for each of two DSM-5 features linked to the case (e.g. chasing losses, lying, risking or losing a job, relying on others for money); 1 mark for the pattern or the four-criteria threshold.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the difference between a delusion and a hallucination.
parts.answer: A delusion is a fixed false belief that persists despite clear evidence against it. A hallucination is a perception experienced without an external stimulus, such as hearing voices.
parts.working: 1 mark for a delusion as a fixed false belief; 1 mark for a hallucination as a perception without external stimulus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of core symptoms that must be present, and the total period of disturbance required, for a DSM-5 diagnosis of schizophrenia.
parts.answer: At least two of the five core symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour, negative symptoms) must be present for a significant portion of one month; the signs of disturbance must last for at least six months in total.
parts.working: 1 mark for at least two of five core symptoms; 1 mark for a total duration of at least six months.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the diathesis-stress model as an explanation of schizophrenia.
parts.answer: The diathesis is an inherited vulnerability, such as genetic risk, which makes a person more likely to develop schizophrenia. Stress from the environment, such as life events, family conflict or drug use, can trigger the disorder in people with the vulnerability. Neither factor alone is usually enough; the disorder results from the interaction of both.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for diathesis as inherited vulnerability; 1 mark for stress as an environmental trigger; 1 mark for the interaction of the two; 1 mark for an example of a stressor or a genetic factor.

stem: In a hypothetical study, 80 patients with schizophrenia were given an atypical antipsychotic for 12 weeks. At the end, 56 patients showed a reduction of at least 50% in their positive symptoms. The data are hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of patients who showed at least a 50% reduction in positive symptoms.
parts.working: M1 divide 56 by 80 and multiply by 100; A1 70.0%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this result cannot show that the antipsychotic caused the reduction in symptoms.
parts.answer: There was no comparison group given a placebo, so improvement may be due to the passing of time, regression to the mean, or expectations of treatment; without a control group, the drug effect cannot be separated from these other causes.
parts.working: 1 mark for the lack of a control or placebo group; 1 mark for another cause of improvement (time, expectation, regression to the mean).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the cognitive explanation of schizophrenia, in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses.
parts.answer: Strengths: Frith's metarepresentation explanation links the symptoms to a specific cognitive deficit, which explains why patients may misattribute their own thoughts or actions to others, and this explains specific symptoms such as delusions of control. The explanation is supported by studies of theory of mind tasks showing difficulties in patients. Weaknesses: the explanation is descriptive rather than causal, as it cannot show whether the deficit causes schizophrenia or is a result of it; it ignores biological evidence such as dopamine, and it may not explain negative symptoms well.
parts.working: Level-based. 9–10 marks: two strengths and two weaknesses, each explained with reference to the cognitive explanation and supporting evidence, with a judgement. 5–8 marks: some explanation but less developed or unbalanced. 1–4 marks: description.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for psychosis, including the aim of the therapy.
parts.answer: CBT for psychosis aims to help patients test their delusional beliefs and reduce their distress rather than remove the belief entirely. The therapist uses questioning to examine the evidence for and against a belief, and considers alternative explanations for experiences such as hearing voices. The aim is to reduce the distress and disruption caused by symptoms, and improve coping.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for a description of testing beliefs or examining evidence; 1 mark for alternative explanations; 1 mark for the aim (reduce distress, improve coping, reduce symptom impact); 1 mark for CBT being used alongside medication where relevant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one ethical problem with using a placebo control group in a trial of antipsychotic medication for people with schizophrenia.
parts.answer: Participants who receive a placebo may not get effective treatment, so their symptoms may worsen or they may relapse, which breaks the principle of protection from harm. This is a serious problem because patients with schizophrenia may be vulnerable and may not be able to give fully informed consent.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying the ethical issue (no effective treatment; risk of relapse or worsening); 1 mark for the harm (protection from harm); 1 mark for the vulnerability or consent issue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the influence of family expressed emotion on relapse in schizophrenia.
parts.answer: Expressed emotion describes family members who are critical, hostile or over-involved with the patient. Research has found that a high level of expressed emotion is associated with a higher rate of relapse. This suggests family stress may act as a trigger for the disorder in vulnerable people. However, the link may be correlational, as relatives may react to the patient's symptoms rather than cause them. Family-based interventions that reduce expressed emotion have been used to lower relapse.
parts.working: Level-based. 5–6 marks: expressed emotion defined and linked to relapse, with a discussion of cause and correlation, and evidence or intervention; judgement made. 3–4 marks: partially developed. 1–2 marks: descriptive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the characteristics of panic disorder, according to DSM-5.
parts.answer: Recurrent, unexpected panic attacks, which are sudden periods of intense fear with physical symptoms such as a racing heart, sweating or shortness of breath. After an attack, the person has at least one month of persistent concern about further attacks or about the consequences of them, or a significant change in behaviour to avoid attacks.
parts.working: 1 mark for recurrent unexpected panic attacks; 1 mark for physical symptoms of an attack; 1 mark for persistent concern or behaviour change for at least one month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two features that distinguish generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) from a specific phobia.
parts.answer: In GAD the worry is about many everyday events and situations, not one object or situation; the anxiety is persistent over months rather than triggered by a specific stimulus.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two correct features (worry about many events vs one object; persistent worry vs fear triggered by a stimulus).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the amygdala contributes to the biological explanation of fear-related disorders.
parts.answer: The amygdala processes emotional information, especially threat, and is involved in learning fear responses through conditioning. In people with anxiety disorders the amygdala may be overactive, which increases fear responses to neutral stimuli. This may make it harder for the prefrontal cortex to reduce fear once it has been learned.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for the amygdala processing threat or emotion; 1 mark for its role in learning fear; 1 mark for overactivity in anxiety; 1 mark for the relationship with the prefrontal cortex or control of fear.

stem: In a hypothetical trial, the mean score on a 0–21 anxiety scale was 14.2 at the start of treatment and 8.6 at the end. The data are hypothetical and the trial had no control group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the mean anxiety score from the start to the end of treatment. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 find the fall (5.6) and divide by the starting mean (14.2) and multiply by 100; A1 39.4%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a within-group design in this trial makes the conclusion weaker than a comparison with a control group.
parts.answer: Without a control group, the fall in scores could be due to time passing, regression to the mean, or expectations, rather than the treatment. A control group would show how much improvement happens without treatment.
parts.working: 1 mark for other causes of change (time, regression to the mean, expectation); 1 mark for a control group allowing the treatment effect to be separated from these.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the use of flooding as a treatment for specific phobias, including one ethical issue.
parts.answer: Flooding involves exposing the person to the feared stimulus at its highest level, without a graded hierarchy, until the anxiety falls. It is based on classical conditioning: the feared stimulus no longer predicts harm, so the conditioned response extinguishes. It can be effective and quick, but it is distressing and may increase fear if the patient cannot cope. Ethical issue: the person must give informed consent and can withdraw at any time, and the therapist must avoid causing harm.
parts.working: Level-based. 5–6 marks: the mechanism (extinction through classical conditioning), an evaluation of effectiveness, and one developed ethical issue. 3–4 marks: partly developed. 1–2 marks: descriptive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a fear hierarchy would be constructed and used in systematic desensitisation for a fear of driving.
parts.answer: The client and therapist list driving-related situations from least to most anxiety-provoking, for example sitting in a parked car, then starting the engine, then driving on a quiet road. The client works up the hierarchy, using relaxation at each step until the anxiety reduces before moving on to the next item.
parts.working: 1 mark for building an ordered list from least to most distressing with the client; 1 mark for an example of items; 1 mark for working up the hierarchy with relaxation at each step.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one biological treatment for generalised anxiety disorder.
parts.answer: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) increase the availability of serotonin in the synapse, which can reduce anxiety over several weeks.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming a treatment (SSRI, or benzodiazepine, or SNRI); 1 mark for a correct outline of how it works or is used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a researcher evaluating a treatment for spider phobia would measure avoidance behaviour, not just the person's self-reported fear.
parts.answer: Self-reported fear can be affected by the participant's wish to show improvement or by how they interpret their feelings. A behavioural test, such as how close a person is willing to get to a spider, measures what the person actually does, so it is a more objective indicator of change.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for the limitation of self-report (bias, demand characteristics, interpretation); 1 mark for behavioural avoidance as objective; 1 mark for a description of a behavioural test; 1 mark for explaining why the behaviour shows the treatment's effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline two features that distinguish obsessive-compulsive disorder from ordinary worry.
parts.answer: The obsessions and compulsions are persistent, intrusive and cause distress; the compulsions are time-consuming (for example more than an hour a day) or cause significant impairment; the person recognises the thoughts may be excessive, and ordinary worry does not usually take up so much time.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct feature (intrusive and persistent thoughts or rituals; time-consuming, more than an hour a day, or impairing; distress or impairment; excessive for the situation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two body-focused repetitive behaviours included in the DSM-5 category of obsessive-compulsive and related disorders.
parts.answer: Trichotillomania (hair pulling) and excoriation (skin-picking) disorder.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correctly named behaviour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the serotonin hypothesis of obsessive-compulsive disorder.
parts.answer: The serotonin hypothesis proposes that OCD is associated with low activity of the neurotransmitter serotonin in certain brain circuits. Evidence includes that SSRIs, which increase serotonin availability, reduce symptoms in many people with OCD. However, the hypothesis is not fully confirmed, because SSRIs take weeks to work and not everyone responds to them.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for low serotonin activity; 1 mark for brain circuits or the role of serotonin; 1 mark for SSRI evidence; 1 mark for a limitation (delay, not everyone responds).

stem: A client with OCD has a Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) total score of 26 before a course of treatment and 14 after it. The total score ranges from 0 to 40. The client's scores are hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the Y-BOCS total score from before to after treatment. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 find the fall (12 points) and divide by the starting score (26) and multiply by 100; A1 46.2%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the Y-BOCS severity band for the score before treatment and after treatment, using the bands 0–7 subclinical, 8–15 mild, 16–23 moderate, 24–31 severe, 32–40 extreme.
parts.answer: Before treatment (26): severe. After treatment (14): mild.
parts.working: 1 mark for severe; 1 mark for mild.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the use of drug treatments for obsessive-compulsive disorder in terms of effectiveness and side effects.
parts.answer: SSRIs are the first-line drug treatment and reduce symptoms in many people with OCD, supporting the serotonin explanation. However, the effect is often modest, and the drugs take several weeks to work. Side effects such as nausea, sexual dysfunction and sleep problems may lead some people to stop taking them. Drugs may also be combined with ERP, which can improve outcomes more than drugs alone.
parts.working: Level-based. 5–6 marks: effectiveness and side effects both discussed, with a judgement and reference to evidence or combined treatment. 3–4 marks: one aspect developed. 1–2 marks: descriptive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a therapist might explain exposure and response prevention (ERP) to a client who fears contamination and washes their hands for an hour a day.
parts.answer: The therapist explains that exposure means touching the feared object (for example a door handle) and that response prevention means not washing afterwards. This allows the anxiety to fall naturally, showing the client that nothing terrible happens, which weakens the link between the fear and the compulsion.
parts.working: 1 mark for explaining exposure (touching the feared object); 1 mark for response prevention (not performing the washing); 1 mark for the reason the anxiety falls and the link between fear and compulsion weakens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one cognitive explanation of obsessive-compulsive disorder, using an example.
parts.answer: Inflated responsibility: the person believes they are responsible for preventing harm, so an intrusive thought (such as leaving the gas on) is treated as a real danger. The person then performs compulsions, such as checking, to reduce their sense of responsibility. Example: a person checks the stove 30 times before leaving home.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming the cognitive explanation (inflated responsibility or thought-action fusion, or similar); 1 mark for explaining how it leads to obsessions or compulsions; 1 mark for an example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher tests whether ERP reduces hoarding in 40 adults. Explain why a waitlist control group, in which participants receive the treatment after the study, would improve the study.
parts.answer: A waitlist group shows how much change occurs over time or from the natural course of the condition without treatment, so the effect of ERP can be separated from these factors. Because the group later receives treatment, it is also ethically more acceptable than no treatment, and participants are less likely to drop out.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for a control group showing change without treatment; 1 mark for separating the treatment effect from time or natural change; 1 mark for the ethical benefit (all receive treatment); 1 mark for reduced dropout or motivation.

stem: The data in this question are hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical study of telephone-delivered CBT for OCD, 30 patients started treatment and 6 dropped out. Of the 24 who completed treatment, 18 showed a clinically meaningful improvement. Calculate the percentage of completers who improved.
parts.working: M1 divide 18 by 24 (the completers, not the 30 starters) and multiply by 100; A1 75.0%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the high dropout rate could bias the findings of the study.
parts.answer: The people who dropped out may have been those who were less improved, or who found the treatment hard, so the completers' results overstate how well the treatment works for everyone who starts it.
parts.working: 1 mark for the dropouts being different from completers; 1 mark for the result overstating effectiveness for those who began treatment.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the behavioural explanation of obsessive-compulsive disorder, in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses.
parts.answer: Strengths: the behavioural explanation (negative reinforcement of compulsions, which reduce anxiety) explains why compulsions persist and why exposure and response prevention is effective, and the approach has good evidence from treatment outcomes. Weaknesses: it cannot explain why some people develop obsessions without a traumatic learning history, and it ignores the biological evidence, such as serotonin and brain-circuit differences; it may also be reductionist as it focuses on observable behaviour.
parts.working: Level-based. 9–10 marks: two strengths and two weaknesses, each explained with reference to the behavioural explanation and evidence, with a balanced judgement. 5–8 marks: less developed. 1–4 marks: descriptive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the DSM-5 criteria for a major depressive episode.
parts.answer: Five or more symptoms present during the same two-week period, at least one of which is either depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure. Other symptoms include changes in appetite or sleep, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, poor concentration, and thoughts of death. The symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment.
parts.working: 1 mark for five or more symptoms over two weeks; 1 mark for the core symptom (depressed mood or loss of interest); 1 mark for distress or impairment (or a named symptom in addition).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two symptoms of a manic episode in bipolar I disorder.
parts.answer: Inflated self-esteem or grandiosity; decreased need for sleep; more talkative than usual; racing thoughts; distractibility; increased goal-directed activity; risky behaviour such as excessive spending.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct symptom (any two from the list).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the learned helplessness explanation of depression.
parts.answer: Repeated experiences of uncontrollable negative events lead a person to believe that they have no control over what happens. This learned helplessness leads to passivity and withdrawal, and the person expects that future efforts will not succeed. Attributions are also important: a person who blames themselves, globally and permanently, is more likely to become depressed.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for uncontrollable events; 1 mark for the belief of no control; 1 mark for passivity or withdrawal; 1 mark for attributions (internal, stable, global).

stem: A patient's Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II) scores on three assessments were 31, 24 and 15. Each item is scored 0 to 3 and the total ranges from 0 to 63. The scores are hypothetical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the BDI-II score from the first to the third assessment. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 find the fall (16 points) and divide by the first score (31) and multiply by 100; A1 51.6%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the severity band for each of the three scores, using the bands 0–13 minimal, 14–19 mild, 20–28 moderate and 29–63 severe.
parts.answer: Score 31: severe. Score 24: moderate. Score 15: mild.
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct label for the first score (severe) and one other score (moderate for 24 or mild for 15); 1 mark for all three correct.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the biological explanation of depression, including the monoamine hypothesis, in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses.
parts.answer: Strengths: the monoamine hypothesis is supported by evidence that drugs increasing serotonin or noradrenaline availability (such as SSRIs) reduce depression, and this gives a plausible biological mechanism. Twin and family studies show genetic influence, supporting a biological basis. Weaknesses: the monoamine hypothesis is correlational for many findings, because low levels of these neurotransmitters may be a consequence of depression rather than its cause; drugs take weeks to work and some people do not respond, which suggests other factors are involved.
parts.working: Level-based. 9–10 marks: two strengths and two weaknesses, each explained with evidence, and a balanced judgement. 5–8 marks: less developed. 1–4 marks: description.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one way a researcher could measure depression in a hypothetical study of older adults, using a self-report measure and a clinician-rated measure.
parts.answer: Self-report: participants complete a questionnaire, such as the BDI-II, rating how often they felt symptoms over the past two weeks. Clinician-rated: a trained clinician interviews the person and scores symptoms, which can detect symptoms the person does not report. Combining the two gives a more complete picture.
parts.working: 1 mark for a self-report measure described; 1 mark for a clinician-rated measure described; 1 mark for a reason to combine them (accuracy, detecting symptoms the person underreports).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the role of negative automatic thoughts in depression.
parts.answer: Negative automatic thoughts are immediate, habitual negative beliefs about oneself, the world or the future, which arise without much reflection. They maintain low mood because they bias how a person interprets events.
parts.working: 1 mark for describing negative automatic thoughts as habitual or immediate negative beliefs; 1 mark for explaining how they maintain or worsen depression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a double-blind design is difficult to use in a trial comparing CBT with antidepressant medication.
parts.answer: Participants can usually tell whether they are receiving a talking therapy or a tablet, so they cannot be blind to the treatment, and therapists who deliver CBT know which therapy they are giving. A placebo also cannot easily be matched to a therapy session, so the participant and the researcher may have expectations that affect the result.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for participants knowing which treatment they have; 1 mark for therapists knowing the treatment; 1 mark for the difficulty of a matched placebo for therapy; 1 mark for the effect of expectations on outcomes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe lithium as a treatment for bipolar disorder, including one limitation.
parts.answer: Lithium is a mood-stabilising drug that reduces the frequency and severity of manic and depressive episodes, particularly for bipolar disorder. It must be carefully monitored using blood tests because the therapeutic range is narrow and high levels are toxic. A limitation is that side effects such as tremor, weight gain and kidney problems may make it difficult for some people to continue the treatment.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for mood stabilising / reduces episodes; 1 mark for monitoring of blood levels (narrow range); 1 mark for a side effect; 1 mark for a clear limitation (side effects or adherence).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength of using a structured clinical interview to diagnose depression.
parts.answer: A structured interview asks the same questions in the same order for every patient, so diagnoses are more consistent between clinicians, which improves reliability. This makes it easier to compare patients and research results.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying the strength (standardised, consistent questions); 1 mark for explaining its effect on reliability; 1 mark for the benefit for comparison or research.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the ethical issues in conducting antidepressant trials with adolescents.
parts.answer: Adolescents are a vulnerable group who may not fully understand the risks of medication, so informed consent must involve both the young person and a parent or guardian. Antidepressants have been linked to increased suicidal thoughts in some young people, so monitoring and protection from harm are essential. A placebo group may leave some adolescents without effective treatment, so researchers must justify the control group. Some adolescents may also feel pressured to take part by parents or clinicians.
parts.working: Level-based. 5–6 marks: at least two ethical issues discussed in relation to adolescents, with safeguards and a balanced view. 3–4 marks: one issue developed or two described. 1–2 marks: names only.
